children.translated_text: * By the lion of logic, the illustrious
is composed for the growth of the seed of <s>smṛti</s> (right knowledge). // NAV_0:0 //
Having bowed to <s>Vardhamāna</s> (Mahāvīra), who teaches <s>sāmānya</s> (universals) and <s>viśeṣa</s> (particulars) as inseparable,
And this is the opening statement of this [work]:
This [work] is undertaken for the purpose of elucidating the <s>pramāṇas</s> (valid means of knowledge).

children.text: ty-ādi anena ca tādātmya-tad-utpatti-lakṣaṇa-saṃbandha-vikalatayā dhvaner bahir-arthaṃ prati prāmāṇyâyogād abhidheyâdi-sūcana-dvarôtpannârtha-saṃśaya-mukhenaśrotāraḥ śravaṇaṃ prati protsāhyanta iti
children.translated_text: and so forth. By this, <s>Dharmottara</s> holds that, since <s>dhvani</s> (verbal sound) lacks <s>prāmāṇya</s> (epistemic validity) with respect to external objects due to the absence of the relation characterized by identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) and origination (<s>tadutpatti</s>), the listeners are encouraged toward listening by means of doubt about the meaning arising through the indication of the referent and so forth.

children.text: manyate. tad ayuktam. yadi hi śabdasyârtha-prakāśanaṃ prati sāmarthyaṃ na samasti, tat katham asāv abhidheyâdi-sūcane 'pi paṭiṣṭhaḥ syāt? na ca tasyâprāmāṇya etac-chravaṇād artha-saṃśayaṃ kurvanti prekṣāvantaḥ, tad-vattā-hāner mithyā-jñānād api pravṛtty-avirāma-prasaṅgāc ca.
children.translated_text: holds [thus]. That is incorrect. For if language has no capacity to illuminate meaning, then how could it be competent even in indicating the referent and so forth? Nor do discerning persons, upon hearing that [language] lacks epistemic validity, develop doubt about its meaning, because [such doubt] would entail the loss of the quality of being discerning, and because there would follow the absurd consequence of unceasing activity even from false knowledge.

children.text: tv āha: "na śrāvakôtsāhakam etat, prāmāṇyâbhāvāt, teṣāṃ câpramāṇād apravṛtter, anyathā prekṣāvattā-kṣateḥ, kiṃ tarhi prakaraṇârtha-kathanâvasarôpasthita-parôpanyasta-hetv-asiddhatôdbhāvanârtham. tathā hi: sambhavaty evaṃ-vādī -- nârabdhavyam idam abhidheyâdi-śūnyatvāt, kāka-danta-parīkṣâdivad iti; tad anenâsya tadvattā-prakāśakena vacasā tad-dhetūnām asiddhatôdbhāvyata" iti. tad ayuktataram: yato yadîdam apramāṇam iti nâbhidheyâdīni sākṣāl lakṣayat pravartayati, tataḥ parôpanyasta-hetv-asiddhatāṃ kathayatîti yukti-riktaṃ paśyāmaḥ, apramāṇasyâkiñcit-karatvād, anyathā pramāṇa-vicāraṇam ānarthakyam aśnuvīta. tasmād idaṃ pramāṇa-bhūtaṃ sad-abhidheyâdīni pratipādayat prekṣāvataḥ pravartayatîti prakaraṇâdāv upanyastam.
children.translated_text: however, says: "This [opening statement] is not meant to encourage listeners, because it lacks epistemic validity, and because those [listeners] would not engage based on what is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>, otherwise their quality of being discerning would be damaged. Rather, it is for the purpose of exposing the unestablished nature of the reasons adduced by the opponent, which have been presented on the occasion of stating the subject matter of the treatise. For thus it is possible that one might argue: 'This [work] should not be undertaken, because it is devoid of referent and so forth, like the examination of a crow's teeth.' Therefore, by this statement that reveals [the work's] possession of such [content], the unestablished nature of those reasons is exposed." That is even more incorrect: because if this [opening statement] is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> and does not directly indicate the referent and so forth and [thereby] motivate [action], then we see that the claim that it states the unestablished nature of the opponent's reasons is devoid of logical force, since what is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> accomplishes nothing — otherwise the investigation of <s>pramāṇas</s> would become purposeless. Therefore, this [opening statement], being a <s>pramāṇa</s>, teaches the referent and so forth and motivates discerning persons — thus it is presented at the beginning of the treatise.

children.text: sambandha-śūnyatvād asya katham arthe pramāṇatêti cet, pratyakṣe 'pi kathaṃ tarhi sêti vācyam. grāhya-grāhaka-bhāva-sambandha-balād iti ced, atrâpi vācya-vācaka-bhāvād iti brūmaḥ. sa eva katham iti ced, adhyakṣe 'pi vedya-vedaka-bhāvaḥ katham iti vācyam. tad-utpatti-tad-ākāratābhyām iti cet, kêyaṃ tad-utpattir nāma? taj-janyatêti cet, pratikṣaṇa-bhaṅguratve sâiva durupapādêty ācakṣmahe. tathā hi: kṣaṇa-naśvaro 'rthaḥ sva-kṣaṇe pūrvaṃ paścād vā kāryaṃ kuryād iti trayī gatiḥ. tatra na tāvad ādyaḥ pakṣaḥ kakṣī-karaṇīyaḥ, sama-kāla-bhāvini vyāpārâbhāvāt, itarathâika-kṣaṇa-vartināṃ samastârtha-kṣaṇānām itarêtaraṃ kārya-kāraṇa-bhāvaḥ prasajyeta, tathā ca tat-prayukto grāhya-grāhaka-bhāvaś cêty asamañjasam āpanīpadyeta. atha sva-kṣaṇāt pūrvam -- acārv etad api, svayam asato bhaviṣyac-chaṅkha-cakravarty-āder iva pūrva-kāla-vartini kārye vyāpārâbhāvāt. atha sva-kṣaṇād ūrdhvaṃ kāryaṃ vidhatta iti manyethāḥ, etad apy asādhīyo, vinaṣṭasya kārya-karaṇâkṣamatvād, anyathā mṛtasya śikhinaḥ kekāyitaṃ syāt. tad-ākāratâpi kim arthâkāra-saṅkrāntyā? atha tat-sadṛśatayôtpatter jñānasyêti? yady ādyaḥ kalpas tad ayuktaṃ, jñāne svâkārârpaṇād arthasya nirākāratânuṣaṅgāt, sva-deha-pṛthutarârthâdarśana-prasaṅgāt, śiraḥ-sphoṭana-plāvanâdy-anartha-prasakteś ca. uta dvitīyas: tathā sati sādṛśya-vaśād artha-vyavasthêty āyātam. na ca sādṛśyaṃ bhavatāṃ darśane tāttvikam asti, vivikta-kṣaṇa-kṣayi-paramâṇu-lakṣaṇa-svalakṣaṇānāṃ pāramārthikatvâbhyupagamāt. anādi-kālâlīna-vāsanā-prabodha-sampādita-sattāka-nirvikalpaka-vivikta-darśanôttara-kāla-bhāvi-vikalpa-vyavasthāpita-sādṛśya-vaśād artha-grahaṇa-niyame saty eka-nīla-svalakṣaṇe kṣaṇe sakala-kāla-kalāpa-vyāpi-kāka-kuvalayâdi-gata-nīlatāyā vyavasthitir aviśeṣeṇânuṣajeta, tathā ca pratiniyato grāhya-grāhaka-bhāvo na ghaṭām-aṭāṭyeta. aṅguly-agra-nirdiśyamāna-puro-varti-nīla-svalakṣaṇa-darśana-balâyātatvān nailya-vikalpasya tad evâdhyavasyati, na bhūtaṃ bhāvi kāka-kuvalayâdi-gataṃ vêti cet, tarhi vikalpaḥ svalakṣaṇa-niṣṭhaḥ prāpto, niyata-deśa-daśâvacchinnârtha-kriyā-samarthârtha-grahaṇāt. tathā hi: tad-adhyavasāyaḥ kiṃ tad-vikalpanaṃ uta tad-grahaṇaṃ? na tāvat tad-vikalpanam, vikalpānāṃ bhavad-abhiprāyeṇa svalakṣaṇântaḥ-praveśâbhāvāt. tad uktam:
children.translated_text: If it is objected that, since [language] is devoid of [the required] relation, how can it have epistemic validity with respect to objects — then the same must be said of perception as well: how does it have [such validity]? If it is said [that it is] by the force of the relation of apprehender and apprehended (<s>grāhya-grāhaka-bhāva</s>) — then we say that here too [it is] by the relation of signifier and signified (<s>vācya-vācaka-bhāva</s>). If asked how that [relation] itself [obtains] — then the same must be asked: how does the relation of knower and known obtain in perception? If [it is said to be] through origination from the object and bearing the form of the object (<s>tad-utpatti-tad-ākāratā</s>) — then what is this so-called 'origination from the object'? If [it means] being produced by it — then we declare that under [the doctrine of] momentariness, that itself is difficult to establish. For the object, being momentarily perishing, would produce its effect in its own moment, either before or after — these are the [only] three possibilities. Of these, the first alternative should not be adopted, because there is no causal activity between things existing at the same time; otherwise, all momentary objects existing in one moment would be mutually related as cause and effect, and consequently the apprehender-apprehended relation based on that would arrive at an absurd conclusion. Now, [if it acts] before its own moment — this too is unacceptable, because a non-existent [thing], like a future conch-shell emperor, has no causal activity with respect to an effect existing at a prior time. If you think that it produces its effect after its own moment — this too is untenable, because what has perished is incapable of producing an effect; otherwise, a dead peacock would cry out. As for bearing the object's form (<s>tad-ākāratā</s>) — is it through the transference of the object's form? Or is it because cognition arises in similarity to it? If the first alternative, then that is wrong, because the object's conferral of its own form upon cognition would entail the object becoming formless, would entail the impossibility of seeing objects larger than one's own body, and would entail absurd consequences such as head-splitting and drowning. Or if the second: in that case, it amounts to [saying that] the determination of objects is by virtue of similarity. But similarity has no ultimate reality in your system, because you accept that <s>svalakṣaṇas</s> (particulars) — characterized as momentarily perishing discrete atoms — alone are ultimately real. If the apprehension of objects is determined by virtue of similarity established through <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction) arising subsequent to the non-conceptual perception of discrete [particulars], a perception whose existence is brought about by the awakening of <s>vāsanā</s> (latent impressions) ingrained since beginningless time — then, with respect to a single <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> (particular) moment of blue, the determination of blueness belonging to crows, blue lotuses, and so forth pervading all times and assemblages would attach without distinction, and consequently the determinate apprehender-apprehended relation would not hold. If it is objected that, because the <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction) of blueness arises from the force of the perception of a particular blue <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> present before [the perceiver] as indicated by the fingertip, it determines only that [particular] and not [something] past, future, or belonging to crows and blue lotuses — then <s>vikalpa</s> would turn out to be grounded in <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> (the particular), since it apprehends an object capable of causal efficacy delimited by a specific place and time. For that <s>adhyavasāya</s> (determination) of it — is it the conceptualization of it, or the apprehension of it? It is not the conceptualization of it, because according to your view <s>vikalpas</s> do not penetrate into <s>svalakṣaṇas</s>. Thus it has been said:
"Therefore words and cognitions are said to have <s>anyāpoha</s> (exclusion of the other) as their object,

children.text: śabdāś ca buddhayaś câiva vastuny eṣām asambhavāt" // NAV_0:1 //
children.translated_text: and to range over <s>sāmānya</s> (universals), because their application to real things is impossible." // NAV_0:1 //

children.text: atha brūyād: yady api vikalpāḥ sāmānyaṃ gocarayanti tattvatas, tathâpi pratyakṣa-vikalpayor yaugapadyena pravṛtter vimūḍhaḥ pratipattā vikalpasya svalakṣaṇa-niṣṭhatāṃ vyavasyati, tathā côktam:
children.translated_text: Now one might say: although <s>vikalpas</s> (conceptual constructions) in reality range over <s>sāmānya</s> (universals), nevertheless, because perception and conceptual construction operate simultaneously, the deluded cognizer determines that <s>vikalpa</s> is grounded in <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> (the particular). And thus it has been said:
"Because the two minds — the conceptual (<s>savikalpa</s>) and the non-conceptual (<s>avikalpa</s>) — operate simultaneously,

children.text: vimūḍho laghu-vṛtter vā tayor aikyaṃ vyavasyati" // NAV_0:2 //
children.translated_text: the deluded [cognizer], or because of the swiftness of [their] operation, determines the unity of the two." // NAV_0:2 //

children.text: tat kim idaṃ śapathaiḥ pratyeyaṃ, yad uta mohād vikalpena svalakṣaṇam adhyavasyati, na punar viśada-nirbhāsena sākṣāt-karoti? evaṃ câdhyakṣam api sakalârtha-vyaktīr gocarayati, vikalpa-mohāt tu sannihita-viṣayaṃ lakṣyata iti paro 'nuṣañjayan durnivāraḥ syāt. uta tad-grahaṇam adhyavasāyaḥ, tadā svalakṣaṇa-niṣṭhatā vikalpasya sva-vācā bhavadbhiḥ pratipannā syāt. evaṃ ca vikalpa-yugalake 'py artha-kriyā-samarthârtha-paryavasita-sattākatā vikalpasyâḍhaukate. yadā ca vikalpaḥ svalakṣaṇa-saudha-madhyam adhyāsta ity abhidadhyās, tathā sati dhvaner api tad-antaḥ-praveśo durnivāraḥ syāt, tat-saha-caratvāt. yad āha bhavad-ācāryaḥ: "sa eva śabdānāṃ viṣayo yo vikalpānām" iti. na ca vikalpaṃ vyatiricya sādṛśya-vyavasthāpakam anyad asti, pratyakṣasya sakala-jagad-vilakṣaṇa-svalakṣaṇa-grahaṇa-pravaṇatvāt. tad yadi tat-sadṛśatayôtpattis tad-ākāratā, tadā pratipādita-nyāyād vikalpasya sannihitârtha-gocaratôrarī-kartavyā, tathā ca dhvanir api tad-viṣayaḥ sidhyatîti siddhaṃ naḥ samīhitam. anyathā tad-ākāratā na samasti, gaty-antarâbhāvāt. tan na tad-utpatti-tad-ākārate grāhya-grāhaka-bhāva-hetū saṃstaḥ.
children.translated_text: Is this to be believed merely on oath — namely, that through delusion one determines <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> (the particular) by means of <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction), but does not directly apprehend it through vivid manifestation? In that case, an opponent who maintains that perception too ranges over all object-instances, but due to the delusion of <s>vikalpa</s> is [merely] regarded as having a proximate object, would be irrefutable. Or if <s>adhyavasāya</s> (determination) is the apprehension of it, then the groundedness of <s>vikalpa</s> in <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> would be acknowledged by you in your own words. And thus, even in the pair of <s>vikalpas</s>, the property of culminating in an object capable of causal efficacy accrues to <s>vikalpa</s>. And when you would assert that <s>vikalpa</s> has entered into the palace of <s>svalakṣaṇa</s>, in that case the entry of <s>dhvani</s> (verbal sound) into that [domain] too would be irrefutable, because it accompanies <s>vikalpa</s>. As your master has said: "The object of words is the very same as the object of <s>vikalpas</s>." And there is nothing other than <s>vikalpa</s> that establishes similarity, because perception is intent upon apprehending <s>svalakṣaṇas</s> that are unique in all the world. Therefore, if origination in similarity to the object is what constitutes bearing the object's form, then, by the reasoning already established, the ranging of <s>vikalpa</s> over proximate objects must be conceded, and consequently <s>dhvani</s> too is established as having that [same proximate object] as its domain — thus our thesis is proven. Otherwise, bearing the object's form does not obtain, because there is no alternative possibility. Therefore, origination from the object and bearing the object's form are not tenable as the basis of the apprehender-apprehended relation.

children.text: saṃstāṃ vā, tathâpi vikalpataḥ paryanuyojyo bhavān: kim ete grahaṇa-kāraṇaṃ pārthakyena uta sāmastyena? tad yady ādyaḥ pakṣaḥ, kapāla-kṣaṇo ghaṭântya-kṣaṇasya grāhakaḥ prāpnoti, taj-janyatvāt, jala-candro vā nabhaś-candrasya grāhakaḥ syāt, tad-ākāratvāt. atha dvitīyas, tathā sati ghaṭôttara-kṣaṇaḥ pūrva-kṣaṇasya grāhakaḥ prasajati, tad-utpattes tad-ākāratvāc ca. jaḍatvād arthasya na grāhakatvam, api tu jñānasya tad-utpatti-tad-ākāratayoḥ satyor iti ced, idam idānīṃ viditam asmābhir, etad api samānârtha-grāhi-prācīna-saṃvedana-kṣaṇa-lakṣaṇa-manaskārôtpādya-jñāne grāhaka-lakṣaṇaṃ vyabhicaraty, utpādaka-prāktana-kṣaṇa-varti-manaskārâgrāhakatvāt. tad-adhyavasāya-sāhityena tad-utpatti-tad-ākāratayor grahaṇa-kāraṇatvaṃ sampūrṇaṃ, manaskāre tan nâstîti cet, kim idaṃ bhinna-gocareṇa saha sāhityam? tathā hy: "adhyavasāyo vāsanā-prabodha-vaśād utpannaḥ sāmānyam anartha-rūpaṃ vikalpayati, pratyakṣaṃ bahir-arthāl labdhâtma-lābhaṃ tad-ākāraṃ tam eva sākṣāt-karotîti" bhavatāṃ darśanam. tan na vikalpa-sāhityaṃ pratyakṣasya kañcana viśeṣaṃ puṣṇāti. tad idam grāhya-grāhaka-bhāva-kāraṇaṃ pratyakṣe 'pi yad bhavadbhir abhyadhāyi, tad yathā yathā vicāryate tathā tathā viśīryata ity anapekṣaṇīyam. tad -- yathā kathañcit pratyakṣasya pratipādita-grāhya-grāhaka-bhāva-lakṣaṇa-vaikalye 'pi grāhakatvam arthasya grāhyatvaṃ, tathā dṛṣṭatvāt, anyathā nikhila-vyavahārôccheda-prasaṅgād bhavadbhir api pratyapādi, tathā śabdasya vācakatvam arthasya vācyatvaṃ pratipadyadhvaṃ yūyam; atrâpi dṛṣṭa-hāner vyavahārôcchedasya samānatvāt. athêttham ācakṣīthāḥ: yathā "nadyās tīre guḍa-śakaṭaṃ paryastaṃ, dhāvata dhāvataḍimbhakā" ity-ādi-vipratāraka-puruṣa-vacana-śravaṇāt pravartamānā vipralambha-bhājo jāyante, 'taḥ sakala-vacaneṣv anāśvāsa iti -- evaṃ tarhi cikicikāyamāna-maru-marīcikā-cakra-cumbi yaj jalôllekhi viśada-darśanam udaya-padavīṃ samāsādayati tad alīkam avalokitam iti; sakalâdhyakṣeṣv anāśvāsa ity abhidadhmahe. pāścātya-viparītârthôpasthāpaka-pramāṇa-bādhitatvād maru-marīcikāsu jala-jñānam apramāṇaṃ, na śeṣa-satya-stambhâdi-jñānāni, bādhā-rahitatvād iti cet, tarhi dhvanāv apy ayaṃ nyāyaḥ kiṃ kākair bhakṣitaḥ? na hi vayaṃ sarva-śabdānāṃ prāmāṇyaṃ pratipadyemahi; kiṃ tarhi suniścitâpta-praṇetṛkāṇām eva. tan na prāmāṇyaṃ prati pratyakṣa-śabdayor viśeṣam upalabhāmahe. eṣa tu viśeṣaḥ syāt, pratyakṣaṃ cakṣur-ādi-sāmagrī-viśeṣa-janyatvāt sannihita-niyatârtha-grāhi spaṣṭa-pratibhāsaṃ, śābdaṃ tu tathā-vidha-kāraṇa-vikalatvān niyatâniyatârtha-grāhy aspaṣṭa-pratibhāsam. na câiṣa viśeṣaḥ prāmāṇya-kṣati-kārī, itarathânumānasyâpy aprāmāṇyam āsajyeta, tasyâpy aviśadâniyatârtha-grāhitvāt. paramârthatas tu tri-kāla-vyāpinaḥ sarvârtha-grahaṇa-svabhāvatve 'py āvaraṇa-tiras-kṛtasya jīva-dravyasya cakṣur-ādi-sāmagrī-sāpekṣâvaraṇa-kṣayôpaśama-vaśāt sannihita-spaṣṭârtha-grahaṇa-pariṇāmaḥ pratyakṣam ity ucyate. śabda-sāpekṣa-kṣayôpaśamān niyatâniyatâviśadârtha-grahaṇa-pariṇāmas tu śābdam iti. tan na tad-utpatti-tad-ākārate pratyakṣe śābde 'nyasmin vā jñāne vāstavyau staḥ. tasmāt pāramārthikâbhidheya-prayojana-sambandha-pratipādakam etad ādi-vākyam iti sthitam.
children.translated_text: Even granting this, you are still open to objection through conceptual analysis: Do these [conditions] constitute the cause of cognition severally or collectively? If the first alternative, then the potsherd-moment would be the cognizer of the final moment of the pot, because it is produced from it; or the moon reflected in water would be the cognizer of the moon in the sky, because it bears its form. If the second alternative, then the moment succeeding the pot would become the cognizer of the preceding moment, because it arises from it and bears its form. If you say that the object, being insentient, cannot be a cognizer, but only cognition can, when both conditions — being produced from it and bearing its form — are present, then we now understand this: but even this definition of a cognizer fails in the case of cognition produced by <s>manaskāra</s> (mental attention) — which is characterized as a prior moment of awareness apprehending the same object — since the <s>manaskāra</s> present in the preceding moment that produces it is not itself a cognizer. If you say that the completeness of the two conditions — being produced from it and bearing its form — as causes of cognition is fulfilled by their conjunction with <s>adhyavasāya</s> (determination), and that this is absent in <s>manaskāra</s>, then what is this conjunction with something having a different domain? For your view is as follows: '<s>Adhyavasāya</s> (determination), arising from the awakening of latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), conceptualizes a universal that has no real existence; perception, having obtained its own existence from the external object, directly apprehends that very object bearing its form.' Therefore, the conjunction with conceptual thought adds no special qualification to perception. Thus, this causal relation of apprehended and apprehender that you posited even for perception — the more it is analyzed, the more it crumbles, and so it should be disregarded. Now — even though the definition of the apprehended-apprehender relation established for perception is defective, the fact that cognition is a cognizer and the object is cognized should be accepted, because this is observed, and because otherwise the annulment of all practical activity would follow — this you yourselves have conceded. In the same way, accept that words have the capacity to signify and objects have the capacity to be signified; for here too, the same situation holds — there would be loss of what is observed and annulment of practical activity. If you were to say: 'Just as when people, hearing the deceitful words of a man saying "A cart of molasses has overturned on the riverbank, run, run, boys!" and acting upon them, become victims of deception — therefore there is no trust in all words whatsoever' — then in that case, the vivid perception that approaches the horizon, kissing the circle of shimmering desert mirages, and that appears like water, is a false perception; therefore there should be no trust in any perceptual cognition whatsoever, we would say. If you say that knowledge of water in desert mirages is not a valid means of knowledge because it is contradicted by a subsequent valid cognition that presents the contrary meaning, but that other cognitions of real pillars and the like are valid because they are free from contradiction — then why has this same principle been devoured by crows when it comes to verbal testimony? For we do not accept the validity of all words whatsoever; rather, only of those whose authors are well-established trustworthy persons (<s>āpta</s>). Therefore we find no difference between perception and verbal testimony with respect to their validity. But this difference may exist: perception, being produced from the specific assemblage of causes such as the eye and so forth, apprehends a determinate proximate object and has a clear appearance; verbal cognition, lacking such a cause, apprehends both determinate and indeterminate objects and has an unclear appearance. But this difference does not damage their validity; otherwise, inference too would be invalid, since it also apprehends objects that are unclear and indeterminate. In the ultimate sense, however, the soul-substance (<s>jīva-dravya</s>), though its nature is to apprehend all objects spanning all three times, is obscured by veils (<s>āvaraṇa</s>); and the transformation of apprehending proximate and clear objects, dependent on the destruction and subsidence of obscurations conditioned by the assemblage of causes such as the eye, is called perception. The transformation of apprehending determinate, indeterminate, and unclear objects, dependent on the destruction and subsidence conditioned by words, is verbal cognition. Therefore, the two properties of being produced from it and bearing its form need not inhere in perception, verbal cognition, or any other cognition. Thus it is established that this opening sentence conveys the subject matter, purpose, and connection in the ultimate sense.

children.text: tatrâbhidheyaṃ vācyaṃ, tac cêha pramāṇam, tasyâiva prakaraṇena pratipādyatvāt; tat pramāṇêty avayavena lakṣayati. prayojanaṃ dvedhā: śrotuḥ kartuś ca. punar api dvividham: anantaraṃ vyavahitaṃ ca. tatra śrotur anantara-prayojanaṃ pramāṇa-viṣayā vyutpattiḥ, kartur vyutpadyamānasya prājñatvāc chiṣyasya vyutpādanam. tatrâtma-prayojanaṃ darśayann ā[hâ]rabhyata iti asya mayêti-pada-savyapekṣatvāt. śiṣya-prayojanaṃ tu vyut-pad-ity anenôpasarga-dhātu-samudāyenâiva tad-antar-agataṃ lapsyata ity abhiprāyavān kartâtma-vyāpāraṃ ṇij-antena nirdiśati:
children.translated_text: Therein, the subject matter (<s>abhidheya</s>) is what is to be expressed (<s>vācya</s>), and here that is <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge), since it alone is what is to be established by this treatise. He defines it by the component word '<s>pramāṇa</s>.' The purpose (<s>prayojana</s>) is twofold: that of the listener and that of the author. Again it is of two kinds: immediate and remote. Therein, the immediate purpose for the listener is proficiency regarding the subject matter of <s>pramāṇa</s>; for the author, it is the instruction of the student, since the student being instructed becomes wise. Showing his own purpose therein, [the author says] 'is commenced' — because this word requires the supplementary expression 'by me.' The author, intending that the student's purpose will be obtained through the combination of prefix and verbal root in '<s>vyutpad</s>' (to instruct) itself, indicates his own activity with the causative form:
'for the purpose of instruction in <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge)'

children.text: iti. vyavahita-prayojanaṃ dvedhā: vyāvahārikaṃ pāramārthikaṃ ca. vyāvahārikaṃ heyôpādeyôpekṣaṇīyeṣv artheṣu hānôpādānôpekṣā-lakṣaṇam. pāramārthikaṃ abhyudaya-niḥśreyasâvāptir iti. etat tu sākṣād anuktam apy anantara-prayojana-phalatvāt tad-vacanenâivâkṣiptam avagantavyam. sambandhas tûpāyôpeya-lakṣaṇaḥ; tatrôpeyaṃ prakaraṇârtha-parijñānam, prakaraṇam upāyas, tatas tad-abhilaṣatā prakaraṇam idam ārambhaṇīyam ity anukto 'pi vacanena sambandho 'rthād gamyata iti tātparyârthaḥ.
children.translated_text: — thus. The remote purpose is twofold: conventional (<s>vyāvahārika</s>) and ultimate (<s>pāramārthika</s>). The conventional purpose is the activity of avoidance, adoption, and indifference with respect to objects that are to be avoided, adopted, or ignored. The ultimate purpose is the attainment of worldly prosperity (<s>abhyudaya</s>) and supreme good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>). Though this is not explicitly stated, it should be understood as implied by the statement of the immediate purpose, since it is the fruit of the immediate purpose. The connection (<s>sambandha</s>) has the character of means and end: therein, the end is the complete understanding of the treatise's subject matter, and the treatise is the means; therefore, one who desires that understanding should undertake this treatise — thus the connection, though unstated, is understood from the meaning of the words. This is the purport.

children.text: adhunâkṣarârtho vivriyate: tatra yady api pramāṇa-śabdasya sarva-kārakair bhāvena ca vyutpatteḥ sukaratvāt "kṛtya-lyuṭo bahulam" anyatrâpîti-vacanād yathā-kramam amī kartr-arthâdi-kāraka-bhāva-vyutpattyā pramāṇa-śabda-vācyāḥ, tad yathā ātmârtha-jñānârtha-kriyā-kāraṇa-kalāpa-kṣayôpaśama-kriyā-rūpāḥ tathâpîha jñānam evâdhikriyate, tasyâiva parīkṣā-kṣamatvād; itareṣāṃ parīkṣāyās tat-puraḥsaratvād vaiyarthāc ca. tathā hi: nârthas tāvad ātmanaḥ parīkṣayā, tasya bhrāntâbhrānta-jñāneṣu samānatvāt. nâpy arthasya, tasyôpeyatvād, upāya-bhūta-jñāna-parīkṣaṇenâiva gatatvāt. nârtha-kriyāyās, tad-avagatau parīkṣā-vaiyarthyāt. nâpi kāraṇa-kalāpasya, jñānôtpatteḥ prāk svarūpânavagateḥ, paścāt tat-svarūpa-nirṇayād eva tat-sādguṇya-vaiguṇyâvagater nairarthakyāt. nâpi kṣayôpaśamasya, tasya jñānôtpādônnīyamāna-rūpatvāt. nâpi pramiti-mātrasya, tasya pramāṇa-sādhyatayā tac-cārutā-dvāreṇâiva samīcīnatā-siddher iti. tad ayam abhiprāyo: yady apy ananta-dharmâdhyāsite vastuni sarva eva śabdârthā nirupacaritā ghaṭante, tathâpi yenârthaṃ paricchidyârtha-kriyā-samarthârtha-prārthanayā pravartante pramātāras tad evêha jñānam ātmanā saha dharmi-rūpatayā tādātmye 'pi dharma-rūpatayā vyatiriktaṃ pramīyate 'nenêti pramāṇam ity ucyate. tasya
children.translated_text: Now the literal meaning of the words is explained. Therein, although proficiency in the word '<s>pramāṇa</s>' is easily derived with all case-relations (<s>kāraka</s>) and with abstract noun formation, and because of the rule 'the suffixes <s>kṛtya</s> and <s>lyuṭ</s> are used variously elsewhere also,' the following are expressible by the word '<s>pramāṇa</s>' according to the respective agent-meaning and other case-relation derivations — namely, the self, the object of cognition, the activity, the assemblage of causes, and the activity of destruction and subsidence of [karmic obscurations] — nevertheless, here it is cognition alone that is the subject, because only cognition is amenable to critical examination; the examination of the others either presupposes cognition or is futile. For: first, the self does not need to be examined, since it is the same in both erroneous and non-erroneous cognitions. Nor does the object, since it is the end to be attained, and is already covered by the examination of cognition, which is the means. Nor does the activity of the object, since once it is understood, examination is pointless. Nor does the assemblage of causes, since before the arising of cognition its own nature is not known, and after cognition, the assessment of its excellence or deficiency follows from the determination of cognition's own nature, making [separate examination] purposeless. Nor does the destruction and subsidence [of karmic veils], since its nature is inferred from the arising of cognition. Nor does the mere result of valid cognition (<s>pramiti</s>), since its correctness is established through the excellence of the <s>pramāṇa</s>, it being what is to be established by the <s>pramāṇa</s>. The intent, then, is this: although in reality, which is pervaded by infinite properties, all word-meanings apply without figurative usage, nevertheless, that by which cognizers discern the object and, desiring an object capable of purposeful activity, engage in action — that cognition alone, here, though identical with the self in being the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>), is distinguished from it as a property (<s>dharma</s>), and is called '<s>pramāṇa</s>' in the sense of 'that by which one knows.' Its
means: the illumination of the true nature of one's own intended definition and so forth, by refuting the definitions and so forth fabricated by opponents. For that
: the word <s>artha</s> is a synonym of <s>prayojana</s> (purpose).

children.text: ity artha-rūpatayā sva-cetasi vivartamānaṃ prakaraṇa-śarīraṃ parāmṛśati; dvividhaṃ hi prakaraṇa-śarīraṃ: śabdo 'rthaś cêti, bahiḥ śabda-rūpatayā prakāśayiṣyamāṇatve 'py antas tattvârthâkāreṇa pratyakṣatvāt.
children.translated_text: refers to the body of the treatise as it takes shape in one's own mind in the form of meaning; for the body of a treatise is twofold: word and meaning — though it will be manifested externally in the form of words, internally it is perceived directly in the form of the true meaning.
means: it is composed by way of the arrangement of words, sentences, verses, and the like.

children.text: iha ca lakṣaṇa-saṃkhyā-gocara-phaleṣu pramāṇaṃ prati vipratipadyante pare. tathā hi: lakṣaṇe tāvat pramāṇam avisaṃvādi jñānam iti
children.translated_text: Now, regarding <s>pramāṇa</s>, others disagree on its definition, enumeration, object, and result. Thus, regarding the definition: '<s>Pramāṇa</s> is non-deceptive cognition' —
'<s>Pramāṇa</s> is that which apprehends an object not previously apprehended' —
'<s>Pramāṇa</s> is the cause of the apprehension of an object' —

children.text: âdayaḥ. tathā saṃkhyāyāṃ: pratyakṣânumāne dve eva pramāṇe iti
children.translated_text: and others. Regarding enumeration: 'Perception and inference alone are the two <s>pramāṇas</s>' —
'Perception, inference, verbal testimony, analogy, presumption, and non-apprehension are the <s>pramāṇas</s>' —
'Perception, inference, verbal testimony, and analogy are the <s>pramāṇas</s>' —
'Perception, inference, and verbal testimony are the <s>pramāṇas</s>' —

children.text: . tathā gocare: paraspara-vinirluṭhita-kṣaṇa-kṣayi-paramânu-lakṣaṇāni svalakṣaṇāni pramāṇa-gocaras tāttvika iti
children.translated_text: Regarding the object: 'The true object of <s>pramāṇa</s> consists of <s>svalakṣaṇas</s> (unique particulars), characterized as momentary atoms that are mutually exclusive and perishing at each instant' —
'The universal has the nature of the three <s>guṇas</s>' —
'The four elements are the ground of <s>pramāṇa</s>' —

children.text: . tathā phale 'pi vipratipadyante: arthâdhigatiḥ pramāṇa-phalam iti
children.translated_text: Regarding the result too, they disagree: 'The apprehension of the object is the result of <s>pramāṇa</s>' —

children.text: . pūrvaṃ pūrvaṃ pramāṇam uttaram uttaraṃ tu phalam iti
children.translated_text: 'The earlier [cognition] is the <s>pramāṇa</s>, the later is the result' —
Therein, wishing first to resolve the disagreements regarding definition and enumeration, [the author] says:
<s>Pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) is cognition that illuminates both itself and other things, and is free from contradiction;

children.text: pratyakṣaṃ ca parokṣaṃ ca dvidhā, meya-viniścayāt || 1 ||
children.translated_text: it is twofold — <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and <s>parokṣa</s> (indirect knowledge) — based on the determination of the object to be known. (NA_1)

children.text: tatrâpi pūrvârdhena lakṣaṇa-vipratipattim uttarârdhena tu saṃkhyā-vipratipattiṃ nirācaṣṭe. lakṣaṇaṃ ca para-rūpebhyo vyāvartana-kṣamo 'sādhāraṇa-dharmaḥ. lakṣyate paricchidyate vijātīyebhyo vyāvṛttaṃ lakṣyaṃ yena tal lakṣaṇam ity ucyate. tac cêha dvaye pratyāyyāḥ, sva-darśanânuraktântaḥ-karaṇās tīrthântarīyā vipratipannās, tathā mugdha-buddhayo laukikā avyutpannāś cêti. tataś ca yadâdau vipratipannān prati lakṣaṇaṃ tadâivaṃ lakṣya-lakṣaṇa-bhāvo draṣṭavyo: yad idaṃ bhavatām asmākaṃ ca
children.translated_text: Therein, by the first half [of the verse], he resolves the disagreement regarding definition; by the second half, the disagreement regarding enumeration. A definition (<s>lakṣaṇa</s>) is a distinctive property capable of distinguishing [the definiendum] from other things. It is called '<s>lakṣaṇa</s>' because by it the <s>lakṣya</s> (definiendum), distinguished from what is of a different kind, is delimited and identified. And here, two [types of audience] are to be instructed: those of other schools who are attached to their own views and are in disagreement, and ordinary people of dull intellect who are unlearned. Therefore, when the definition is first directed toward those in disagreement, the relation of definiendum and definition should be understood as follows: that which is well-known to you and to us as
should be understood as 'cognition that illuminates both itself and other things, and is free from contradiction';

children.text: mantavyam; prasiddhaṃ pramāṇam anūdyâprasiddhaṃ sva-parâbhāsitvâdi vidhīyate. yadā tv avyutpanna-matīn pratîdaṃ lakṣaṇam, tadā pratiprāṇi sva-para-prakāśino jñānasya bādha-rahitasya kasyacit siddhatvād, anyathā pratiniyata-vyavahārôccheda-prasaṅgād, evaṃ te bodhyante: yad ado bhavatāṃ kvacin niyatârtha-grāhi sva-para-prakāśakaṃ bādha-rahitaṃ jñānaṃ prasiddhaṃ tat pramāṇam iti budhyantām. atrâpi siddhasyânuvādo 'siddhasya vidhānaṃ yojyam.
children.translated_text: the well-known [term] '<s>pramāṇa</s>' is repeated (restated), and the not-yet-known property of illuminating itself and others, and so forth, is predicated. When, however, this definition is directed toward the unlearned, then, since for each living being some cognition that illuminates itself and others and is free from contradiction is established — for otherwise, the annulment of all determinate practical activity would follow — they are instructed thus: that cognition of yours which apprehends a determinate object in some domain, which illuminates both itself and the other, and which is free from contradiction — let them understand that to be <s>pramāṇa</s>. Here too, the restatement of what is established and the predication of what is not yet established should be applied.
Now the literal meaning of the words: therein,
means the self, one's own nature;

children.text: 'rthas, tāv ābhāsayituṃ prakāśayituṃ śīlam yasya tat-tathā. jñāyate nirṇīyate tattvaṃ yena taj
children.translated_text: [That which has as] its nature the illumination, i.e., the making manifest, of objects — thus [is it described]. That by which reality is known, i.e., ascertained, is
That by which [something] is contradicted is

children.text: ; viparītârthôpasthāpaka-pramāṇa-pravṛttir iti yāvat. tena viśeṣeṇa varjitaṃ rahitaṃ yaj jñānaṃ tat pramāṇam iti saṇṭaṅkaḥ.
children.translated_text: that is to say, the operation of a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) that presents the opposite meaning. Knowledge that is free from, i.e., devoid of, that particular [sublation] is <s>pramāṇa</s> — such is the connected meaning.
Now, since the qualifying terms in the definition are introduced with respect to what is to be excluded,

children.text: ty anena ye svâbhāsy eva jñānaṃ manyante
children.translated_text: by this [term], those who consider knowledge to be illuminating only itself —
i.e., particular [schools of] Buddhists, and those who [consider it to be] illuminating only the other [object] —

children.text: âdayas te nirastāḥ. te hi bahir-arthâbhāvāj jñānaṃ svâṃśa-paryavasita-sattākam ity ācakṣīran, tad ayuktam, jñeyârthâbhāve jñānâbhāva-prasaṅgāt. athârthâbhāve 'pi svapna-daśāyāṃ vana-deva-kulâdi-nānā-pratibhāsaṃ jñānam avalokitam iti tathā-bhūtaṃ sakalaṃ brūṣe, tan na, tasyâpi jāgrad-avasthā-bhāvi-sadbhūtârtha-darśana-sampāditâtma-saṃskāra-middhâdi-kāraṇa-kalāpa-sannidhāna-prabodha-savyapekṣatvād; itarathâtyantânanubhūta-bhūta-pañcakâtirikta-ṣaṣṭha-bhūta-pratibhāsaḥ syāt. kiṃ ca, katham ekaṃ jñānaṃ sita-pītâdy-anekâkāra-vivartam iti praṣṭavyo bhavān. anādy-avidyā-vāsanād iti ced, atrâpi vikalpa-yugalam amalam avatarati: tato jñānāt sā vāsanā vyabhaitsīd vā na vā? vyatyaraikṣīc ced, evaṃ sati tad-grāhaka-pramāṇam abhidhānīyam, jñāna-vyatiriktāyāḥ saṃvedanâbhāvāt, tat-saṃvedane cârthasyâpi vyatiriktasya saṃvedanam iti sa duṣpratiṣedhaḥ syāt. vedya-vedakâkāra-kaluṣitāj jñānād eva vyatiriktā tat-kāraṇa-bhūtā jñāna-rūpâiva sânumīyata iti cen, na, tayā saha sambandha-grahaṇâbhāvād, dṛṣṭa-hāny-adṛṣṭa-parikalpanā-prasaṅgāc ca. kiṃ ca, yathā vyatirikta-vāsanā-vaśād ekam api jñānaṃ nānâkāram, tathā jaḍam api tad-vaśād eva bodha-rūpaṃ prakāśata iti viparītâpatter artha eva siddhim āskanden, na jñānam. athâvyatiriktā, hanta jñānam eva tan, na vāsanā tad-avyatiriktatvāt tat-svarūpavad ity āstāṃ tāvat. parâbhāsy api sva-prakāśâbhāvād abhidadhīraṃs, tad apy asambaddham, sva-prakāśâbhāve para-prakāśâyogāt. na hi pradīpaḥ svarūpam anuddyotayan ghaṭâdy-uddyotane vyāpriyate. svayaṃ câpratītam api yady arthaṃ grāhayati jñānaṃ, devadattasyôtpannaṃ yajñadattaṃ grāhayed, viśeṣâbhāvāt. anyac ca, para-prakāśana-mātre dūrâsannâdi-bhedaḥ prathamānānām arthānāṃ kim-apekṣaś cakāsti? śarīrâpekṣa iti cen, na, tasyâpi prakāśyatâviśeṣāt, tasmād antar-mukhâkārasya bahir-artha-grahaṇe saty ayaṃ ghaṭām āṭīkate nânyathā. athârthâpatty-ādinā pramāṇântareṇa tad antar-niviṣṭaṃ gṛhyate, tatas tad-apekṣayā yokṣyate dūrâsannâdi-bheda iti cen, na, tatrâpi vikalpa-yugalakânativṛtteḥ; tathā hi: tat pramāṇântaraṃ sva-prakāśam anya-prakāśaṃ vā? sva-prakāśaṃ cet, prathamasya kiṃ kṣūṇam?! anya-prakāśaṃ cet, tatrâpîyam eva vārtêty anavasthā. tasmāt svarūpam avabhāsayad eva jñānam artha-grahaṇāya vyāpriyata iti sthitam.
children.translated_text: and others — are refuted. For they would declare that, due to the non-existence of external objects, knowledge has its existence confined to its own aspect — but that is untenable, because in the absence of a knowable object, knowledge itself would be absurd. If [you say that] even in the absence of [real] objects, in the dream state, knowledge is observed manifesting various appearances such as forests, temples, etc., and [if] you assert that all [knowledge] is of such a nature — no, because even that [dream knowledge] depends on the awakening produced by the assemblage of causes such as latent impressions generated by the perception of real objects occurring in the waking state, drowsiness, etc.; otherwise there would be the appearance of a sixth element beyond the five elements that have never been experienced at all. Moreover, you should be asked: how does a single knowledge undergo transformation into many forms such as white, yellow, etc.? If [you say] due to beginningless <s>avidyā</s>-impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), here too a pair of alternatives inescapably descends: Did that <s>vāsanā</s> differ from that knowledge, or not? If it did differ, then a means of valid knowledge that apprehends it must be specified, since there is no awareness of it apart from knowledge; and if there is awareness of it [as separate], then awareness of the object too as separate [would follow], and that would be difficult to deny. [If you say] it is inferred as having the nature of knowledge itself, as distinct [yet] being the cause of that [knowledge], from knowledge that is tainted with the forms of the known and the knower — no, because there is no apprehension of a relation with it, and because there would be the absurd consequence of abandoning what is observed and fabricating what is unobserved. Moreover, just as due to a distinct <s>vāsanā</s>, even a single knowledge takes on many forms, so too an inert [thing] could, due to that same [<s>vāsanā</s>], appear as having the nature of consciousness — thus, through this reductio ad absurdum, it is rather the [external] object that would be established, not knowledge. If [the <s>vāsanā</s> is] non-distinct [from knowledge], then well — it is knowledge itself, not <s>vāsanā</s>, since it is non-distinct from it, like its own nature — but let that be for now. Those who would maintain that [knowledge] illuminates the other but lacks self-illumination — that too is incoherent, because in the absence of self-illumination, illumination of the other is impossible. For a lamp does not engage in illuminating a pot, etc., without illuminating its own form. And if knowledge, though itself unperceived, causes an object to be known, then knowledge arising in <s>Devadatta</s> should cause <s>Yajñadatta</s> to know [it], since there is no distinguishing feature [between the two cases]. Furthermore, in the mere illumination of the other, with respect to objects apprehended as having distinctions such as far and near — on what does [the distinction] depend? If [you say] on the body — no, because the body too is equally something to be illuminated. Therefore, when there is the apprehension of an external object by [knowledge] whose form is inward-facing, this [view] limps and cannot be otherwise. If [you say that] the internally situated [knowledge] is apprehended by another <s>pramāṇa</s> such as <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption), and therefore the distinction of far and near will be explained with reference to that — no, because even there the pair of alternatives is not transcended. For is that other <s>pramāṇa</s> self-illuminating or other-illuminating? If self-illuminating, what was lacking in the first [knowledge]?! If other-illuminating, then even there the same problem applies — hence an infinite regress. Therefore, it is established that knowledge engages in the apprehension of objects only while illuminating its own form.

children.text: âdibhiḥ paryakalpi sannikarṣaḥ pramāṇam iti tasya prāmāṇyaṃ nirasyati. yataḥ snāna-pānâvagāhanâdy-artha-kriyā-nirvartana-kṣamam arthaṃ niścityâvyavadhānena pravartante pramātāras tad eva jñānaṃ pramāṇam, na sannikarṣo jaḍatayâsti, avyavahita-nirṇayâbhāvād ity ākūtam. arthôpalabdhi-hetutvāt tasya prāmāṇyam iti ced, viśīrṇêdānīṃ pramāṇêyattā, dehâder api tat-kāraṇatayā prāmāṇyâpatter ity āstāṃ tāvat.
children.translated_text: and others have imagined — namely that contact (<s>sannikarṣa</s>) is a <s>pramāṇa</s> — its status as a valid means of knowledge is rejected. For the knowers, having ascertained an object capable of fulfilling a practical purpose such as bathing, drinking, or immersion, engage [with it] without any intervening [medium] — that very knowledge is the <s>pramāṇa</s>, not contact, since [contact], being insentient, lacks unmediated ascertainment — such is the purport. If [you say that] its status as <s>pramāṇa</s> is due to being the cause of the apprehension of objects, then the scope of what counts as <s>pramāṇa</s> is now shattered, since even the body and such, being causes of that [apprehension], would absurdly qualify as <s>pramāṇa</s> — but let that be for now.

children.text: ity amunā tu yat timirâdi-tiras-kṛta-nayana-dīdhiti-prasarâdīnāṃ nabhas-talâvalambi-niśīthinī-nātha-dvayâdi-pratibhāsaṃ, yac ca kutarka-bhrānta-cetasāṃ nija-nija-darśanâkarṇana-prabhavaṃ kṣaṇa-kṣayi-sāmānya-viśeṣâikântêśvarâdikṛta-bhuvana-pratibhāsaṃ jñānaṃ tat-pratyanīkârtha-pratyāyaka-pramāṇântarôpanipāta-plāvitatvāt pratikṣipati. viśeṣârtha-vi-śabdôpādānāt tu yaḥ khalu bahula-kāmalâvalepa-lupta-locana-balānāṃ dhavale jalaje pītimānam ādadhāno bodhaḥ samullasati, sa yady api sakala-kālaṃ tad-doṣâvyuparame pramātur nija-darśanena na bādhyate, tathâpi taj-jalaja-dhavalatā-grāhinā janântara-darśanena bādhitatvān na pramāṇam ity uktaṃ bhavati.
children.translated_text: by this [term], that knowledge of those whose visual faculty has been obstructed by cataracts and the like, which manifests [appearances] such as two moons suspended in the sky, and that knowledge of those whose minds are bewildered by faulty reasoning, which manifests a world created by momentary [entities], universals, particulars, the One Lord, etc. — produced through the hearing and contemplation of their respective doctrines — [such knowledge] is rejected, because it is overwhelmed by the onset of another <s>pramāṇa</s> that demonstrates the opposite. However, by the inclusion of the qualifying word '<s>viśeṣa</s>' (particular), that cognition which arises attributing yellowness to a white lotus in those whose visual capacity is impaired by a heavy coating of bile — although it is never sublated by their own perception as long as the defect persists in the perceiver — is nevertheless not a <s>pramāṇa</s>, because it is sublated by the perception of another person who apprehends the whiteness of that lotus — this is what is stated.

children.text: samasta-lakṣaṇena tu yat pare pratyapīpadann "anadhigatârthâdhigantṛ pramāṇam", "avisaṃvādakaṃ pramāṇam", "arthôpalabdhi-hetuḥ pramāṇam" ity-ādi tan nirāsthat. tathā hy: anadhigatârthâdhigantṛtvaṃ kim abhidhīyate? jñānântareṇânadhigatam arthaṃ yad adhigacchati tat pramāṇam iti cet, tarhi taj jñānântaraṃ parakīyaṃ svakīyaṃ vā? tad yadi parakīyaṃ, tad ayuktaṃ, sarva-jña-jñānasya sakalârtha-gocaratayā sarva-prākṛta-loka-jñānānām adhigatârthâdhigantṛtvenâprāmāṇya-prasaṅgāt, tad-artha-grāhi-janântara-darśana-sambhavāc ca. atha svakīyaṃ, tatrâpi so 'dhigamyo 'rthaḥ kiṃ dravyam uta paryāyo yad vā, dravya-viśiṣṭaḥ paryāyaḥ paryāya-viśiṣṭaṃ vā dravyam iti, tathā kiṃ sāmānyam uta viśeṣa, āhosvit sāmānya-viśiṣṭo viśeṣaḥ, viśeṣa-viśiṣṭaṃ vā sāmānyam ity aṣṭau pakṣāḥ. tatra yady ādyam urarī-kuruṣe, tad ayuktaṃ, dravyasya nityatvâikatvābhyām anadhigatâṃśâbhāvāt. atha dvitīyaṃ, tad apy acāru, paryāyasya prācīna-saṃvedanôdaya-samaya-dhvastasya saṃvedanântara-prabhava-kālaṃ yāvat pratīkṣaṇâsambhavena viśeṣaṇânarthakyāt. uta tṛtīyaṃ, tad apy asādhīyo, vikalpa-dvayânatikramāt. sa hi dravya-viśiṣṭaḥ paryāyaḥ sama-kāla-bhāvinā jñānenânadhigato 'dhigamyate, yad vā kālântara-bhāvinêti. na tāvat sama-kāla-bhāvinā, tat-sambhavâbhāvena viśeṣaṇa-vaiphalyāt. na hi sambhavo 'sty ekasya pramātur eka-kālaṃ dravya-kroḍī-kṛtâika-paryāya-viṣaya-saṃvedana-dvaya-vṛtteḥ, tathânubhavâbhavāt, parasparam adhigatârthâdhigantṛtvenâprāmāṇya-prasaṅgāc ca. nâpi kālântara-bhāvinā, gṛhyamāṇa-paryāyasya kālântarânāskandanāt, pūrvôttara-kṣaṇa-truṭita-vartamāna-kṣaṇa-mātra-sambaddhatvāt tasya. etena paryāya-viśiṣṭa-dravya-pakṣo 'pi prativyūḍhaḥ, samāna-yoga-kṣematvāt. atha sāmānyaṃ, tad apy asambaddhaṃ, tad-ekatayā prathama-jñānena sākalya-grahaṇād uttareṣāṃ sāmānya-jñānānām adhigatârtha-gocaratayâprāmāṇya-prasaṅgāt. atha viśeṣaḥ, sa nityo 'nityo vêti vaktavyam. nityaś ced, evaṃ saty ādya-saṃvedanenâiva tasya sāmastya-grahaṇād uttareṣāṃ tad-viṣayāṇām adhigata-gocaratvenâprāmāṇya-prasaktiḥ. anityaś cet, paryāya-dūṣaṇena pratikṣiptiḥ. atha sāmānya-viśiṣṭo viśeṣaḥ, kâsya viśiṣṭatā: kiṃ tādātmyam uta tat-sannidhi-mātram? tādātmyaṃ cet, prathama-jñānena sāmānyavat tasyâpi grahaḥāt, anyathā tādātmya-kṣates, tad-viṣayânya-jñānānām aprāmāṇyaṃ prasajyeta. tat-sānnidhya-pakṣe tu dvayor api parasparaṃ viśakalita-rūpatvāt pakṣa-dvayôditaṃ dūṣaṇaṃ paścāl-lagnaṃ dhāvati. viśeṣa-viśiṣṭa-sāmānya-pakṣe punar etad eva viparītaṃ yojyam. tan nânadhigatârthâdhigantṛtvaṃ jñānasya kathañcid vicāra-bhāra-gauravaṃ sahata ity alakṣaṇam iti sthitam. avisaṃvādakatvam adhunā vicāryate: tat kiṃ pradarśitârtha-prāptyâhosvid prāpti-yogyârthôpadarśakatvena utâvicalitârtha-viṣayatvena bhavān jñānasya prāmāṇyaṃ kathayati? yadi prathamaḥ kalpas, tad ayuktaṃ, jala-budbud-ādi-mumūrṣu-padârthôtpādita-saṃvedanasyâpramāṇatôtpatteḥ, prāpti-kāle tasya dhvastatvāt. atha dvitīyas, tad apy acāru, prāpty-ayogya-deśa-sthita-graha-nakṣatrâdi-gocara-jñānasyâprāmāṇya-prasakter, anucita-deśâvasthānenâiva prāpty-anarhatvāt teṣām. atha tṛtīyaḥ pakṣas, tatrâpy avicalita-viṣayatāṃ katham avaiṣi? jñānântareṇa tad-viṣaya-nirākaraṇâbhāvād iti ced, etad evâsmābhir uditaṃ; kiṃ bhavataḥ paruṣam ābhāti? na hi sva-para-prakāśi jñānaṃ bādhā-rahitaṃ vimucyânyasya viṣayânirākaraṇaṃ jñānântareṇa prekṣāmahe. tat tad eva nyāyāt pramāṇaṃ bhavadbhir abhyupagatam iti. "arthôpalabdhi-hetuḥ pramāṇam" ity etad api na parīkṣāṃ kṣamate, śarīrâder api tat-kāraṇatayā prāmāṇya-prasaṅgāt. avyavahitam arthôpalambha-kāraṇaṃ pramāṇaṃ, na dehâdikam iti ced, evaṃ tarhi jñānam eva sva-parâvir-bhāvakaṃ nirbādhakaṃ ca pramāṇaṃ, na sannikarṣâdi, tad-sadbhāve 'py artha-paricchedâbhāvāt. tasmād etad eva cāru pramāṇa-lakṣaṇam iti.
children.translated_text: By the complete definition, that which others have proposed — 'a <s>pramāṇa</s> is that which apprehends a previously unapprehended object,' 'a <s>pramāṇa</s> is that which is non-deceptive,' 'a <s>pramāṇa</s> is the cause of the apprehension of objects,' and so forth — is rejected. For: what is meant by 'apprehending a previously unapprehended object'? If [you say] that which apprehends an object not apprehended by another cognition is a <s>pramāṇa</s> — then is that other cognition another person's or one's own? If another person's, that is untenable, because since the omniscient one's knowledge has all objects as its domain, all ordinary people's cognitions would absurdly become non-<s>pramāṇa</s> as apprehending already-apprehended objects, and because another person's perception grasping that object is [always] possible. If one's own, then too: is the object to be apprehended a substance (<s>dravya</s>), or a mode (<s>paryāya</s>), or a mode qualified by substance, or a substance qualified by mode? Likewise, is it a universal (<s>sāmānya</s>), or a particular (<s>viśeṣa</s>), or a particular qualified by a universal, or a universal qualified by a particular? — [thus] eight positions [arise]. Among these, if you accept the first — that is untenable, because substance, being permanent and unitary, has no unapprehended aspect. If the second — that too is unattractive, because the mode, having been destroyed at the time of the arising of the prior awareness, cannot wait until the time of the arising of the next awareness, making the qualifier pointless. Or if the third — that too is not sound, because the pair of alternatives cannot be transcended. For is that mode qualified by substance apprehended by a cognition simultaneous [with a prior one], or by one at a different time? Not by a simultaneous one, because the qualifier would be futile since such [simultaneous cognition] is impossible — for it is impossible for one knower to have two awarenesses at one time having as their object one mode embedded in substance, because such experience does not occur, and because each would absurdly become non-<s>pramāṇa</s> as apprehending each other's already-apprehended object. Nor by one at a different time, because the mode being apprehended does not extend to another time, being connected only with the present moment severed from prior and subsequent moments. By this, the position of substance qualified by mode is also refuted, since it shares the same logical fate. If [you say] the universal — that too is incoherent, because being unitary, it is grasped in its entirety by the first cognition, and subsequent cognitions of the universal would absurdly become non-<s>pramāṇa</s> as having an already-apprehended domain. If the particular — it must be said whether it is permanent or impermanent. If permanent, then in that case, since it too is grasped in its entirety by the first awareness, there would be the absurd consequence that subsequent cognitions having it as their object become non-<s>pramāṇa</s> as having an already-apprehended domain. If impermanent, it is rejected by the refutation [already given] for modes. If a particular qualified by a universal — what is its qualification: identity (<s>tādātmya</s>), or mere proximity? If identity, then since, like the universal, it too is grasped by the first cognition — otherwise the identity would be broken — other cognitions having it as their object would absurdly become non-<s>pramāṇa</s>. In the position of proximity, since the two [universal and particular] have mutually separated natures, the objection raised against both positions follows closely behind. In the position of universal qualified by particular, the same [refutation] is to be applied in reverse. Therefore, the [criterion of] 'apprehending a previously unapprehended object' cannot in any way bear the weight of scrutiny for [defining] knowledge — hence it is an invalid definition; this is established. Non-deceptiveness is now examined: Does your lordship say that knowledge's validity consists in the attainment of the presented object, or in presenting an object fit for attainment, or in having an unshaken object-domain? If the first option — that is untenable, because the awareness produced by objects about to perish, such as water-bubbles, would become non-<s>pramāṇa</s>, since at the time of attainment, that [object] has been destroyed. If the second — that too is unattractive, since there would be the absurd consequence that knowledge of planets, stars, etc. located in places unfit for attainment would become non-<s>pramāṇa</s>, since they are unworthy of attainment simply by being situated in an improper location. If the third position — there too, how do you know the object-domain is unshaken? If [you say] because there is no negation of that object by another cognition — this is exactly what we have stated; why does it appear harsh to your lordship? For we do not see any other [criterion for] the non-negation of an object by another cognition, beyond knowledge that illuminates both self and other and is free from sublation. Therefore, that very [definition] has in effect been accepted as <s>pramāṇa</s> by your lordships on [our] reasoning. The [definition] 'the cause of the apprehension of objects is <s>pramāṇa</s>' — this too does not withstand examination, since even the body and such, being causes of that [apprehension], would absurdly qualify as <s>pramāṇa</s>. If [you say] the <s>pramāṇa</s> is the unmediated cause of the apprehension of objects, not the body and such — then in that case, knowledge itself, which makes both self and other manifest and is free from sublation, is the <s>pramāṇa</s>, not contact and the like, because even when those exist, ascertainment of the object may be absent. Therefore, this alone is the proper definition of <s>pramāṇa</s>.

children.text: êty-ādi; tatra siddhânta-prasiddha-pāramārthika-pratyakṣâpekṣayâkṣa-śabdo jīva-paryāyatayā prasiddhaḥ. iha tu vyāvahārika-pratyakṣa-prastāvād akṣa-dhvanir indriya-vacano gṛhyate. tataś câkṣaṃ pratigataṃ pratyakṣaṃ. yad indriyam āśrityôjjihīte 'rtha-sākṣāt-kāri jñānaṃ tat pratyakṣam ity arthaḥ. etac ca pratyakṣa-śabda-vyutpatti-nimittaṃ, na tu pravṛtti-nimittam. sa hy evaṃ vyutpāditaḥ sākṣād grāhya-grāhakaṃ jñāna-viśeṣaṃ lakṣayati, tatrâiva rūḍhatvāt, yathā gamana-kriyāyāṃ vyutpādito 'pi go-śabdaḥ kakud-ādimantaṃ piṇḍa-viśeṣaṃ gacchantam agacchantaṃ vā gocarayati, tatrâiva tasya prasiddhatvāt, na gamana-kriyā-yuktam api puruṣâdikaṃ, viparyayād iti. tataś ca sarva-jñānānāṃ yat svarūpa-saṃvedanaṃ tad api pratyakṣam ity uktaṃ bhavati, tatrâpi svarūpasya grāhyasya sākṣāt-karaṇa-sadbhāvād iti. akṣebhyaḥ parato vartata iti parokṣam. akṣa-vyāpāra-nirapekṣaṃ mano-vyāpāreṇâsākṣād-artha-paricchedakaṃ yaj jñānaṃ tat parokṣam iti-bhāvaḥ.
children.translated_text: And so forth; therein, with respect to <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) in its ultimate sense as established in the <s>siddhānta</s> (doctrine), the word <s>akṣa</s> is well-known as a synonym for <s>jīva</s> (soul). But here, since the topic at hand is empirical <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), the term <s>akṣa</s> is taken to mean sense-organ (<s>indriya</s>). Thus, <s>pratyakṣa</s> means 'directed toward the sense-organ' (<s>akṣaṃ pratigataṃ</s>). The meaning is: that cognition which arises depending on a sense-organ and directly apprehends its object is <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception). This is the etymological derivation of the word <s>pratyakṣa</s>, not its operative definition. For the word, having been thus etymologically derived, denotes a particular cognition that directly grasps the object-of-knowledge and the knower, being conventionally fixed in that usage alone—just as the word <s>go</s> ('going'), though etymologically derived from the action of going, denotes only a particular bodily form possessing a hump and so forth, whether moving or not, since it is established in that usage alone, and does not denote a person or the like even though engaged in the action of going—because of the converse. From this it follows that the self-awareness (<s>svarūpa-saṃvedana</s>) of all cognitions is also called <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), since even there the direct apprehension of one's own nature as the object-of-knowledge exists. <s>Parokṣa</s> (indirect knowledge) means that which operates beyond the senses (<s>akṣebhyaḥ parataḥ</s>). The intended meaning is: that cognition which, independent of the operation of the senses, indirectly ascertains objects through the operation of the mind alone, is <s>parokṣa</s> (indirect knowledge).

children.text: -śabdau pratyakṣa-parokṣayos tulya-kakṣatāṃ lakṣayataḥ. tena yat pare prāhuḥ: "pratyakṣaṃ sakala-pramāṇa-jyeṣṭham" ityâdi tad apāstam bhavati, dvayor api prāmāṇyaṃ praty aviśeṣāt, viśadâviśada-pratibhāsa-viśeṣasya sato 'pi jyeṣṭhatāṃ praty anaṅgatvāt. pratyakṣasya puraḥsaratvāt parokṣasya kaniṣṭhatêti cen, nâyam ekântaḥ, sarvatrânyathânupapannatâvadhāritôcchvāsa-niḥśvāsâdi-jīva-liṅga-sadbhāvâsadbhāvābhyāṃ jīva-sākṣāt-kāri-pratyakṣa-kṣūṇe 'pi jīvan-mṛta-pratīti-darśanād, anyathā loka-vyavahārâbhāva-prasaṅgāt. kvacit pratyakṣa-parigṛhīta-sambandha-balāt parokṣaṃ pravartata iti pratyakṣasya jyeṣṭhatva-kalpane "paśya mṛgo dhāvatîty"-ādi-śabda-balāt kṛkâṭikā-moṭana-dvāreṇa mṛga-viṣayam, tathā smaraṇāt saṅketa-grahaṇād vâpūrvâpūrvârtha-darśana-kutūhalâdinā vana-deva-kulâdi-gocaraṃ parokṣa-pūrvaṃ pratyakṣaṃ dṛṣṭam iti parokṣasya jyeṣṭhatâsajyeta.
children.translated_text: indicate the equal status of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and <s>parokṣa</s> (indirect knowledge). Thereby, what others declare—"<s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) is the foremost of all <s>pramāṇas</s> (valid means of knowledge)" and so forth—is refuted, since there is no distinction between the two with respect to their validity as <s>pramāṇa</s>, and since the difference of vivid versus non-vivid appearance, even though it exists, is irrelevant to establishing superiority. If one objects that <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) is superior because it precedes and <s>parokṣa</s> (indirect knowledge) is inferior—this is not universally the case, since we observe the cognition of living and dead even when <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) that directly apprehends the <s>jīva</s> (soul) is impaired, through the presence or absence of signs of life such as breathing and exhalation, which are ascertained as otherwise inexplicable in all cases; otherwise, the absence of worldly conventions would follow. If one argues that <s>parokṣa</s> (indirect knowledge) operates on the strength of relations grasped by <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), and therefore <s>pratyakṣa</s> is superior, then by the force of words such as 'Look, a deer is running!' one turns the neck and perceives the deer—but similarly, <s>pratyakṣa</s> preceded by <s>parokṣa</s> is observed when, through recollection, grasping of conventions, or curiosity about seeing unprecedented objects, one goes to a forest temple and the like; thus the superiority of <s>parokṣa</s> (indirect knowledge) would equally follow.

children.text: ti. "sarvaṃ vākyaṃ sâvadhāraṇaṃ pravartata" iti nyāyād, anyathā niyatârthâpradarśakatvena tad-uccāraṇa-vaiyarthya-prasaṅgād, viparītâkāra-nirākaraṇa-cāturyâyogena nirākāṅkṣa-pravṛtty-asiddher dvidhâivêty avadhāraṇena para-parikalpita-viparīta-saṃkhyântaraṃ tiras-kurute, tasya yukti-bādhitatvāt.
children.translated_text: by the maxim that 'every statement operates with a restrictive force,' since otherwise, by failing to indicate a definite meaning, the utterance would become pointless, and since without the skill of excluding contrary forms, unrestricted application would not be established—by the restriction 'only twofold,' the alternative number proposed by opponents is dismissed, because it is contradicted by reasoning.

children.text: tathā hi: pratyakṣam evâikaṃ pramāṇam ity asat, parokṣâbhāve tasyâiva prāmāṇyâyogāt. sa hi kāścit pratyakṣa-vyaktīr artha-kriyā-samarthârtha-prāpakatvenâvyabhicāriṇīr upalabhyânyās tad-viparītatayā vyabhicāriṇīś ca, tataḥ kālântare punar api tādṛśêtarāṇāṃ pratyakṣa-vyaktīnāṃ pramāṇatêtarate samācakṣīta. na ca pūrvâpara-parāmarśa-śūnyaṃ puro-varty-artha-grahaṇa-paryavasita-sattākaṃ pratyakṣaṃ pūrvâpara-kāla-bhāvinīnāṃ pratyakṣa-vyaktīnāṃ sādṛśyaṃ prāmāṇya-nibandhanam upalakṣayituṃ kṣamate. na câyaṃ sva-pratīti-gocarāṇām api pratyakṣa-vyaktīnāṃ prāmāṇyaṃ paraṃ pratipādayitum īśaḥ. tasmād avaśyantayā yathâdṛṣṭa-pratyakṣa-vyakti-sādharmya-dvāreṇâdhunātana-pratyakṣa-vyaktīnāṃ prāmāṇya-pratyāyakaṃ para-paripādakaṃ ca parokṣântar-gatam anumāna-rūpaṃ pramāṇântaram urarī-kartavyam. parâvabodhârthaṃ ca pratyakṣam evâikaṃ pramāṇaṃ nânyad astîty ullapann unmattatām ātmano lakṣayati, pratyakṣeṇa para-ceto-vṛtti-sākṣāt-karaṇâbhāvād vyāpāra-vyāhāra-ceṣṭā-viśeṣa-darśanād bodha-viśeṣâvagatau parokṣasya prāmāṇyaṃ balād āpatatîti nyāyāt. svargâdṛṣṭa-devatâdi-pratiṣedhaṃ na pratyakṣeṇa kartum arhati, tasya sannihita-mātra-viṣayatvāt. na câyaṃ tad-pratiṣedhena khara-kharaka-
children.translated_text: For instance: it is wrong to hold that <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) alone is the sole <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge), because in the absence of <s>parokṣa</s> (indirect knowledge), even its own validity would be impossible. For one who, having perceived certain particular instances of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) as non-deviating because they lead to objects capable of practical efficacy, and others as deviating because they are contrary to that, would subsequently determine the validity or otherwise of similar and dissimilar perceptual instances at another time. But <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), whose existence is confined to grasping only the present object and is devoid of reference to past and future, is incapable of discerning the similarity of perceptual instances occurring at earlier and later times that constitutes the basis of their validity. Nor is this person able to demonstrate to others the validity of perceptual instances that are within the range of his own experience alone. Therefore, one must necessarily accept another <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) of the nature of <s>anumāna</s> (inference), included within <s>parokṣa</s> (indirect knowledge), which establishes the validity of present perceptual instances through their similarity with previously observed perceptual instances, and which communicates this to others. Moreover, one who proclaims for the sake of informing others that <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) alone is the only <s>pramāṇa</s> and nothing else exists thereby marks himself as insane, since by <s>pratyakṣa</s> one cannot directly apprehend another's mental states, and the validity of <s>parokṣa</s> (indirect knowledge) forcibly imposes itself by the principle that knowledge of another's particular mental states is obtained from observing particular actions, transactions, and gestures. Nor can one use <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) to negate heaven, unseen merit (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>), deities, and the like, since perception has only presently proximate objects as its domain. And yet this person, by denying those,

children.text: tām āpnoti, pramāṇântaraṃ ca tat-pratiṣedhârthaṃ nêcchatîti viṣamam etat kathaṃ kuryād iti savismayaṃ naś cetaḥ. kiṃ ca, pratyakṣam api kathaṃ pramāṇatāṃ svī-karotîti vaktavyam, gṛhyamāṇa-padârthânvaya-vyatirekânukaraṇāt. tathā hi: tat samagra-sāmagrīka-padârtha-balenônmajjati, tat-abhāve visphāritêkṣaṇa-yugalasyâpi pramātur nôdīyata iti yadi brūṣe, parokṣe 'pi tarhi samānam evâitat, tad api bahir-artha-sāmarthyād evôllasati, tat-sambaddha-liṅga-śabda-dvāreṇa tasyôtpatter, anyathā parokṣâbhāsatā-prasaṅgāt, tasya câlīkatve pāramārthika-parokṣa-prāmāṇya-kṣater ayogād, anyathā pratyakṣam api gagana-talâvalambi-śaśa-dhara-yugalâvalokana-caturam alīkam avalokitam iti sakala-viśada-darśanāni satyatâbhimatāny apy alīkatām aśnuvīran. tan na pramāṇa-bhūtaṃ parokṣaṃ kadācana gṛhyamāṇa-padârtha-sattāṃ vihāyôtpattum utsahata iti pratyakṣavat pramāṇa-koṭim ārohati balād iti sthitam.
children.translated_text: and does not accept another <s>pramāṇa</s> for the purpose of negating them—this is contradictory; how could one manage this?—thus our mind is filled with wonder. Furthermore, one must explain how <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) itself assumes the status of a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge), since it follows the pattern of concomitance and non-concomitance with apprehended objects. For if you say that it arises by the force of an object possessing a complete set of conditions, and does not arise for the perceiver even with eyes wide open in the absence of that—then the same applies equally to <s>parokṣa</s> (indirect knowledge), for it too manifests only through the capacity of external objects, since it arises through the medium of <s>liṅga</s> (inferential marks) and <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) connected with those objects; otherwise, it would be mere semblance of <s>parokṣa</s> (pseudo-indirect knowledge). And if its falsity were admitted, the damage to the genuine validity of <s>parokṣa</s> (indirect knowledge) would be unwarranted, since otherwise even <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception)—clever at beholding a pair of moons hanging in the sky—would be observed as false, and then all vivid cognitions, though considered true, would attain falsity. Therefore, <s>parokṣa</s> (indirect knowledge), being a <s>pramāṇa</s>, is never capable of arising while abandoning the reality of the objects being apprehended, and thus it forcibly ascends to the rank of <s>pramāṇa</s> just like <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception)—this is established.

children.text: tathā yad api parair ukta-dvayâtiriktaṃ pramāṇa-saṃkhyântaraṃ pratyajñāyi, tatrâpi yat paryālocyamānam upamānârthâpattivat pramāṇatām ātmasāt-karoti, tad anayor eva pratyakṣa-parokṣayor antar-bhāvanīyam. yat punar vicāryamāṇaṃ
children.translated_text: Similarly, whatever alternative number of <s>pramāṇas</s> (valid means of knowledge) beyond the two stated has been acknowledged by others—even among those, whatever, when carefully examined, assumes the status of <s>pramāṇa</s> in the manner of <s>upamāna</s> (analogy) or <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption), should be subsumed under these two, <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and <s>parokṣa</s> (indirect knowledge). But whatever, when scrutinized,
like the <s>abhāva</s> (absence) postulated by the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s> (Mīmāṃsā philosopher),

children.text: -parikalpitâbhāvavat prāmāṇyam eva nâskandati, na tena bahir-bhūtenântar-bhūtena vā kiñcin naḥ prayojanam avastutvād ity apakarṇanīyam.
children.translated_text: does not even attain the status of a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge), we have no concern with it whether it falls outside or within these two, since it is a non-entity—and so it should be disregarded.

children.text: atha katham upamānasya prāmāṇyam iti brūṣe, tad ucyate: prathamaṃ hi viśada-darśanâdhigata-go-piṇḍa-viśeṣasya "yathā gaus tathā gavaya" iti vākyâkarṇanâhitâtma-saṃskārasya puṃso 'ṭavyāṃ paryaṭato gavaya-piṇḍa-viśeṣa-viṣaya-vivikta-darśana-puraḥsaraṃ yat pūrvâpara-go-gavaya-piṇḍa-gocara-darśana-vyāpāra-sampādita-janmakam ayaṃ tena sadṛśo 'nayor vā sādṛśyam iti sādṛśya-viśiṣṭaṃ piṇḍaṃ piṇḍa-viśiṣṭaṃ sādṛśyaṃ vā gocarayat saṃvedanam udīyate tad upamānam iti. yathâhus tad-vādinaḥ:
children.translated_text: Now, if you ask how <s>upamāna</s> (analogy) has validity as a <s>pramāṇa</s>, the answer is as follows: First, a person who has apprehended a particular form of a cow through vivid perception, and in whom a mental impression has been deposited by hearing the statement 'As is a cow, so is a <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox),' while wandering in the forest, preceded by a distinct perception of a particular form of a <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox)—there arises a cognition born from the perceptual activity encompassing both the earlier and later forms of cow and <s>gavaya</s>, which apprehends either a particular bodily form qualified by similarity—'this is similar to that, or there is similarity between these two'—or similarity qualified by particular bodily form: that cognition is <s>upamāna</s> (analogy). As the proponents of that view state:

children.text: "tasmād yad dṛśyate tat syāt sādṛśyena viśeṣitaṃ /
children.translated_text: "Therefore, that which is perceived, qualified by similarity,

children.text: prameyam upamānasya sādṛśyaṃ vā tad-anvitam" // NAV_1.12:1 //
children.translated_text: is the object of <s>upamāna</s> (analogy); or the similarity accompanied by that [object]." [NAV_1.12:1]

children.text: tataś ca pūrvâpara-darśanayoḥ puro-varti-go-gavaya-piṇḍa-grahaṇa-paryavasita-sattākatvāt pūrvâpara-parāmarśa-śūnyatvād viśada-nirbhāsitayā śabdôllekha-rahitatvāt tad-adhikam avyabhicaritaṃ vyavahāra-kāri sādṛśyam avasyad upamānaṃ sva-para-prakāśitayā nirbādhakatvāc ca pramāṇam. pūrvâpara-piṇḍâtiriktam aparaṃ sādṛśyaṃ nôpalabhyata iti cet, ko 'yam upalambho yena nôpalabhyate sādṛśyaṃ yadi pratyakṣaṃ tat? yadi pratyakṣe sādṛśyam upamāna-gocaratvān na pratibhāti, ko 'syâparādhaḥ? na hi jñānântare tad-gocaro na pratibhātîti nirgocaraṃ tad iti vaktuṃ śakyam, itarathôpamāne 'pi pratyakṣa-nirgrāhyā vyaktir na bhātîti nirgocaram adhyakṣam anuṣajyeta. tad yathā sva-viṣaye 'dhyakṣaṃ pramāṇaṃ tathôpamānam api. na hi dvayoḥ prathamānayor ekaṃ prati viśeṣâbhāve pakṣa-pātaḥ kartuṃ yuktaḥ. etena pratyabhijñā-jñāna-smṛty-ūhâdīnām avisaṃvādakānāṃ parokṣa-viśeṣāṇāṃ prāmāṇyaṃ vyākhyātam avagantavyaṃ, samāna-nyāyânupātitvāt. tathā hi: prathamam artha-darśanam ātmani saṃskāram ādhatte, tādṛśa-darśanād asau saṃskāraḥ prabudhyate, prabuddhaḥ pūrvârtha-viṣayaṃ sa evâyaṃ taj-jātīyo vêty ullekhena pratyabhijñā-jñānam utthāpayati, tasyôrdhva-tiraścīna-bheda-sāmānya-dvayâvasthāpakatvād, asañjāta-pūrvârtha-gocara-darśanasya tad-udayâbhāvāt. tathā sa eva saṃskāras tādṛśârtha-darśanenâbhogâdinā vā prabuddho 'nubhūta-viṣayâsampramoṣa-lakṣaṇaṃ smaraṇam upajanayaty, adṛṣṭârthasya puṃsaḥ smaraṇânupapatter iti. ūho 'pi pratyakṣânumānâsaṃvedya-sādhyârthânyathânupapannatva-lakṣaṇa-liṅga-sambandha-grahaṇa-pravaṇaḥ pramāṇântaram iti kathayiṣyate.
children.translated_text: And since both the earlier and later perceptions have their existence confined to grasping the present cow and <s>gavaya</s> forms, since they are devoid of reference to past and future, since by their vivid manifestation they are free from verbal overlay—the similarity that is additional to them, invariable, and productive of practical activity, must necessarily be <s>upamāna</s> (analogy), and because it is self-luminous and other-luminous and unobstructed, it is a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge). If one objects that no similarity is perceived apart from the earlier and later particular forms—what is this perception by which similarity is not perceived? If it is <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), then since similarity is the domain of <s>upamāna</s> (analogy) and does not appear in <s>pratyakṣa</s>, what is its fault? For one cannot say that because the object of one type of cognition does not appear in another type of cognition, it therefore has no object at all; otherwise, since the particular object graspable by <s>pratyakṣa</s> does not appear in <s>upamāna</s>, <s>pratyakṣa</s> too would be deemed objectless. Therefore, just as <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) is a <s>pramāṇa</s> in its own domain, so too is <s>upamāna</s> (analogy). For when two things are being evaluated and there is no distinguishing feature between them, it is not proper to show partiality to one. By this, the validity of <s>pratyabhijñā</s> (recognition), <s>smṛti</s> (memory), <s>ūha</s> (conjecture), and similar non-deceptive particular forms of <s>parokṣa</s> (indirect knowledge) should be understood as explained, since they follow the same principle. For first, the perception of an object deposits a mental impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) in the self; from a similar perception, that impression is awakened; once awakened, it gives rise to <s>pratyabhijñā</s> (recognition) with the thought 'this is the same one' or 'this is of the same kind,' since it establishes both the vertical and horizontal aspects of the universal; for one who has never had perception of a prior object, that recognition would not arise. Likewise, that same impression, awakened by a similar perception or by attention and the like, produces <s>smaraṇa</s> (recollection) characterized as the non-loss of experienced objects, since recollection is impossible for one who has never seen the object. <s>Ūha</s> (conjecture) too, being inclined to grasp the connection with an inferential mark characterized as the otherwise-inexplicability of an object to be established that is not perceivable by <s>pratyakṣa</s> or <s>anumāna</s>, will be described as a separate <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge).

children.text: arthâpattis tu pratyakṣâdi-gocarī-kṛta-sphoṭâdi-padârthânyathânupapattyā dahana-śakty-ādikaṃ pāvakâder arthântaraṃ pūrva-darśana-gocarāt samadhikam avyabhicaritaṃ parikalpayantîti pramāṇatāṃ svī-karoty eva, tal-lakṣaṇa-yogāt. evam anyad api pratyakṣa-gocarâdhikya-sampādakaṃ nirākāṅkṣatayā vyavahāra-kāri yad yat saṃvedanaṃ tat tat pramāṇam iti samarthanīyaṃ, sva-para-prakāśi-nirbādhatvāt, pūrvâpara-sopāna-paddhati-darśanôttara-kāla-bhāvi-tat-saṃkhyā-saṃvedanavat. sarveṣāṃ câiteṣāṃ parokṣe 'ntar-bhāvo, 'nyathânupapannârthântara-darśana-dvāreṇa prastutârtha-saṃvedana-caturatvād iti. kiñcid-viśeṣāt tu pramāṇântara-parikalpane pramāṇêyattā viśīryetânantya-prāpter,āvaraṇa-kṣayôpaśama-vicitratayā jñāna-pravṛtter vicitratvād iti. nanu câivaṃ sati yat parokṣasya dvaividhyaṃ vakṣyamāṇam anumāna-śābda-bhedena tad api katham upapatsyate, tatrâpi hy āpta-praṇīta-vacana-prabhava-jñānasyârthânyathânupapannatvenânumānântar-bhāvo na durupapādaḥ? tataś cânumānam evâikam avaśiṣyate, tad eva parokṣa-śabdena, yady ucyate yuktam āste, viduṣām abhidhānaṃ praty anādarāt; satyam etad, evaṃ tu manyate: yady api kayācit prakriyayânumāne śābdam antar-bhāvayituṃ śakyaṃ, tathâpi tat prati vipratipadyante pare; 'tas tasyâhatya prāmāṇyaṃ samarthanīyam. na câpṛthag-bhūtasya tad-viviktaṃ vaktuṃ śakyam iti, ataḥ pārthakyenôpanyāsaḥ. anena câitad upalakṣayaty anyeṣām api parokṣa-viśeṣāṇām anumānântar-bhāva-sambhave 'pi yaṃ yaṃ prati pareṣāṃ vipratipattis taṃ taṃ parokṣān niṣkṛṣya vivikta-yukty-upanyāsena tasya tasya prāmāṇyam āvedanīyam. tathā ca śāstrântare yad ūhâdīnāṃ lakṣaṇam akāry ācāryais tad yuktam evêty uktam bhavati.
children.translated_text: <s>Arthāpatti</s> (presumption), however, by postulating something additional beyond what was previously observed — such as the burning power and so forth of fire — through the impossibility of otherwise explaining entities like <s>sphoṭa</s> (the meaning-bearing phonemic unit) and the like, which have been brought within the range of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and other means, does indeed accept the status of a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge), since it possesses the defining characteristics thereof. Similarly, whatever cognition that produces knowledge exceeding the range of perception and that gives rise to practical activity without any further expectation — all that should be maintained as a <s>pramāṇa</s>, because it is self-luminous, other-luminous, and unobstructed — just like the cognition of that number which arises after seeing the sequence of earlier and later steps of a staircase. And all of these are included under <s>parokṣa</s> (indirect knowledge), because they are skilled at cognizing the matter at hand through the door of perceiving something other than what would otherwise be inexplicable. However, if one were to postulate separate means of knowledge on the basis of minor differences, the definite number of <s>pramāṇas</s> would be shattered, since there would be an infinite regress — because the variety of knowledge-activity arises from the variety of the destruction and subsidence of obscurations. Now, if this is so, how will the twofold division of <s>parokṣa</s> that will be stated — namely the distinction between <s>anumāna</s> (inference) and <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) — be justified? For there too, the inclusion of knowledge born from the words of a reliable authority within <s>anumāna</s> is not difficult to establish, since it involves what would otherwise be inexplicable. Thus only <s>anumāna</s> alone would remain, and if that alone is designated by the term '<s>parokṣa</s>,' that would be proper, since the learned are indifferent to mere terminology. This is true; however, the view is as follows: although by some method it is possible to include <s>śabda</s> within <s>anumāna</s>, nevertheless others dispute this; therefore its validity as a <s>pramāṇa</s> must be established independently. And since what is not separate cannot be discussed distinctly from it, therefore it is presented separately. By this he indicates that even when the inclusion of other particular types of <s>parokṣa</s> within <s>anumāna</s> is possible, whichever ones others dispute should be extracted from <s>parokṣa</s> and their validity as <s>pramāṇas</s> should be demonstrated through the presentation of separate reasoning. And thus whatever definitions of <s>ūha</s> (reasoning) and the like were given by the teachers in other treatises — that too is said to be proper.

children.text: -parikalpito 'bhāvo na pramāṇam? nirgocaratvād iti brūmaḥ. tathā hi: pratyakṣam evânvaya-vyatireka-dvārena "bhū-talam evêdaṃ, ghaṭâdir nâstîti" vastu-pariccheda-prāvīṇyam ābibhrāṇaṃ tad-adhika-grāhyârthâbhāvāt pramāṇântaraṃ parikalpyamānaṃ nirasyatîti kiṃ naś cintayā, tasya sad-asad-rūpa-vastu-grāhiṇaḥ pratiprāṇi-prasiddhatvāt. atha kadācid abhidadhyād: adhyakṣaṃ bhāvâṃśam evâkalayatîndriya-dvāreṇôtpattes, tasya ca bhāvâṃśa eva vyāpārān; nâstitā-jñānaṃ tu vastu-grahaṇôttara-kālaṃ pratiyogi-smaraṇa-sadbhāve mānasam akṣa-vyāpāra-nirapekṣam unmajjati. tad uktam:
children.translated_text: not a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge)? We say: because it lacks an object. For <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) itself, through the method of positive and negative concomitance, bearing the proficiency of determining a real entity such as 'this is just the ground-surface, a pot and the like do not exist here,' refutes any additional means of knowledge that might be postulated, since there is no object to be grasped beyond that. So what need have we of further deliberation, since that [perception], which grasps entities both existent and non-existent in nature, is well-established for every sentient being?
