As for the Voidist (<s>śūnya-vādin</s>), since he denies everything, he is simply unfit for the discourse of <s>pramāṇas</s> and objects of knowledge, and therefore one need not address faults in one's own proof with reference to him, since his position never arises at all, his thesis being contradicted by his own statement. For consider: does the statement that establishes the non-existence of everything exist or not? If it exists, then the thesis is abandoned. If it does not exist, then the existence of all things is established, since there is no negator.

children.text: punar vedya-vedakâkāra-vikalaṃ sakala-vikalpa-gocarâtītaṃ nirvikalpakaṃ vivikta-pāramārthika-sva-saṃvedana-vedyaṃ saṃvedanam āgūryânādi-kālâlīna-vāsanā-bala-prabhāvitaṃ grāhya-grāhakâkāra-kaluṣitaṃ bahiṣ-prathamānaṃ nikhilam api jñānaṃ viparyastatayā pratijānānaḥ samakṣa-lakṣaṇasya prakṛta-dṛṣṭântasya sādhya-śūnyatām abhidadhyād, atas tan-mata-vikuṭṭanârtham āha:
children.translated_text: again, one who maintains that all cognition is erroneous because it manifests externally, being tainted by the forms of apprehended-object and apprehending-subject (<s>grāhya-grāhaka</s>), influenced by the power of beginningless latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), while [true] awareness is to be known only through the isolated, ultimately real self-awareness (<s>sva-saṃvedana</s>), devoid of the forms of known and knower, beyond the scope of all conceptual thought (<s>vikalpa</s>), and non-conceptual (<s>nirvikalpaka</s>)—such a one might declare the example of perception under discussion to be devoid of the <s>sādhya</s> [i.e., non-erroneousness]. Therefore, to demolish his doctrine, [the author] says:
Even perception is not erroneous, because of the ascertainment of its validity as a <s>pramāṇa</s>;

children.text: bhrāntaṃ pramāṇam ity etad viruddhaṃ vacanaṃ yataḥ || 6 ||
children.translated_text: for 'erroneous [and yet] a <s>pramāṇa</s>'—this is a contradictory statement. || NA_6 ||

children.text: yad bhavataś cetasi vivartate, yad uta na kevalam anumānaṃ bhrāntaṃ, kiṃ tarhi yad bhavadbhir dṛṣṭântatayôpāttaṃ pratyakṣaṃ tad api bhrāntam eva, "sarvam ālambane bhrāntam" ity vacanāt, tad etan na. kuta ity āha:
children.translated_text: What revolves in your mind—namely, that not only inference is erroneous, but that perception too, which you have adduced as an example, is also erroneous, because of the statement 'all [cognition] is erroneous with respect to its object (<s>ālambana</s>)'—that is wrong. Why? He says:
'Because of the ascertainment of its validity as a <s>pramāṇa</s>'—
that is, because of the determination of its <s>pramāṇa</s>-nature. This is the meaning.

children.text: nanu ca pramāṇatām abhrāntatânyathânupapannāṃ yadi paraḥ pratipadyate, tatas tām abhyupagacchan kathaṃ bhrāntatā-vipratipattiṃ vidadhyād iti pārśva-sthita-vacanâvakāśam āśaṅkya, bhrāntatā-pramāṇatayor virodha-sādhanena tataḥ pramāṇatāṃ vyāvartyânanya-śaraṇatayā pratijñātâbhrāntatâkrāntāṃ tāṃ darśayann āha:
children.translated_text: Now, anticipating the objection of a bystander—'If the opponent accepts <s>pramāṇa</s>-hood as inexplicable without non-erroneousness, then how, while accepting that [<s>pramāṇa</s>-hood], could he maintain the counter-position of erroneousness?'—[the author], establishing the contradiction between erroneousness and <s>pramāṇa</s>-hood, thereby setting aside <s>pramāṇa</s>-hood, and showing that the [thus] established non-erroneousness, having no other recourse, pervades [the <s>pramāṇa</s>], says:
i.e., a cause of the ascertainment of the object to be apprehended;
i.e., this utterance that conveys such meaning—
because it contains meanings that are mutually inconsistent between the earlier and later parts.

children.text: nanu ca nâivâsya viruddhatā, tathā hy: avidita-paramârtha-vyāvahārikâbhiprāyeṇa loka-saṃvṛtiṃ ghaṭayanto vayaṃ dṛḍhatara-vāsanā-prabodha-sampādita-sattākayoḥ pratyakṣânumānayoḥ pramāṇatām ācakṣmahe, tad-abhiprāyeṇa darśitârtha-prāpakatvena tayor avisaṃvādakatvāt. śithila-vāsanâunmukhya-nirmita-janmakayoḥ punar apramāṇatāṃ, tad-ākūtenâiva darśite 'rthe vipralambhanād iti, bhrāntatāṃ punas tattva-cintakâbhiprāyeṇa sakalasya bahir upaplavamānasya grāhya-grāhakâkāra-kāluṣya-dūṣitasya pratibhāsasya pāramārthikâdvaya-saṃvedana-viparyasta-rūpatvād abhidadhmahe, bahiḥ pratibhāsasya tad-grāhyârtha-vicārâkṣamatayôpapluta-rūpatvāt. tathā hy: artho 'vayavi-rūpo 'vayava-rūpo vā syād, gaty-antarâbhāvāt. na tāvad avayavi-rūpo vicāraṃ kṣamate, 'vayava-virahe 'vayavitvâyogāt, teṣu ca tad-vṛtti-vikalpânupapatteḥ. tathā hi: teṣv asāv ekadeśena vartate sāmastyena vā. na tāvad ekadeśena, tasya svayaṃ niravayavatvāt. avayava-vṛtti-nimittam aṃśântara-kalpane tad-vṛttāv apy aṃśântara-kalpana-prasaṅgas, tathā cânavasthā. nâpi sāmastyena, praty-avayavaṃ parisamāpta-rūpatayâvayavi-bahutva-prasaṅgāt. bheda-pakṣe doṣo 'yam, abheda-pakṣe nâstîti cen, na: tatrâpy avayava-mātram avayavi-mātraṃ vā syād, itarêtarâvyatiriktatvād, itarêtara-svarūpavat. kiṃ ca, samastâvayava-vyāpino 'vayavino 'bhyupagame paṭâder eka-deśa-rāga-kampa-darśanâdiṣu sakala-rāga-kampa-darśanâdīni durnivārāṇi syur, ekasya rāgârāgâdi-viruddha-dharmâdhyāsâyogād iti. nâpy avayava-rūpo 'rtho vicāra-gocara-cārī kara-caraṇa-śiro-grīvâdīnām avayavānāṃ svâvayavâpekṣayâvayavi-rūpatayā tad-dūṣaṇenâivâpāstatvāt. paramâṇūnāṃ niraṃśatayâvayavatvam upapadyata iti cen, na, teṣām api dik-ṣaṭka-sambandhena ṣaṭ-aṃśatâpatter, anyathâvasthānâbhāvāt. tataś cârtha-virahāt tad-unmukho grāhyâkāro 'līkas, tad-alīkatāyāṃ grāhakâkāro 'pi nâvasthānam ābadhnāti, grāhyâbhāve grāhakâyogāt. tad-apekṣayâiva tat-svarūpa-sthitiḥ, grāhya-grāhakâkāra-vilaye ca bodhâkāro 'vaśiṣyate, tasya sarvatrâvyabhicarita-rūpatvāt, tasmāt sa eva pāramārthika iti.
children.translated_text: Now, [the Yogācāra says:] 'There is no contradiction here. For we, harmonizing worldly convention (<s>loka-saṃvṛti</s>) with an intent toward the conventional that is unaware of the ultimate truth, declare the <s>pramāṇa</s>-hood of perception and inference, whose existence is brought about by the awakening of firmly rooted latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), since from that standpoint they are non-deceiving, having been shown to lead to their objects. But we declare the non-<s>pramāṇa</s>-hood of those [cognitions] whose arising is fashioned by the tendency of weakened impressions, since from that intent they deceive with respect to the object shown. And we declare erroneousness from the standpoint of the truth-investigator, because all appearances that manifest externally, tainted by the impurity of apprehended-object and apprehending-subject forms, have a nature that is the reverse of the ultimately real non-dual awareness (<s>advaya-saṃvedana</s>), since what appears externally, being incapable of withstanding examination of its [supposed] object, has a distorted nature. For an object must be either a whole (<s>avayavin</s>) or parts (<s>avayava</s>), there being no third alternative. The whole, first, does not withstand examination, because whole-ness is impossible in the absence of parts, and because the conception of the whole's subsistence in the parts is untenable. For does it subsist in them partially or entirely? Not partially, because [a part] is itself without parts. If one posits another portion [of the whole] as the basis for partial subsistence, then in the subsistence of that [portion] too, yet another portion would have to be posited, and so on to infinite regress. Nor entirely, because if the whole were fully realized in each individual part, there would be a plurality of wholes. If [one says] this fault applies to the position of difference [between whole and parts] but not to the position of non-difference—no: even there, the parts alone would be the whole alone or vice versa, since they are non-different from each other, having the nature of each other. Moreover, if the whole pervading all parts is accepted, then when color, trembling, etc. are seen in one part of a cloth and the like, it would be unavoidable that color, trembling, etc. would be seen in the entirety, since it is impossible for contradictory properties like colored-and-uncolored to be superimposed on one thing. Nor does the object as parts fare better under examination, because the parts such as hands, feet, head, and neck, being themselves wholes with respect to their own sub-parts, are refuted by the very same objection. If [one says] atoms (<s>paramāṇu</s>), being partless, qualify as genuine parts—no, because even they, through connection with the six directions, incur six-partedness, since otherwise they could not be spatially situated. Therefore, since the object is absent, the apprehended-object form directed toward it is false. And when the apprehended-object form is false, the apprehending-subject form too has no standing, since without an apprehended there can be no apprehender. Its own nature subsists only in dependence on that [apprehended]. And when the forms of apprehended and apprehender dissolve, the awareness-form (<s>bodhākāra</s>) alone remains, since its nature is invariable everywhere. Therefore that alone is ultimately real.'

children.text: atra pratividhīyate -- yad avādi saṃvedanam advayaṃ pāramārthikaṃ, grāhya-grāhakâkāra-pravṛttaṃ punar atāttvikam iti, tad ayuktaṃ, pramāṇâbhāvāt. tathā hi: bahir antaś cânekâkāratayā harṣa-viṣādâdibhiḥ sthira-sthūratâdy-aneka-dharma-parikaritârtha-grahaṇa-pariṇāmaiś ca vivartamānaṃ saṃvedanam upalabhyate, na punar vedya-vedakâkāra-viviktaṃ yādṛg bhavadbhir upavarṇyate jñānaṃ tādṛśaṃ kasyacit kadācana pratīti-gocara-cāritām anubhavaty, advaya-pratibhāsasya svapna-daśāyām apy ananubhūteḥ. na ca tattva-cintakā api pramāṇam antareṇa svâkūtaṃ pratiṣṭhāpayantaḥ prekṣāvatām avadheya-vacanā bhavanty, anyathâikam acetanam avyayam api brahmânekaṃ cetanaṃ kṣaṇa-bhaṅguratâkrāntam avidyātaḥ prathata iti bruvāṇo 'nirākāryaḥ syāt. yad api bahir-artha-nirākaraṇa-dhiyā avayavy-avayava-dvāreṇa dūṣaṇam adāyi, tad api bahir antaḥ prathamāna-sakalâsumat-pratīta-pratibhāsa-mudgara-nirdalita-śarīratayā bhakta-madhya-niṣṭhyūta-darśinaḥ purato vipratāraṇa-pravaṇa-kuṭṭinī-śapatha-prāyam iti na vidvaj-jana-manāṃsi rañjayati, pratyakṣa-pratibhāsâpahnave tan-mūlakatvāt kuyukti-vikalpānām utthānâbhāvāt. kiṃ ca, saṃvedanasyâpi sitâsitâdy-anekâkāreṣv ekasya vartane bhedâbheda-sāmastyâika-deśâdi-codyaṃ samānam evêti na dūṣaṇam. anekâkāra-vivartasyâlīkatvān na tena saha saṃvedanasya pāramārthikasya bhedâbhedâdi-cintêti cen, nanv evam itarêtarâśrayaṃ duruttaram āḍhaukate. tathā hi: tad-alīkatva-siddhāv advaya-saṃvedana-siddhis, tat-siddhau ca tad-alīkatvam iti nyāyāt. anyac câdvayam apy eka-kṣaṇa-varti saṃvedanaṃ yathā pūrvôttara-kṣaṇābhyāṃ sambandham anubhavati, tathā niraṃśā api yadi paramâṇavo dig-aṃśaiḥ paramâṇv-antarair vā saṃśleṣamāgaccheyuḥ kim ayuktaṃ syāt. na câvayavy-avayavayor ekânta-vyatirekâvyatireka-pakṣe yad dūṣaṇaṃ tad asmat-pakṣa-bādhā-karaṃ, parasparâvinirluṭhita-rūpayor vivakṣayā sandarśanīya-bhedayos tayor abhyupagamād, bahir antaś ca tathâiva prakāśamānatayā tayor nihnotum aśakyatvāt. etena rāgârāga-kampâkampâdi-virodhôdbhāvanam api prativyūḍhaṃ, pramāṇa-prasiddhe 'rthe virodhâbhāvāt, pramāṇa-bādhitasyâiva viruddhatvāt, kuyukti-vikalpānāṃ ca pratyakṣâpahnave nirmūlatayā bādhakatvâyogāt, tad-uddalitatvenôtthānâbhāvād, bhinna-pravṛtti-nimittatvāc ca sarva-dharmānāṃ tad-viparyaya-sampādyo virodho dūrâpāsta eva. kiṃ ca, svayam eva saṃvedanaṃ paramârtha-saṃvyavahārâpekṣayā pratyakṣâpratyakṣa-savikalpakâvikalpaka-bhrāntâbhrāntâdi-rūpam abhyupayato bahir-arthe viruddha-dharmâdhyāsa-pratiṣedha-buddhiḥ kevalaṃ jāḍyaṃ sūcayati. tan na pramāṇaṃ kathañcid bhrāntaṃ samasti, svarūpa-pracyava-prasaṅgād iti sthitam.
children.translated_text: Here is the counter-argument: The claim that non-dual awareness is ultimately real while [cognition] manifesting in apprehended-apprehender form is non-ultimate—that is untenable, for lack of a <s>pramāṇa</s>. For cognition is observed to manifest externally and internally in manifold forms, with transformations of apprehension accompanied by diverse properties such as joy, sorrow, stability, density, and so on; but no one ever, at any time, experiences cognition of the kind you describe—devoid of the forms of known and knower. For even in the dream state the appearance of non-duality is never experienced. And even truth-investigators, when they establish their own intention without a <s>pramāṇa</s>, do not deserve the attention of the discerning; otherwise, one who says that from ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) a single, unconscious, immutable <s>Brahman</s> manifests as a multiplicity of conscious, momentarily perishing [things] would be irrefutable. As for the objection raised through the analysis of whole and parts with a view to refuting external objects—that too, since its body is shattered by the pestle of the well-known appearance manifest both externally and internally, is like the oath of a deceitful procuress in front of one who has seen [her client] spitting out food in mid-meal, and does not charm the minds of the learned; for when the appearance of perception is denied, there is no ground for the arising of sophistic constructions, since they are rooted in that [perception]. Moreover, the same objections regarding difference, non-difference, entirety, and partial subsistence apply equally to awareness itself when a single [awareness] is held to subsist in manifold forms such as white, dark, etc., so this is no refutation. If [one says:] 'Since the manifold-formed manifestation is false, there is no consideration of difference or non-difference between it and the ultimately real awareness'—then surely this unavoidably incurs the charge of mutual dependence (<s>itaretarāśraya</s>). For: the establishment of non-dual awareness depends on the establishment of the falsity of that [duality], and the establishment of that falsity depends on the establishment of that [non-dual awareness]—such is the logical situation. Furthermore, just as non-dual awareness, though existing in a single moment, experiences connection with prior and subsequent moments, so too if partless atoms were to come into conjunction with directional portions or with other atoms, what would be wrong with that? And the objection raised against the strict positions of difference or non-difference of whole and parts does not damage our position, since we accept both [whole and parts] as having mutually non-excluded natures, to be pointed out as different according to context, since both manifest thus externally and internally and cannot be denied. By this, the charge of contradiction regarding colored/uncolored, trembling/not-trembling, etc. is also repelled: there is no contradiction in an object established by <s>pramāṇa</s>; only what is contradicted by <s>pramāṇa</s> is truly contradictory; and sophistic constructions, being rootless when perception is denied, are incapable of being contradictors, since they cannot arise having been uprooted by it; and since all <s>dharmas</s> have distinct grounds for their operation, the contradiction produced by [assuming] the opposite is far removed indeed. Moreover, when one accepts that awareness itself assumes the forms of perceptual/non-perceptual, conceptual/non-conceptual, erroneous/non-erroneous, etc. with respect to the ultimate and the conventional, the notion of prohibiting the superimposition of contradictory properties on external objects merely betrays dullness. Therefore, a <s>pramāṇa</s> is in no way erroneous—since that would entail the loss of its very nature. This is established.

children.text: nanu ca tad-darśitârthâlīkatayā jñānasya bhrāntatā, na svarūpeṇa, na ca tad-udaya-samaye kasyacid idam alīkârtham idaṃ tv analīkârtham iti vivekenâvadhāraṇaṃ samasti, bhrāntâbhrāntâbhimatayos tad-eka-rūpatayā prakāśanāt. yadā ca viśada-darśana-patha-cāriṇo 'pi śaśa-dhara-yugalâdayo 'līkatām āviśanto dṛśyante, tadā sakala-satyârthatâbhimata-pratibhāseṣv apy alīkârthatâśaṅkânivṛtter anāśvāsa eva. na ca tad-artha-prāpty-ādikam ārekā-nirākaraṇa-kāraṇaṃ kalpanīyaṃ, svapnâvasthāyāṃ tat-sadbhāve 'py alīkârthatā-siddheḥ. bādhaka-pratyayôpanipātāt tasyâsatyârthatêti cen, na, tasya sva-gocara-paryavasitatvena bādhakatvâyogāt. anyathā nīlam ādadānā devadatta-buddhiḥ prāk-pravṛtta-pīta-buddher bādhikâpadyeta. sarva-pratibhāsasya bādhakâbhāva-siddheś ca samānatā. tasmād bhrāntâbhrānta-jñāna-bhrāntir iyaṃ bhavatāṃ, vivekâbhāvena sarvasyâlīkârthatvād iti.
children.translated_text: [The Yogācāra replies:] 'The erroneousness of cognition is due to the falsity of the object it presents, not in its own nature. And at the time of its arising, no one has the discriminating determination that "this has a false object" and "this has a real object," since both what is considered erroneous and what is considered non-erroneous appear in the same form. And when even things that are within the range of clear vision, like a double moon, are seen to be false, there can be no reassurance against the suspicion of false-objecthood even in appearances taken to be entirely real. Nor should one suppose that the attainment of the object, etc. is a reason to ward off [the charge of falsity], since falsity of the object is established even in the dream state where such [attainment] obtains.' If [one says] 'Its false-objecthood [is known only] from the occurrence of a sublating cognition (<s>bādhaka-pratyaya</s>)'—no, because that [sublating cognition] terminates in its own domain and therefore cannot be a sublator [of the prior cognition]; otherwise, a cognition of <s>Devadatta</s> apprehending blue would become the sublator of a previously arisen cognition of yellow. And since for all appearances there is equally no sublator—[the Yogācāra concludes:] 'Therefore this belief of yours in erroneous and non-erroneous cognition is itself an error, since due to the absence of a discriminating criterion, all [appearances] have false objects.'
Since the erroneousness of all appearances is not established, it is clear
that a <s>pramāṇa</s>, which ascertains both self and other, is established when both [its validity and non-erroneousness] are established. || NA_7 ||

And thus other [cognitions] of the same kind too would be non-erroneous. Therefore,

children.translated_text: Having thus explained the definition of inference-for-oneself (<s>svārthānumāna</s>) and refuted the error and misunderstanding of those who possess it, now — since the definition of inference-for-others (<s>parārthānumāna</s>), which has not yet been explained, requires only a brief statement — he first states the definition of verbal testimony (<s>śābda</s>):
From a sentence that is uncontradicted by what is perceived and intended,
and that communicates the highest truth — the knowledge born from its capacity to convey reality is declared to be verbal <s>pramāṇa</s> (testimonial valid knowledge). NA_8

children.text: pasargârthena śābde parasyâprāmāṇya-buddhiṃ tiras-kurute, tad-aprāmāṇye parârthânumāna-pralaya-prasaṅgāt, tasya vacana-rūpatvāt. try-avayava-hetu-sūcakatvenôpacāratas tasya prāmāṇyaṃ, na tattvata iti cen, nâpramāṇasya sūcakatvâyogāt. nanu ca hetu-pratipādane yadi tat pramāṇaṃ, tato hetu-samarthaka-pramāṇântara-pratīkṣaṇaṃ viśīryeta, tenâiva nirṇīta-svarūpatvāt tasya, pramāṇa-prasiddhe punaḥ pramāṇântara-vaiyarthyāt. nâitad asti, bhavat-parikalpitâdhyakṣasyâpy aprāmāṇya-prasaṅgāt: tad-darśite 'rthe vikalpa-pratīkṣaṇāt tasyâiva prāmāṇyam āsajyeta. tad-gṛhītam evârtham asāv abhilāpayatîti cec chabda-pratipāditaṃ hetuṃ pramāṇântaraṃ samarthayata iti samāno nyāyaḥ.
children.translated_text: included within it, he dispels the other party's notion that verbal testimony lacks <s>prāmāṇya</s> (validity); for if verbal testimony were invalid, inference-for-others would collapse, since it has the form of a verbal statement. If one objects that verbal testimony is valid only figuratively, as indicating a three-membered proof-reason (<s>hetu</s>), and not in reality — this is not so, because something that is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> cannot serve as an indicator. Objection: if it is a <s>pramāṇa</s> with respect to establishing the reason, then the expectation of another <s>pramāṇa</s> to validate the reason would be undermined, since its nature is already determined by that very [testimony]; and when something is already established by a <s>pramāṇa</s>, another <s>pramāṇa</s> becomes superfluous. This is not so, because the same absurdity would apply to the perception (<s>adhyakṣa</s>) postulated by you: since deliberation (<s>vikalpa</s>) is expected for the object shown by it, the same <s>prāmāṇya</s> would apply to that alone. If you say that [perception] merely makes one verbalize the object already grasped by it — then the same logic applies: another <s>pramāṇa</s> validates the reason conveyed by verbal testimony.

children.text: śābdaṃ ca dvidhā bhavati: laukikaṃ śāstra-jaṃ cêti. tatrêdam dvayor api sādhāraṇaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ pratipāditaṃ. samarthanaṃ punar avipratāraka-vacana-prabhavasyêhâdi-vākya-prastāva eva laukikasya vihitaṃ, śāstra-jasya tu vidhātavyam iti yādṛśaḥ śāstrāt taj-jātaṃ pramāṇatām anubhavati tad darśayati:
children.translated_text: Verbal testimony is of two kinds: worldly and scripture-born. Here, the definition stated applies commonly to both. The validation of the worldly kind, arising from non-deceptive speech, has been done in the context of sentences such as 'here' and the like; but for the scripture-born kind, it must still be done. He now shows what kind of scripture gives rise to [knowledge that] attains the status of <s>pramāṇa</s>:
Originated by one who is <s>āpta</s> (authoritative and trustworthy), not to be overridden, not contradicting what is perceived or intended,
teaching reality, universal — [such] scripture is the shattering of false paths. NA_9

children.text: ādāv upalabdham. anenâpauruṣeyâpoham āha, tasya pramāṇa-bādhitatvāt, puruṣa-vyāpārâbhāve vacanânupalabdher, upalambhe 'pi tad-arthânavagamāt, tad-artha-niścayârthaṃ puruṣâśrayaṇe gaja-snāna-nyāya-prasaṅgāt, tasya rāgâdi-kaluṣitatvena vitathârtha-kathana-pravṛtteḥ. tad-anuṣṭhānād api sva-kārya-siddhau praṇayanârtham api puruṣaḥ kiṃ nêṣyate, viśeṣâbhāvāt. tan na kṣīṇa-doṣa-vacanaṃ vyatiricyânyataḥ prekṣāvatāṃ para-lokâdāv adṛṣṭe 'rthe pravṛttir yuktā; tat tad eva śāstraṃ, nirupacarita-śabdârthôpapatter ity āstāṃ tāvat.
children.translated_text: means: first perceived [or composed]. By this, he rejects the doctrine of <s>apauruṣeyatva</s> (authorlessness [of the Veda]), since it is contradicted by <s>pramāṇa</s>: in the absence of human activity, speech cannot be apprehended; even if apprehended, its meaning cannot be understood; and if one resorts to a person for determining its meaning, the fallacy of 'the elephant's bath' (futile effort) arises, since that person, being sullied by passion and the like, would tend to speak false meanings. If one argues that even from following such [authorless scripture] one achieves one's purpose — then why not accept a person [as author] for the sake of composition as well, since there is no difference? Therefore, apart from the speech of one whose defects are destroyed, no activity of discerning persons toward unseen objects such as the next world is justified; hence that alone is scripture — since the meaning of words can be established without figurative usage. But let that rest for now.

children.text: adhunā parârthânumāna-lakṣaṇaṃ vaktavyam, tac ca pratyakṣe 'pi paśyann eka-yoga-kṣematvāt sāmānyenâha:
children.translated_text: Now the definition of inference-for-others (<s>parārthānumāna</s>) is to be stated; and since he sees that it applies to perception also, due to their sharing a single benefit, he states it generally:
The production in others of an ascertainment similar to one's own ascertainment —
