children.text: nanu ca yadi niścayôtpādanaṃ parârtha-mānaṃ, tathā jñānam api para-pratyāyanāya vyāpriyamānaṃ parârthaṃ prāpnotîty āha: vākyaṃ parârthaṃ, na jñānaṃ, tasyâivânantaryeṇa vyāpārāt, para-prayojana-mātratvāc ca, itarasya tu vyavahitatvāt, sva-parôpakāritvāc ca. kathaṃ vacanam ajñāna-rūpaṃ pramāṇam ity āha:
children.translated_text: Objection: if the production of ascertainment in others is <s>pramāṇa</s>-for-others, then knowledge too, when engaged in convincing others, would become 'for others' sake.' He responds: the statement (<s>vākya</s>) is [the <s>pramāṇa</s>] for others' sake, not knowledge, because only the statement operates with immediate efficacy [toward others], and because it serves merely as the other's instrument — whereas knowledge operates at a remove, and serves both oneself and others. How can a statement, which is not of the nature of knowledge, be a <s>pramāṇa</s>? He responds:

children.text: , tasya jñānasyôpacāro 'tad-rūpasyâpi tad-aṅgatayā tad-rūpatvena grahaṇam, tataḥ. idam uktaṃ bhavati: pratipādya-gatam utpatsyamānaṃ yaj jñānaṃ tad avyavahita-kāraṇatvād vacanam apy upacāreṇa pramāṇam ity ucyate. tatrânumānasya pārārthyaṃ parair abhyupagatam eva, pratyakṣasya na pratipadyante, kilêdaṃ śabda-praveśa-śūnya-svalakṣaṇa-grāhîti nâitad-gocaraḥ parebhyaḥ pratipādayituṃ pāryate. na ca śabdāt parasya svalakṣaṇa-grahaṇa-dakṣaṃ pratyakṣam unmaṅkṣyati, śabdasya vikalpôtpāditatvena parasyâpi vikalpôtpādakatvāt. tad uktaṃ:
children.translated_text: means: the figurative transfer (<s>upacāra</s>) of knowledge consists in grasping something that is not of that nature as being of that nature, by virtue of its being a component of it; from that. What is meant is this: the knowledge that will arise in the person to be instructed — because the statement is its immediate cause, the statement too is figuratively called a <s>pramāṇa</s>. In this regard, the 'for-others' character of inference is already accepted by others; but they do not accept it for perception, [arguing that] since it grasps the particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>), which is devoid of verbal access, its domain cannot be communicated to others. Nor will perception, which is capable of grasping the particular, arise in another from words, since words produce conceptual constructions (<s>vikalpa</s>) and thus produce conceptual constructions in the other as well. As it is said:
'Words are the source of conceptual constructions, and conceptual constructions are the source of words;

children.text: kārya-kāraṇatā teṣāṃ nârthaṃ śabdāḥ spṛśanty api" //
children.translated_text: there is a cause-effect relation between them — words do not touch the real object at all.'

children.text: nirvikalpakaṃ ca pratyakṣam, ato na śabda-janyam ity ato 'numānaṃ dṛṣṭântī-kṛtya pratyakṣasyâpi parārthatāṃ sādhayitum āha:
children.translated_text: And perception is non-conceptual (<s>nirvikalpaka</s>), hence it is not produced by words. Therefore, taking inference as the example, to establish that perception too can serve others' purposes, he says:
Since both perception and inference illuminate an object that is [already] established,
and since they serve as means for the other [person's cognition] — both have the character of serving others' purposes. NA_11
means: because of causing the other to cognize the knowable that one has oneself apprehended,
means: having the function of [benefiting] the person to be instructed,

children.text: pratyakṣânumānayos, tulya-kāraṇatvān, nânumānasyâivâikasyêty abhiprāyaḥ. iha câśrūyamāṇatvāt tad-artha-gamanāc câpîva-śabdau lupta-nirdiṣṭau draṣṭavyau. pratyakṣa-pratītârtha-pratyāyanaṃ ca pratijānānasyâyam abhiprāyo: yat paro manyate -- nâitad-gocaraṃ parebhyaḥ pratipādayituṃ pāryata iti -- tad ayuktaṃ, nirvikalpakâdhyakṣâpohena vyavasāya-rūpasya pratyakṣasya prāg eva sādhitatvāt, tad-gocarasya kathañcid vikalpa-gamyatvena śabda-pratipādyatvāt. tad yathânumāna-pratīto 'rthaḥ parasmai pratipādyamāno vacana-rūpâpannaḥ parârtham anumānaṃ, tathā pratyakṣa-pratīto 'pi parârthaṃ pratyakṣaṃ, para-pratyāyanasya tulyatvād, vacana-vyāpārasyâiva bhedāt. tathā hy: anumāna-pratītaṃ pratyāyayann evaṃ vacanayaty -- agnir atra dhūmād, yatra yatra dhūmas tatra tatrâgnir, yathā mahānasâdau; vaidharmyeṇa vâgny-abhāve na kvacid dhūmo, yathā jalâśayâdau, tathā ca dhūmo 'yaṃ, tasmād dhūmād agnir atrêti, avyutpanna-vismṛta-sambandhayos tathâiva pratipādayituṃ śakyatvāt. smaryamāṇe sambandhe punar evam: agnir atra dhūmôpapatter; vaidharmyeṇa: agnir atra, anyathā dhūmânupapatteḥ. pratyakṣa-pratītaṃ punar darśayann etāvad vakti: ‘paśya rāja gacchati'. tataś ca vacanād dvividhād api samagra-sāmagrīkasya pratipādyasyânumeya-pratyakṣârtha-viṣayā yataḥ pratītir ullasaty, ato dvayor api parârthatêty āha:
children.translated_text: [belongs] to both perception and inference, because the cause is the same — the purport is that it does not belong to inference alone. Here, the words 'iva' (like) and 'api' (also), though not heard [in the verse], should be understood as implicitly indicated, because the meaning requires them. The intention of one who claims that the object apprehended through perception can be communicated to others is this: what the opponent holds — that 'this domain cannot be communicated to others' — is unjustified, because it has already been established above that perception, in the form of determinate cognition (<s>vyavasāya</s>), [is valid] by excluding non-conceptual direct perception; and because its domain, being somehow accessible to conceptual thought, can be conveyed through words. Thus, just as an object apprehended through inference, when communicated to another, takes the form of a verbal statement and becomes inference-for-others, so too an object apprehended through perception [when communicated becomes] perception-for-others, since the communication to the other is the same, with only the verbal operation differing. For instance: one communicating what is apprehended through inference speaks thus: 'There is fire here because of smoke; wherever there is smoke, there is fire, as in a kitchen; or by dissimilarity: where there is no fire, there is never smoke, as in a lake; and there is this smoke, therefore from this smoke there is fire here' — since this can be conveyed in exactly this way to one who is uninstructed or has forgotten the connection. When the connection is remembered, then thus: 'There is fire here because smoke is present'; by dissimilarity: 'There is fire here, since otherwise smoke would be impossible.' But one showing what is apprehended through perception says only this much: 'Look — the king is going.' And since from both kinds of verbal statement, the cognition of the person to be instructed — when all conditions are complete — flashes forth with respect to the objects of both the inferable and the directly perceived, therefore both have the character of serving others' purposes. Thus he says:
'Because they serve as means for the other'

children.text: pratipādyasya pratītiṃ prati pratipādaka-stha-pratyakṣânumāna-nirṇītârtha-prakāśana-kāraṇatvād ity arthaḥ. etena pūrva-kārikôktôpacāra-kāraṇaṃ ca lakṣayati.
children.translated_text: means: because they are causes of the illumination of the object determined by the perception and inference residing in the instructor, for the cognition of the person to be instructed — this is the meaning. By this, he also indicates the reason for the figurative usage stated in the previous verse.

children.text: yac côktaṃ: ‘na śabdāt parasya pratyakṣôtpattis, tasya vikalpa-janakatvāt, pratyakṣasya svalakṣaṇa-viṣayatvena nirvikalpakatvāt'; -- tad ayuktaṃ, sāmānya-viśeṣâtmakârtha-viṣayasya nirṇaya-rūpasya tasya kathañcid eka-viṣayatayā śabdôtpādyatvâvirodhād, evaṃ-vidhasya ca prāg eva samarthanāt. cakṣur-ādi-sāmagrītas tad utpadyate, na śabdād iti ced, anumānam api pratyakṣâdi-niścitād dhetor avismṛta-sambandhasya pramātur ullasati, na śabdād, atas tasyâpi parârthatā viśīryeta. samartha-hetu-kathanāt tatra vacanasya parârthatêti ced, atrâpi darśana-yogyârtha-pratipādanād iti brūmaḥ. tan na pratyakṣa-parokṣayoḥ pārārthyaṃ prati viśeṣôpalabdhir iti mucyatāṃ pakṣa-pātaḥ.
children.translated_text: And as for what was stated: 'From verbal testimony, there is no arising of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), since it [verbal testimony] generates <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction), and since <s>pratyakṣa</s>, having <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> (the particular) as its object, is <s>nirvikalpaka</s> (non-conceptual)' — that is incorrect. For there is no contradiction in [<s>pratyakṣa</s>] being produced by verbal testimony, since it [<s>pratyakṣa</s>], being a determination whose object is a thing possessing both universal and particular nature, can in some manner share the same object [as verbal testimony]; and this kind [of view] has already been established earlier. If it is objected that [<s>pratyakṣa</s>] arises from the aggregate of causes such as the eye and so forth, not from verbal testimony — then <s>anumāna</s> (inference) also flashes forth in a knower whose connection [between reason and probandum] has not been forgotten, from a reason ascertained by <s>pratyakṣa</s> and other means, not from verbal testimony. Therefore, the other-serving nature of inference too would be undermined. If [you say] that verbal statement serves others there because it communicates a capable reason — here too, we say, [verbal statement serves others] because it conveys an object fit to be perceived. Therefore, no distinguishing ground is found between <s>pratyakṣa</s> and <s>parokṣa</s> (non-perceptual knowledge) with respect to serving others; so let go of partisanship.

children.text: tad evaṃ dvayor api parârthatāṃ pratipādya tat-svarūpam āha:
children.translated_text: Having thus established the other-serving nature of both [<s>pratyakṣa</s> and <s>anumāna</s>], he states their essential nature:
That verbal statement which conveys an object apprehended by <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception)
Is called <s>pratyakṣa</s>, because it is the cause of a [perceptual] manifestation. || 12 ||
that is, which is skilled in describing the domain of directly apprehending cognition —

children.text: pratyakṣa-rūpam evôcyamānaṃ pratyakṣaṃ, vipratipannaṃ prati punar anumāna-dvāreṇôcyamānam anumānam evêti ca-śabdenânekârthatvād darśayati. vacanaṃ kutaḥ pratyakṣam ity āha:
children.translated_text: when stated in the form of <s>pratyakṣa</s> itself, it is [called] <s>pratyakṣa</s>; when stated through the channel of <s>anumāna</s> to one who has misapprehended, it is <s>anumāna</s> itself — by the word "and" he indicates [that it has] multiple meanings, since [the particle] has multiple senses. Why is the verbal statement called <s>pratyakṣa</s>? He says:
"Because it is the cause of a manifestation" —
The meaning is: it is called so by metaphorical extension, because it is the cause of the illumination of the <s>pratyakṣa</s> to be conveyed.
That verbal statement which conveys a <s>hetu</s> (reason) that is invariably concomitant with the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum),
That is <s>parārthanumāna</s> (inference for the sake of others), consisting of statements of <s>pakṣa</s> (thesis) and so forth. || 13 ||
That which impels or leads [one] to an object — that is
because it is the cause of the illumination of inference,
is <s>parārtham anumānam</s> (inference for the sake of others)."

children.text: . tat kī-dṛśaṃ? ity āha: pakṣo vakṣyamāṇa-lakṣaṇaḥ sa
children.translated_text: What is its nature? He says: the <s>pakṣa</s> (thesis), which has the characteristics to be described,
of those — namely, <s>hetu</s> (reason), <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (example), <s>upanaya</s> (application), <s>nigamana</s> (conclusion), and so forth — and they are so [named]; of those,
the sounds that convey [them]; those very [sounds]
"that [inference] consists of statements of <s>pakṣa</s> and so forth."

children.text: nanu ca hetu-pratipādakaṃ vacaḥ parârtham anumānam ity abhidhāya
children.translated_text: Objection: Having stated that the verbal statement conveying the <s>hetu</s> is <s>parārtham anumānam</s> (inference for the sake of others), when he then says
"that consists of statements of <s>pakṣa</s> and so forth" —

children.text: iti vadataḥ pūrvâpara-vyāhatā vāco yuktiḥ. nâitad asty; evaṃ manyate nâikaḥ prakāraḥ parârthânumānasya, kiṃ tarhi yathā parasya sukhena prameya-pratītir bhavati tathā yatnataḥ pratyāyanīyaḥ. tatra daśâvayavaṃ sādhanaṃ pratipādanôpāyaḥ. tad yathā -- pakṣâdayaḥ pañca, tac-chuddhayaś ca. tatra yadā pratipādyaḥ prakramād eva nirṇīta-pakṣo 'vismṛta-dṛṣṭânta-smārya-pratibandha-grāhaka-pramāṇo vyutpanna-matitvāc cheṣâvayavâbhyūhana-samarthaś ca bhavati, yad vâtyantâbhyāsena parikarmita-matitvāt tāvatâiva prastuta-prameyam avabudhyate, tadā hetu-pratipādanam eva kriyate, śeṣâbhidhānasya śrotṛ-saṃskārâkāritayā nairarthakyād ity-ādau hetu-pratipādanaṃ sūtra-kṛtā parârtham anumānam uktam. yadā tu pratipādyasya nâdyâpi pakṣa-nirṇayas, tadâkāṇḍa eva hetûpanyāso 'dṛṣṭa-mudgara-pātāyamānaḥ syād iti pakṣo 'pi nirdiśyate. tathâsmaryamāṇe pratibandha-grāhiṇi pramāṇe dṛṣṭânto 'pi varṇyetânyathā hetoḥ sāmarthyânavagateḥ. smṛte 'pi pramāṇe dārṣṭāntike yojayitum ajānānasyôpanayo darśyate. tathâpi sākāṅkṣasya nigamanam ucyate, 'nyathā nirākula-prastutârthâsiddheḥ. tathā yatra pakṣâdau svarūpa-vipratipattis tatra tac-chuddhiḥ pramāṇena kartavyêtarathā teṣāṃ sva-sādhyâsādhanāt. sarveṣāṃ câmīṣāṃ sādhanâvayavatvaṃ, pratipādya-pratīty-upāyatvāt.
children.translated_text: there is a contradiction between the earlier and later parts of his speech, which is illogical. [Reply:] This is not so. His view is that <s>parārthānumāna</s> (inference for the sake of others) is not of a single type. Rather, whatever method most easily produces in the other person a cognition of the object to be proved — that method must be diligently employed for the purpose of persuasion. Therein, the ten-membered proof is the means of demonstration. It is as follows: the five [members] beginning with <s>pakṣa</s> (thesis), and their respective purifications. When the person to be persuaded has already determined the <s>pakṣa</s> from the very progression [of argument], possesses the <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) that grasps the invariable connection by recalling the <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (example), and is capable of inferring the remaining members due to his trained intellect — or when, through extensive practice, his intellect is so refined that he comprehends the matter at hand from just that much — then only the statement of the <s>hetu</s> is made, since stating the rest would be pointless, being merely a reflection of the listener's prior conditioning. Thus, in the <s>sūtra</s> [text], the author of the aphorisms called <s>parārthānumāna</s> simply the statement of the <s>hetu</s>. But when the person to be persuaded has not yet even determined the <s>pakṣa</s>, then presenting the <s>hetu</s> abruptly would be like an unseen mallet-blow; therefore the <s>pakṣa</s> too must be stated. Likewise, when the <s>pramāṇa</s> grasping the invariable connection is not being recalled, the <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> too must be described, for otherwise the capacity of the <s>hetu</s> would not be understood. Even when the <s>pramāṇa</s> is recalled, the <s>upanaya</s> (application) is shown for one who does not know how to apply it to the particular case. Even so, for one still in doubt, the <s>nigamana</s> (conclusion) is stated; otherwise the clear establishment of the matter at hand would not be achieved. Furthermore, wherever there is a misconception about the proper form of the <s>pakṣa</s> and so forth, there the purification of each must be carried out through <s>pramāṇa</s>; otherwise they would not establish what is to be proved. And all of these are members of the proof, because they are means for the cognition of the person to be persuaded.

children.text: nanu ca sva-niścayavat para-niścayôtpādanaṃ parârtham anumānam uktaṃ, na ca svârthânumāna-kāle kramo 'yam anubhūyate, sambandha-vedino hetu-darśana-mātrāt sādhya-pratīti-siddher, na hi pratipattā pakṣaṃ kṛtvā tato hetuṃ nibhālayati, nâpi dṛṣṭântâdikaṃ viracayati, tathā pratīter abhāvāt. kiṃ cânvaya-vyatirekābhyāṃ hetor eva sāmarthyam unnīyate, na pakṣâdīnāṃ, tad-vyatirekeṇâpi sādhya-siddheḥ, tathâpi teṣāṃ sādhanâṃśatva-kalpane 'navasthā-prasaṅgāt. yadi ca tat-sāmarthyaṃ syāt, tadā pakṣôpanyāsa-mātrād eva sādhyâvagater hetur ānarthakyam aśnuvīta, uttarâvayavāś ca, evaṃ hi tat-sāmarthyaṃ siddhyen nânyathā. tasmād ya eva para-nirapekṣaṃ sādhyaṃ bodhayati sa eva hetuḥ sādhanaṃ, na pakṣâdaya iti.
children.translated_text: Objection: It has been said that <s>parārtham anumānam</s> (inference for the sake of others) is producing in another a determination similar to one's own determination. But this sequential procedure [of <s>pakṣa</s>, <s>hetu</s>, etc.] is not experienced at the time of <s>svārthānumāna</s> (inference for one's own sake), since for one who knows the invariable connection, the cognition of the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum) is established merely from perceiving the <s>hetu</s> (reason). For the cognizer does not first formulate the <s>pakṣa</s> and then examine the <s>hetu</s>, nor does he construct the <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (example) and so forth, since cognition does not occur in that manner. Moreover, it is through positive and negative concomitance that the capacity of the <s>hetu</s> alone is inferred, not of the <s>pakṣa</s> and so forth, since the <s>sādhya</s> is established even without them. Even so, if one tries to posit them as parts of the proof, there would be an infinite regress. And if they did possess such capacity, then the <s>sādhya</s> would be cognized from the mere statement of the <s>pakṣa</s> alone, rendering the <s>hetu</s> useless, and the subsequent members too — for only thus would their capacity be established, not otherwise. Therefore, that alone which communicates the <s>sādhya</s> independently of others is the <s>hetu</s>, the proof — not the <s>pakṣa</s> and so forth.

children.text: atrôcyate -- ‘sva-niścayavat para-niścayôtpādanaṃ parârtham anumānam uktam'; ity-ādi yad uktaṃ tad yuktam uktaṃ, kevalaṃ tad-arthaṃ na jānīṣe, niścayâpekṣayâiva ‘vat'-inā tulyatâbhidhānān; na punaḥ sarva-sāmānyam abhipretam, anyathā dhvanim anuccārayan svârthânumāne sādhyam avabudhyata iti, tad-anuccāraṇena para-niścayôtpādanaṃ prasajyeta. na câitad asti, śabdânuccāraṇe para-pratipādanâsambhavāt, tad-arthaṃ śabdâṅgī-karaṇe yena yena vinā para-pratipādanâsambhavas tat tad urarī-kartavyaṃ, samāna-nyāyāt. na ca pakṣâdi-virahe pratipādya-viśeṣaḥ pratipādayituṃ śakyo, hetu-gocarâdi-tat-sādhyârtha-pratīti-vikalatayā tasya sākāṅkṣatvāt. tathā ca bubhutsitârtha-bodhâbhāvād apratyāyita eva tiṣṭhed; atas tad-bodhanârthaṃ pakṣâdayo darśanīyā iti te 'pi sādhanâṃśāḥ syuḥ. yac côktam: anvaya-vyatirekânukaraṇâbhāvān na sādhanaṃ, hetu-mātrād api sādhya-siddhes, tad ayuktam, avipratārakatā-niścita-puruṣa-vacana-mātrād apy agnir atrêty-ādi-rūpāt kvacit prameyo 'rthaḥ sidhyatîti hetor apy asādhanatā-prasaṅgāt. tad-viraheṇâpi sādhya-siddheḥ. yuktaṃ câitad, avipratāraka-vacanasya prāg eva prāmāṇya-prasādhanāt. yac côktam: yady amīṣāṃ sāmarthyaṃ syāt, tadā pakṣa-mātrād eva sādhya-pratīter hetor vaiyarthyaṃ syād iti, tad ayuktataraṃ, bhavat-pakṣe 'pi samānatvāt, tatrâpi samartha-hetûpanyāsād eva sādhyâvagater, anyathā samarthatâyogāt. paścāt tasyâiva pramāṇena samarthanaṃ sarvatra gṛhīta-vyāptikasya ca punaḥ pakṣa-dharmiṇy upasaṃharaṇam anarthakatāṃ prāpnuvat kena nivāryeta? tad-abhāve hetoḥ sāmarthyaṃ nâvagamyate, tena sārthakam iti cet, pakṣâdīn api virahayya pratipādya-viśeṣaḥ pratipādayituṃ na pāryata iti teṣām api sārthakatā na durupapādêti mucyatām āgrahaḥ. tasmād dhetuvat pakṣâdayo 'pi sādhanaṃ, hetor api kvacit pratipādye tad-apekṣatayā nirapekṣatâsiddher iti. tad idaṃ sakalam ākalayyôktaṃ
children.translated_text: To this we reply: As for what was said — 'producing in another a determination similar to one's own determination is called <s>parārtham anumānam</s>' — and so forth, that was correctly stated. Only you do not understand its meaning. For the comparison by means of the suffix '-vat' ('like') is stated only with reference to the determination [itself, not the entire process]. It is not intended to mean complete identity [of process]. Otherwise, since in <s>svārthānumāna</s> one comprehends the <s>sādhya</s> without uttering a sound, it would follow that producing determination in another could also be done without uttering a sound. But this is not the case, since without the utterance of words, conveying [knowledge] to another is impossible. For the purpose of that [communication], verbal expression must be accepted. And whatever [element] without which conveying [knowledge] to another is impossible — that [element] must be admitted, by parity of reasoning. Without the <s>pakṣa</s> and so forth, the specific matter to be conveyed cannot be demonstrated, because without them, cognition of the domain of the <s>hetu</s> and the object to be proved thereby remains incomplete, leaving the hearer in doubt. And thus, since the desired object would not be understood, [the hearer] would remain unpersuaded. Therefore, the <s>pakṣa</s> and so forth must be presented for the purpose of communicating that [knowledge], and thus they too are parts of the proof. As for the objection that [the <s>pakṣa</s> etc.] are not [parts of the] proof because they do not follow the pattern of positive and negative concomitance, and because the <s>sādhya</s> is established from the <s>hetu</s> alone — that is incorrect. For even from the mere words of a person known to be trustworthy, without [formal proof], a knowable object of the form 'there is fire here' and so forth is sometimes established; thus the same absurd consequence would apply to the <s>hetu</s> itself — that it too is not a proof, since the <s>sādhya</s> is established even without it. And this is reasonable, since the authority of trustworthy speech has been established already. As for the objection that if [<s>pakṣa</s> etc.] had such capacity, then the <s>sādhya</s> would be cognized from the mere statement of the <s>pakṣa</s>, rendering the <s>hetu</s> useless — that is even more unreasonable, since the same [objection] applies equally to your own position. For there too, the <s>sādhya</s> is cognized from the presentation of a capable <s>hetu</s> alone; otherwise, it could not have the capacity [you attribute to it]. The subsequent corroboration of that very [<s>hetu</s>] through <s>pramāṇa</s>, and the re-application of the already-grasped <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) to the <s>pakṣadharmin</s> (subject of the thesis) — [on your view] these would turn out to be useless. By what would they be prevented [from being useless]? If [you say] that without them the capacity of the <s>hetu</s> is not understood, and therefore they are purposeful — then the <s>pakṣa</s> and so forth too: without them, the specific matter to be proved cannot be demonstrated, so their purposefulness too is not difficult to establish. Therefore, let go of your stubbornness. Hence, like the <s>hetu</s>, the <s>pakṣa</s> and so forth are also [parts of the] proof, since even the <s>hetu</s>, in certain cases of proving, requires them, and its independence is not established. Comprehending all this, he said:
"That [inference] consists of statements of <s>pakṣa</s> and so forth" —

children.text: tad evam arthataḥ pakṣâdīn prastutya tāvat pakṣa-lakṣaṇam āha:
children.translated_text: Having thus presented the <s>pakṣa</s> and so forth with respect to their substance, he first states the definition of <s>pakṣa</s> (thesis):
The <s>pakṣa</s> is the acceptance of the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum), not contradicted by <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and other [means of valid knowledge];
Therein, the employment of that [<s>pakṣa</s>] must be made, as it illuminates the domain of the <s>hetu</s> (reason). || 14 ||

children.text: pacyata iti pakṣo, vyaktī-kriyata iti-bhāvaḥ. kiṃ-bhūta ity āha:
children.translated_text: That which is 'cooked' (examined) — that is the <s>pakṣa</s>; meaning: that which is made manifest. Of what nature? He says:
that is, of the object to be inferred —

children.text: 'ṅgī-karaṇaṃ, prāśnikâdīnāṃ purataḥ pratijñā-svī-kāra ity arthaḥ. kim abhyupagama-mātram? nêty āha:
children.translated_text: the acknowledgment; meaning: the undertaking of a <s>pratijñā</s> (proposition) before the examiners and others. Is it mere acceptance? No, he says:
"Not contradicted by <s>pratyakṣa</s> and other [means of valid knowledge]" —
<s>anumāna</s> (inference), one's own prior statement, and common consensus are included; by these,

children.text: 'bādhitaḥ pakṣa iti sambandhaḥ. tad yathā -- ‘sarvam anekântâtmakam', ‘asti sarva-jña'; ity-ādi vā. ayaṃ ca kevalam eṣṭavyo, na punaḥ parârthânumāna-kāle vacanenâbhidhātavya iti yo manyeta taṃ pratyāha:
children.translated_text: not refuted — that is the <s>pakṣa</s>: this is the syntactic connection. For example: 'All things are of manifold nature (<s>anekāntātmaka</s>),' or 'The <s>sarvajña</s> (omniscient being) exists' — and so forth. Now, one might think that this [<s>pakṣa</s>] should merely be intended [mentally], and need not be verbally stated at the time of <s>parārthānumāna</s>. To counter that, he says:
in the context of <s>parārthānumāna</s> (inference for the sake of others) —

children.text: vidheyaḥ. kuta ity āha: hetoḥ prāṅ-nirūpitasya
children.translated_text: must be carried out. Why? He says: "Of the <s>hetu</s>," as previously defined,

children.text: iti, ‘nimitta-kāraṇa-hetuṣu sarvāsāṃ prāyo darśanam'; iti-vacanād, bhāva-pradhānatvāc ca nirdeśasya, viṣaya-sandarśakatvād ity arthaḥ. ayam atrâbhiprāyo: na hi sarvatra prativādinaḥ prakramād eva nirṇīta-pakṣasya kūrca-śobhā-puraḥ-saraṃ hetur upanyasyate, 'pi tu kvacit kathañcit.
children.translated_text: thus. Since, according to the statement 'among the terms <s>nimitta</s>, <s>kāraṇa</s>, and <s>hetu</s>, usage of all [these synonyms] is generally seen,' and since the expression is primarily about the entity [rather than the agent], the meaning is: because it reveals the domain [of the <s>hetu</s>]. The intent here is this: it is not the case that everywhere the <s>hetu</s> is presented to the opponent with the preliminary flourish of one whose <s>pakṣa</s> has already been determined from the progression [of argument]; rather, sometimes and in some manner [the <s>pakṣa</s> must be stated explicitly].

children.text: tato yadâdyâpi pratipādyaḥ pakṣârthaṃ na jānīte, tadâkāṇḍa eva hetāv ucyamāne viṣaya-vyāmohād bhrānti-lakṣaṇo doṣaḥ syād ity āha:
children.translated_text: Therefore, when the person to be persuaded does not yet even know the content of the <s>pakṣa</s>, then if the <s>hetu</s> is stated abruptly, there would arise the fault characterized as confusion due to bewilderment about the domain [of the <s>hetu</s>]. He states this:
Otherwise, for the person to be persuaded, who is confused about the intended domain of the <s>hetu</s> of the proponent,
The <s>hetu</s> would appear to be tainted with the flaw of being contradictory. || 15 ||
this means: in the contrary case, i.e., when the <s>pakṣa</s> is not stated — this is the meaning.
that is, accepted by him, and [it is] that

children.text: ; tatra muhyati dolāyate tac chīlaś ca yas, tasya
children.translated_text: one who is confused therein, who vacillates — having that disposition; of such
"would appear tainted with the flaw of being contradictory" —

children.text: virodha-śaṅkā-kalaṅkitaḥ syād ity arthaḥ. tataś ca samyag-ghetāv api ‘vipakṣa evâyaṃ vartata'; iti vyāmohād viruddha-dūṣaṇam abhidadhīta, pakṣôpanyāsāt tu nirṇīta-hetu-gocarasya nâiṣa doṣaḥ syād ity abhiprāyaḥ. amum evârthaṃ spaṣṭa-dṛṣṭântenâha
children.translated_text: meaning: it would be blemished by the suspicion of contradiction. And thus, even though the <s>hetu</s> is valid, due to confusion [the opponent] might charge it with the defect of being contradictory, [thinking] 'this [<s>hetu</s>] applies only to the counter-thesis.' But if the <s>pakṣa</s> is stated, this fault would not arise for one whose domain of the <s>hetu</s> has been determined — this is the intent. He illustrates this very point with a clear example:
this is for the purpose of presenting that [example].
"For the people observing the skill of an archer who is shooting,
Without the indication of the target, [the archer's] merits [appear as] their opposites." || 16 ||

children.text: yathā lakṣya-nirdeśaṃ vinā dhānuṣkasyêṣuṃ prakṣipato yau guṇa-doṣau tau tad-darśi-janasya viparyastāv api pratibhātaḥ -- guṇo 'pi doṣatayā, doṣo 'pi vā guṇatayā -- tathā pakṣa-nirdeśaṃ vinā hetum upanyasyato vādino yau svâbhipreta-sādhya-sādhana-samarthatvâsamarthatva-lakṣaṇau guṇa-doṣau tau prāśnika-prativādyâdīnāṃ viparītāv api pratibhāta iti bhāvârthaḥ. akṣarârthas tu dhanuṣā carati
children.translated_text: Just as, without the indication of the target, for an archer releasing an arrow, the merits and defects — as seen by the observing people — appear reversed, such that even a merit appears as a defect, or a defect as a merit; so too, without the statement of the <s>pakṣa</s>, for a proponent who presents the <s>hetu</s>, the merits and defects — characterized as the capability and incapability of proving his intended <s>sādhya</s> — appear reversed to the examiners, opponents, and others. This is the purport. As for the literal meaning: one who practices with a bow —

children.text: lakṣya-vedha-prāvīṇya-lakṣaṇas tatra prekṣakāṇāṃ kutūhalam iti tasyâivôpādānam, anyathā doṣo 'pi draṣṭavyaḥ. tat-
children.translated_text: characterised by skill in hitting the target — that is what arouses the curiosity of the spectators, and hence only that is taken up; otherwise, a fault too must be observed. That —
of the world accustomed to observing that,

children.text: yathā -- kathañcid bāṇaṃ muñcata ity arthaḥ;

children.translated_text: of the archer, without indicating the target —
of the bow-bearer, without fixing on the object to be pierced,

children.text: guṇa-doṣau tau yathā viruddhārekitau bhavatas, tathā vādino 'pîty arthaḥ. tasmād avijñāta-tad-arthe prativādini vādi-dhānuṣkeṇa pakṣa-lakṣyaṃ nirdiśyâiva hetu-śaraḥ proktavya iti sthitam.
children.translated_text: that is, merit and fault — just as these two are contradictorily related (for the archer), so too for the debater. Therefore, it is established that the debater-archer must indicate the target of the thesis (<s>pakṣa</s>) before releasing the arrow of the reason (<s>hetu</s>), when the opponent does not know the intended meaning.

children.text: sāmprataṃ hetor lakṣaṇâvasaras, tac ca svârthânumānavan nirviśeṣaṃ draṣṭavyaṃ; prayogas tu tatra na darśitaḥ, svârthânumānasya bodha-rūpatvād; iha tu darśanīyaḥ, parârthânumānasya vacana-rūpatvād; atas taṃ darśayati:
children.translated_text: Now is the occasion for the definition of the reason (<s>hetu</s>), and this should be seen as no different from inference for oneself (<s>svārthānumāna</s>); however, the formulation (<s>prayoga</s>) was not shown there, since inference for oneself has the nature of cognition; but here it must be shown, since inference for another (<s>parārthānumāna</s>) has the nature of verbal statement. Therefore he presents it:

children.text: hetos tathôpapattyā vā syāt prayogo 'nyathâpi vā /
children.translated_text: The formulation of the reason may be either by its positive concomitance, or otherwise; || NA_17 ||
the proof of the provable (<s>sādhya</s>) may be accomplished by either of the two kinds.

children.text: svârthânumāna-prastāve hi para-praṇīta-lakṣaṇântara-vyapohena sādhya-vyatirekāt sāmastyena hetor vyāvṛttir evâikaṃ lakṣaṇam iti nirṇītam. parârthânumāne 'pi tad eva prakāśanīyaṃ, vacana-racanā tu kvacit kathañcit pravartata ity abhiprāyavāṃs tad-dvaividhyam āha: hetor dvividhaḥ prayogaḥ syād iti sambandhaḥ. katham ity āha:
children.translated_text: In the context of inference for oneself (<s>svārthānumāna</s>), by refuting alternative definitions proposed by others, it was determined that the sole definition of the reason (<s>hetu</s>) is, collectively, its invariable exclusion from what is other than the provable (<s>sādhya</s>). In inference for another (<s>parārthānumāna</s>) too, the same must be made manifest; but the verbal formulation may proceed in different ways in different contexts — with this intention, he states its twofold nature: 'The formulation of the reason is of two kinds' — this is the connection. How? He says:
precisely in the presence of the provable (<s>sādhya</s>),
i.e. the existence; by means of that,
as in: 'There is fire here, because smoke obtains precisely thus' — i.e. through its positive concomitance.
by this, through the figure of speech of applying the collective term to a part, he indicates the impossibility of being otherwise (<s>anyathānupapatti</s>).
in the absence of the provable (<s>sādhya</s>), non-obtaining, i.e. non-existence itself; by means of that,

children.text: nyathânupapattyā hetoḥ prayogaḥ syād, yathâgnir atra, dhūmasyânyathânupapatter iti. ‘ete ca dve apy ekasmin sādhye prayoktavye'; iti yo manyeta,tac-chiṣyaṇârthaṃ āh
children.translated_text: by the impossibility of being otherwise, the formulation of the reason would be, as in: 'There is fire here, because of the impossibility of smoke being otherwise.' And lest someone think: 'Both of these must be formulated for one and the same provable,' to instruct such a person he says:
either by the formulation of positive concomitance or by the formulation of the impossibility of being otherwise,
i.e. the meaning one wishes to establish,
i.e. the completion — the ascent to the cognition of what is to be established — would occur.

children.text: yasmāt, tasmān na dve api prayoktavye, prayoga-dvaye 'pi yasmād vacana-racanā bhidyate, nârthaḥ; prayogasya ca sādhya-sādhanaṃ phalaṃ; tac ced ekenâiva sidhyati, dvitīya-prayogaḥ kevalaṃ vaktur akauśalamācakṣīta, nairarthakyād ity abhiprāyaḥ.
children.translated_text: therefore both need not be formulated, because even though the verbal formulation differs in a twofold formulation, the meaning does not; and the purpose of the formulation is the establishment of the provable; if that is accomplished by just one, the second formulation would merely indicate the speaker's lack of skill, since it would be pointless — this is the intention.

children.text: adhunā dṛṣṭânta-lakṣaṇâvasaraḥ. sa ca dvedhā: sādharmyeṇa vaidharmyeṇa ca. tatra sādharmya-dṛṣṭântam adhikṛtyâha:
children.translated_text: Now is the occasion for the definition of the example (<s>dṛṣṭānta</s>). It is of two kinds: by similarity (<s>sādharmya</s>) and by dissimilarity (<s>vaidharmya</s>). Regarding the example by similarity, he says:
Where the <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) of the provable (<s>sādhya</s>) and the prover (<s>sādhana</s>) is ascertained most firmly, || NA_18 ||
that is considered the example by similarity, [employed] for the recollection of the connection.
Of the two that have been observed,
i.e. that have been perceived — by virtue of their capacity, of the provable (<s>sādhya</s>) and the prover (<s>sādhana</s>),
determination — the establishment of the relation of provable and prover, whether by positive concomitance or by negative concomitance, having its basis in this —

children.text: ; samāno dharmo 'syêti sadharmā tad-bhāvaḥ sādharmyaṃ tena
children.translated_text: That which has a similar property is <s>sadharma</s>; its state is <s>sādharmya</s> (similarity); by that,
[is the example]. What kind is it? He says:
— that whose nature is the meaning to be investigated,
— the reason (<s>hetu</s>) that leads to it; of those two,
the <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) of the provable and the prover
— of the form 'this does not exist without that,'

children.text: atiśayena nirṇīyate sa sādharmya-dṛṣṭântaḥ. yathâgnir atra, dhūmasya tathâivôpapatter, mahānasâdivad iti. ayaṃ câvismṛta-pratibandhe prativādini na prayoktavya ity āha:
children.translated_text: i.e. is determined with special certainty — that is the example by similarity. As in: 'There is fire here, because smoke obtains precisely thus, as in a kitchen and the like.' And this should not be employed when the opponent already remembers the connection — thus he says:
this is an ablative after the elision of the <s>lyap</s> suffix, meaning: with reference to the recollection of a previously grasped but forgotten connection.

children.text: 'bhipreto 'yaṃ nītividām, nânyadā. yadā hi pratipādyo 'dyâpi sambandhaṃ sādhyâvinâbhāvitva-lakṣaṇaṃ nâvabudhyate, tadā pramāṇena sambandhaṃ grāhaṇīyo, na dṛṣṭânta-mātreṇa, na hi saha-darśanād eva kvacit sarvatrêdam amunā vinā na bhavatîti sidhyaty, atiprasaṅgāt. gṛhīte ca pratibandhe smaryamāṇe kevalaṃ hetur darśanīyaḥ, tāvatâiva bubhutsitârtha-siddher dṛṣṭânto na vācyo, vaiyarthyāt. yadā tu gṛhīto 'pi vismṛtaḥ kathañcit sambandhas, tadā tat-smaraṇârthaṃ dṛṣṭântaḥ kathyate.
children.translated_text: i.e. intended by the knowers of logic, and not otherwise. For when the person to be instructed still does not understand the connection characterised by the inseparability of the provable, then the connection must be grasped by a means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>), not merely by an example; for merely from the co-observation in some place, it does not follow that everywhere this does not exist without that, because of over-extension. And when the connection has been grasped and is being remembered, only the reason needs to be presented, since the desired meaning is accomplished by that alone — the example need not be stated, as it would be purposeless. But when a connection once grasped has somehow been forgotten, then the example is stated for the purpose of recollecting it.

children.text: nanu ca kathaṃ tri-kāla-samasta-deśa-vyāpi-sambandhâvagatiḥ? na tāvan nirṇayâtmakam api pratyakṣaṃ deśa-kālântara-saṃcariṣṇunoḥ sādhya-sādhanayoḥ sambandhaṃ nirīkṣituṃ kṣamate, sannihite 'rthe viśadâdhyavasāyena pravṛtteḥ. nâpi śabdāt tan-nirṇayas, tasya parôpadeśa-rūpatayā svârthânumānâbhāva-prasaṅgāt, tatra parôpadeśâbhāvāt, tad-abhāve sambandhâsiddes, tad-asiddhāv anumānânutthānād iti. anumānāt sambandha-grahaṇe niravadhir anavasthânuṣajyeta, sambandha-grāhiṇo 'py anumānasya punaḥ sambandhântara-grahaṇa-savyapekṣatvād iti. atrôcyate -- pratyakṣânumāne dve eva pramāṇe iti yeṣāṃ mithyâbhiniveśas, teṣāṃ eṣa doṣo nâsmākam, anvaya-vyatireka-grāhi-pratyakṣânupalambhôttara-kāla-bhāvino 'vyabhicarita-tri-kāla-vyāpi-gocarasya mati-nibandhanasyôha-saṃjñitasya pramāṇântarasya sambandha-grāhitayêṣṭatvāt, tad-aniṣṭau dṛṣṭa-vyavahāra-vilopa-prasaṅgāt, tad-vilope ca vicārânarthakya-prāpter iti. atra prakaraṇe punar anumānāt pārthakyenôho na darśitaḥ, saṅkṣipta-ruci-sattvânugraha-pravṛttatvād asya, śābdaṃ tu pṛthak samarthitaṃ, tasyâtrâiva parârthânumānôpayogitvād ity āstāṃ tāvat.
children.translated_text: But how can there be cognition of a connection pervading all times and all places? Direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>), even of the determinative kind, is not capable of examining the connection of the provable and prover when they extend to other places and times, since it operates with clear determination only regarding proximate objects. Nor is there determination from verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>), since that, being of the nature of instruction by another, would lead to the absurd consequence of there being no inference for oneself — because in that case there would be no instruction by another, and without that the connection would be unestablished, and without that established, inference would not arise. If the connection is grasped by inference, an endless regress would follow without limit, since the inference grasping the connection would itself require the grasping of yet another connection. To this we say: this fault belongs to those who wrongly insist that perception and inference are the only two means of valid knowledge — not to us, because we accept as a separate means of valid knowledge the one called <s>ūha</s> (tarka, reasoning), which has its basis in cognition (<s>mati</s>), which arises subsequent to the perception and non-perception that grasp positive and negative concomitance, and whose scope is the unfailing three-time-pervading [connection]; if that is not accepted, the absurd consequence of the collapse of observed practice would follow, and with that collapse, inquiry would become purposeless. In this treatise, however, <s>ūha</s> is not separately presented as distinct from inference, since this work proceeds with the aim of benefiting beings of concise taste; but verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>) has been separately justified, since it is useful here in inference for another — but let that be for now.
Now, presenting the example by dissimilarity, he says:
Where, in the example, it is made known that when the provable (<s>sādhya</s>) is absent, || NA_19 ||

children.text: khyāpyate yatra dṛṣṭânte vaidharmyeṇêti sa smṛtaḥ || 19 ||
children.translated_text: the prover (<s>sādhana</s>) too is impossible — that is regarded as [the example] by dissimilarity.

children.text: visadṛśo dharmo 'syêti vidharmā, tad-bhāvo vaidharmyaṃ, tena
children.translated_text: That which has a dissimilar property is <s>vidharma</s>; its state is <s>vaidharmya</s> (dissimilarity); by that,
is the example. What kind is it? He says:
i.e. what is to be inferred,
is for the purpose of restriction, with inverted word-order; and it
alone — this is to be understood here.
by the word 'iti,' [it is implied:] 'for the recollection of the connection.'

children.text: idam atrâpi sambadhnāti: asyâpi smaryamāṇe sambandhe prayogâyogād iti kim arthaṃ vismṛta-sambandha eva prativādini dṛṣṭântaḥ prayujyate, nânyadêti para-vacanâvakāśam āśaṅkyâha:
children.translated_text: He connects this here as well: since even here, when the connection is being remembered, there is no occasion for the formulation [of the example] — for what purpose then is the example employed only when the opponent has forgotten the connection, and not otherwise? Anticipating such an objection, he says:
Since the provable is established by the internal <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) alone, the external illustration || NA_20 ||

children.text: vyarthā syāt tad-asadbhāve 'py evaṃ nyāya-vido viduḥ || 20 ||
children.translated_text: would be purposeless; even in the absence of that — thus the knowers of logic know.

children.text: anyadāhi smaryamāṇe vā sambandhe prayujyetâgṛhīte vā. yady ādyaḥ pakṣaḥ, so 'yuktaḥ. yadā sarvatra sādhyâvinâbhāvinaṃ hetuṃ smarati pratipādyas, tadā pakṣe 'pi tam avabudhya kathaṃ sādhyaṃ na pratipadyeta? tataś c
children.translated_text: For otherwise, [the example] would be employed either when the connection is being remembered or when it has not been grasped. If the first alternative, that is improper. When the person to be instructed remembers the reason as invariably concomitant with the provable everywhere, then, understanding it in the thesis (<s>pakṣa</s>) as well, how would he not cognise the provable? Therefore,
the prover's being pervaded by the provable,
of what is to be inferred,
in the example-subject (<s>dṛṣṭānta-dharmin</s>), which is other than the intended subject (<s>dharmin</s>),
which has the form of showing the pervasion,

children.text: niṣprayojanā, tat-pratyāyyârthâbhāvād iti. dvitīya-pakṣasyâpi nirdoṣatāṃ nirasyann āha:
children.translated_text: i.e. without utility, since there is no meaning to be conveyed by it. Rejecting the faultlessness of the second alternative as well, he says:
'Even in the absence of that' — thus:

children.text: sambandhâgrahaṇād antar-vyāpty-abhāve 'py evam iti vyarthâiva bahir-udāhṛtiḥ. na hi saha-darśanāt kvacit sarvatra tad-rūpatā sidhyati, vyabhicāra-darśanāt. tasmād agṛhīta-sambandhe pratipādye pramāṇena pratibandhaḥ sādhyaḥ. tat-siddhau tata eva sādhya-siddher akiñcit-karī dṛṣṭântôdāhṛtir iti
children.translated_text: even in the absence of internal <s>vyāpti</s> due to the non-grasping of the connection, the external illustration is equally purposeless. For from mere co-observation in some place, the nature of that [connection] is not established everywhere, because of the observation of deviation. Therefore, when the connection has not been grasped by the person to be instructed, the invariable concomitance must be established by a means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>). Once that is established, the illustration of the example is of no avail, since the provable is established from that alone — thus

children.text: avabudhyanta iti. iha ca prakaraṇe śeṣâvayavānām upanaya-nigamana-śuddhi-pañcaka-lakṣaṇānāṃ saṅkṣipta-ruci-sattvânugraha-paratvād asya, yady api sākṣāl lakṣaṇaṃ nôktaṃ, tathâpy ata eva pratipāditâvayava-trayād buddhimadbhir unneyaṃ; yato 'vayavâpekṣayā jaghanya-madhyamôtkṛṣṭās tisraḥ kathā bhavanti. tatra hetu-pratipādana-mātraṃ jaghanyā. dvy-ādy-avayava-nivedanaṃ madhyamā. sampūrṇa-daśâvayava-kathanam utkṛṣṭā. tatrêha madhyamāyāḥ sākṣāt kathanena jaghanyôtkṛṣṭe arthataḥ sūcayati, tad-sadbhāvasya pramāṇa-siddhatvād iti.
children.translated_text: i.e. understand. And in this treatise, although the definitions of the remaining members — <s>upanaya</s> (application), <s>nigamana</s> (conclusion), and the five-fold purity — have not been directly stated, since this work is devoted to benefiting beings of concise taste, nevertheless the intelligent can infer them from the three members that have been explained; for in relation to the members, there are three kinds of discourse: minimal, middling, and excellent. Among these, the minimal consists of presenting the reason alone. The middling consists of presenting two or more members. The excellent consists of stating all ten members. Here, by directly stating the middling, he implicitly indicates the minimal and the excellent, since their existence is established by valid knowledge.

children.text: evaṃ pakṣâdi-lakṣaṇaṃ pratipādyêdānīṃ heya-jñāne saty upādeyaṃ viviktataraṃ vedyata iti tad-vyudastāḥ pakṣa-hetu-dṛṣṭântâbhāsā vaktavyāḥ. tatra tāvat pakṣa-lakṣaṇa-vyudastān pakṣâbhāsān āha:
children.translated_text: Having thus explained the definitions of the thesis (<s>pakṣa</s>) and the rest, now, since when what is to be rejected is known, what is to be accepted is understood more distinctly, the semblances (<s>ābhāsa</s>) of thesis, reason, and example — which fall short of those definitions — must be stated. Among these, he first states the semblances of the thesis that fall short of its definition:
That which is already established for the person to be instructed is a semblance of a thesis; || NA_21 ||
also that which is contradicted by perception, inference, common opinion, and one's own statement — it is regarded as being of many kinds.

children.text: pakṣa-sthānôpanyastatvāt tat-kāryâkaraṇatvāc ca pakṣavad ābhāsata iti
children.translated_text: Because it is placed in the position of a thesis and because it fails to accomplish the function of a thesis, it appears like a thesis — hence
it is a semblance of a thesis (<s>pakṣābhāsa</s>).
this is the connection. How? He says:
For the person to be instructed,

children.text: pratītāv ārūḍha eva sa pakṣâbhāsaḥ, sādhyasyâiva pakṣatvāt, siddhasya sādhanânarhatvād, atiprasakteḥ. tath
children.translated_text: i.e. has already ascended to cognition — that is a semblance of a thesis, because only what is to be proved is a proper thesis, and what is already established does not merit proof, since there would be over-extension. Likewise,
i.e. by direct perception and inferential reasons,
and by common opinion and one's own statement — that which is contradicted,

children.text: tiras-kṛto yaḥ sa pakṣâbhāsaḥ. tatra pratipādya-siddho yathā: paudgaliko ghaṭaḥ,
children.translated_text: i.e. refuted — that is a semblance of a thesis. Among these, an example of what is already established for the opponent: 'The pot is a substance' [said to a <s>Pudgalavādin</s>],

children.text: vā prati: sarvaṃ kṣaṇikam ity-ādi. pratyakṣa-bādhito yathā: niraṃśāni svalakṣaṇāni, paraspara-viviktau vā sāmānya-viśeṣāv iti. anumāna-bādhito yathā: nâsti sarva-jña iti. loka-bādhito yathā: gamyā mātā iti. sva-vacana-bādhito yathā: na santi sarve bhāvā iti.
children.translated_text: 'Everything is momentary,' and so forth. An example of what is contradicted by perception: 'Particulars (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) are partless,' or 'The universal and the particular are mutually separate.' An example of what is contradicted by inference: 'An omniscient being does not exist.' An example of what is contradicted by common opinion: 'One's mother is a fit object of sexual intercourse.' An example of what is contradicted by one's own statement: 'All entities do not exist.'

children.text: sāmprataṃ hetu-lakṣaṇaṃ smārayaṃs tad-apāstān hetv-ābhāsān āha:
children.translated_text: Now, recalling the definition of the reason, he states the semblances of the reason that fall short of it:
The definition of the reason has been declared to be the impossibility of being otherwise; || NA_22 ||
its semblance [arises] through non-cognition, doubt, and contrary cognition regarding that.
that which has the form of a distinctive property,

children.text: gamitam anekârthatvād vā pratipāditaṃ svârthânumāna-prastāve yad ut
children.translated_text: i.e. conveyed — or, due to the multiplicity of meanings, established in the context of inference for oneself — which is

children.text: vaiparītya-nirṇayo; 'pratītiś ca sandehaś ca viparyāsaś cêti dvandvaḥ; paścāt tadā saha tat-puruṣas: tais
children.translated_text: the determination of contrariety; '<s>pratīti</s> (cognition) and <s>sandeha</s> (doubt) and <s>viparyāsa</s> (error)' — this is a <s>dvandva</s> (copulative compound); then with those, a <s>tatpuruṣa</s> (determinative compound): by those —
by that non-cognition, doubt, and error,
that which has the appearance [of a valid reason]

children.text: ābhānam ābhā tasyêva samyag-ghetor ivâbhâsyêti tad-ābhas, tad-bhāvas tattā, hetv-ābhāsatā bhavatîty arthaḥ.
children.translated_text: appearance is <s>ābhā</s>; of that very thing — of a correct <s>hetu</s> (reason) — there is the appearance; thus it is <s>tad-ābhāsa</s> (that which has [mere] appearance); the state of being that is <s>tattā</s>; [thus] the meaning is that it constitutes <s>hetvābhāsatā</s> (the state of being a fallacious reason).

children.text: adhunā yena lakṣaṇena yan-nāmā hetv-ābhāso bhavati tad darśayati:
children.translated_text: Now he shows by which characteristic a fallacious reason (<s>hetvābhāsa</s>) of a given name comes about:

That which is uncognized is <s>asiddha</s> (unestablished); that which is established only otherwise is <s>viruddha</s> (contradictory); that which is compatible even otherwise here is <s>anaikāntika</s> (inconclusive). (NA_23)

children.text: viruddho yo 'nyathâpy atra yukto 'naikāntikaḥ sa tu || 23 ||
children.translated_text: That which is uncognized is <s>asiddha</s> (unestablished); that which is established only otherwise is <s>viruddha</s> (contradictory); that which is compatible even otherwise here is <s>anaikāntika</s> (inconclusive). (NA_23)
rendered beyond the reach of cognition, i.e., unascertained — that
serves to distinguish all three [types]. That which
that is, exclusively in the counter-instance (<s>vipakṣa</s>), without [establishing] the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum) —
even with the opposite of the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum) —
should be known as bearing the designation '<s>anaikāntika</s>'
(inconclusive). Therein, all reasons whatsoever that are put forward by the disciples of <s>Kaṇabhakṣa</s> (Kaṇāda), <s>Akṣapāda</s> (Gautama),

children.text: di-śiṣyakair upanyasyamānāḥ sarva eva hetavaḥ, tad yathâikântenânityaḥ śabdo nityo vā, sattvād, utpattimattvāt, kṛtakatvāt, pratyabhijñāyamānatvād ity-ādayo vivakṣayâsiddha-viruddhânaikāntikatāṃ svī-kurvantîty avagantavyam.
children.translated_text: and others — [disciples] who are established in the intellects of the one-sided (<s>ekānta</s>), contradictory, and well-known-to-every-being through <s>pramāṇa</s> — all those reasons, such as 'Sound is exclusively impermanent (or permanent), because of existence, because of being produced, because of being made, because of being re-cognized,' and so forth — these, according to [each disputant's] intention, assume the character of being unestablished, contradictory, or inconclusive. This should be understood.

children.text: tathā hy: anityâikânte tāvad asiddhāḥ sarva eva hetavaś, cākṣuṣatvavat teṣāṃ dhvanāv avidyamānatvād, asad-ādi-vyavacchedenâlīka-saṃvṛti-vikalpitatvāt, pāramārthikatve tv ekasyâneka-rūpâpattyânekânta-vādâpatteḥ, kalpanā-racita-sattākānāṃ ca sarva-śakti-viraha-rūpatayā niḥsvabhāvatvāt, tathâpi teṣāṃ sādhanatve sādhyam api niḥsvabhāvam iti khara-viṣāṇaṃ śaśa-viṣāṇasya sādhanam āpadyata iti śobhanaḥ sādhya-sadhana-vyavahāraḥ. sarva evâyam anumānânumeya-vyavahāro buddhy-ārūḍhena dharma-dharmi-nyāyena na bahiḥ-sad-asattvam apekṣate, tenâyam adoṣa iti ced, evaṃ tarhi cākṣuṣatvam api śabde buddhyâdhyāropya hetutayôcyamānaṃ nâsiddhatayôdbhāvanīyaṃ, viśeṣâbhāvāt. acākṣuṣatva-vyavacchedena cākṣuṣatvaṃ buddhyâdhyāropayituṃpāryate, na yathā kathañcin, na câsau śabde 'sty, acakṣur-grāhyatvāt tasya, tenâyam adoṣa iti cet, ko 'yam acākṣuṣatva-vyavacchedo nāma: vyavaccheda-mātraṃ nīrūpaṃ, vyavacchinnaṃ vā svalakṣaṇaṃ, vyavacchedikā vā buddhiḥ svâṃśa-magnâpi bahir-vastu-grahaṇa-rūpatayā plavamānā? nâparo vastu-dharmo yatra bhedâbheda-vikalpa-dvāreṇā dūṣaṇaṃ ditsur bhavān iti cet, tarhi sa śabde nâstîti kâiṣā bhāṣā? evaṃ hi nabhaḥ-puṇḍarīkaṃ tatra nâstîti sattvâdikam api kalpayituṃ na śakyam iti prasajyeta. kiṃ ca, te sādhana-dharmā dharmiṇi bhavanto 'pi na bhavad-darśane pratītim ārohanti, pratyakṣasya vikalpa-vikalatayā dharma-nirṇaya-śūnyatvāt, tad-uttara-kāla-bhāvinyā vāsanā-prabodha-janyāyā vikalpa-buddheḥ svâṃśa-grahaṇa-paryavasita-śarīratvena bahiḥ-svalakṣaṇe praveśâbhāvāt, tataś câpratītatvāt sarvasyâsiddhatvam.
children.translated_text: For: In the one-sided position of impermanence, to begin with, all reasons whatsoever are unestablished, because they are absent in sound just as visual perceptibility [is absent in sound]; because they are fabricated by the conceptual constructs of conventional reality through the exclusion of non-existence, etc.; and if they were ultimately real, the consequence would be the doctrine of <s>anekānta</s> (non-one-sidedness), since one thing would take on multiple forms; and because those whose existence is constructed by conceptual elaboration are devoid of intrinsic nature (<s>niḥsvabhāva</s>) due to being devoid of all capacities; and even granting that, if they serve as means of proof, then the probandum too would be devoid of intrinsic nature, and it would follow that a donkey's horn would be the means of proving a hare's horn — what a splendid establishment of the <s>sādhya-sādhana</s> (probandum-probans) relationship! If one objects: 'This entire system of <s>anumāna</s> (inference) and <s>anumeya</s> (what is to be inferred) operates through the principle of property and property-bearer as superimposed upon cognition, and does not depend on external existence or non-existence, hence there is no fault' — then in that case, visual perceptibility too, when superimposed upon sound by the intellect and stated as a reason, should not be criticized as unestablished, since there is no distinguishing ground. [If one responds:] 'Through the exclusion of non-visual-perceptibility, visual perceptibility can be superimposed by the intellect, but not in just any way, and that [visual perceptibility] does not exist in sound, since sound is not apprehensible by the eye, hence there is no fault' — [we ask:] what is this so-called exclusion of non-visual-perceptibility? Is it mere exclusion, which is formless? Or the excluded <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> (particular)? Or the excluding cognition, which, though absorbed in its own aspect, floats about in the form of grasping an external object? [If you say:] 'It is no other real property, where you wish to raise an objection through the dilemma of difference and non-difference' — then how can you say 'that does not exist in sound'? For in that case it would follow that, just as a sky-lotus does not exist there, so too existence and the like could not be imputed [to sound either]. Moreover, those proving properties, even while existing in the property-bearer, do not — in your system — ascend to cognition, because perception is devoid of the determination of properties due to the infirmity of being free from conceptual construction; and because the conceptual cognition that arises subsequently, generated by the awakening of latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), has its scope terminated in grasping its own mental aspect and has no access to the external particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>); and consequently, since everything is uncognized, everything would be unestablished.

children.text: nityâikânte 'pi dharmiṇo 'tyanta-vyatiriktānām apāramārthikānāṃ vā sva-sādhana-dharmāṇāṃ pramāṇenâpratītatvād asiddhatā draṣṭavyā, dharmiṇo 'vinirluṭhita-rūpāṇāṃ pāramārthikānāṃ sakala-dharmāṇāṃ pratyakṣâdi-pramāṇa-prasiddhatvena nihnotum aśakyatvād iti.
children.translated_text: In the one-sided position of permanence too, the unestablished character should be recognized, because the property-bearer's own proving properties — which are either entirely distinct [from it] or ultimately unreal — are not cognized by any <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge); [yet the opponent cannot deny all properties,] since the ultimately real properties of the property-bearer, whose nature has not been overturned, being well-established through <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and other <s>pramāṇas</s>, cannot be denied.

children.text: tathā viruddhatâpi pakṣa-dvaye 'pi sarva-sādhana-dharmāṇām unneyânekânta-pratibaddha-svabhāvatvena tat-sādhana-pravaṇatvāt. etac côttaratra vakṣyāmaḥ.
children.translated_text: Likewise, the contradictory character [of reasons] also [applies] in both positions, because all proving properties, being by nature bound to <s>anekānta</s> (non-one-sidedness) which can be demonstrated, tend toward proving that [non-one-sidedness]. And this we shall explain further on.

children.text: evaṃ pakṣa-dvaye 'pi nirdiśyamānāḥ sarva eva hetavo 'naikāntikatām ātmasāt-kurvanti, paraspara-viruddhâvyabhicāritvāt, samāna-yukty-upanyāsena vipakṣe 'pi darśayituṃ śakyatvāt.
children.translated_text: Thus, all reasons whatsoever, as presented in both positions, assume inconclusiveness (<s>anaikāntikatā</s>), because they are unfailing with respect to mutually contradictory [conclusions], and because through the presentation of equal reasoning they can be shown [to apply] in the counter-instance (<s>vipakṣa</s>) as well.

children.text: tathā hi: anitya-vādī nitya-vādinaṃ prati pramāṇayati. sarvaṃ kṣaṇikaṃ, sattvād, akṣaṇike krama-yaugapadyābhyām artha-kriyā-virodhād, artha-kriyā-kāritvasya ca bhāva-lakṣaṇatvāt, tato 'rtha-kriyā vyāvartamānā sva-kroḍī-kṛtāṃ sattāṃ vyāvartayed iti kṣaṇikatva-siddhiḥ. na hi nityo 'rtho 'rtha-kriyāyāṃ krameṇa pravartitum utsahate, pūrvârtha-kriyā-karaṇa-svabhāvôpamarda-dvāreṇôttara-kriyāyāṃ pravṛtter, anyathā pūrvârtha-kriyā-karaṇâvirāma-prasaṅgāt; tat-svabhāva-pracyave ca nityatâpayāty, atādavasthyasyânitya-lakṣaṇatvāt. nityo 'pi krama-vartinaṃ saha-kāri-kāraṇam artham udīkṣamāṇas tāvad asīt, paścāt tam āsādya krameṇa kāryaṃ kuryād iti cen, na, saha-kāri-kāraṇasya nitye 'kiñcit-karatvād, akiñcit-karasyâpi pratīkṣaṇe 'navasthā-prasaṅgāt. nâpi yaugapadyena nityo 'rtho 'rtha-kriyāṃ kurute, 'dhyakṣa-virodhāt. na hy eka-kālaṃ sakalāḥ kriyāḥ prārabhamāṇaḥ kaścid upalabhate; karotu vā, tathâpy ādya-kṣaṇa eva sakala-kriyā-parisamāpter dvitīyâdi-kṣaṇeṣv akurvāṇasyânityatā balād āḍhaukate, karaṇâkaraṇayor ekasmin viruddhatvād iti.
children.translated_text: For instance: the proponent of impermanence proves against the proponent of permanence: 'Everything is momentary, because of existence; for in the case of the non-momentary, causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyā</s>) would be contradicted by both succession and simultaneity; and causal efficacy is the defining characteristic of being (<s>bhāva</s>); therefore, when causal efficacy ceases, it would remove the existence that it encompasses — thus momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatva</s>) is established. For a permanent entity cannot undertake causal activity successively, since engagement in a subsequent activity requires the destruction of the nature that was [the basis of] the prior causal activity; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of non-cessation of the prior causal activity; and upon the dissolution of that nature, permanence would depart, since instability is the defining characteristic of impermanence. [If one says:] a permanent entity, while awaiting a successive auxiliary cause, first existed [without acting], and then, having obtained that [auxiliary cause], would act successively — no, because an auxiliary cause has no effect whatsoever on a permanent entity; and if something having no effect is still awaited, there would be an infinite regress. Nor does a permanent entity perform causal activity simultaneously, because that contradicts direct experience (<s>adhyakṣa</s>). For no one observes all activities being undertaken at a single moment; or even if it did [act simultaneously], still, since all activities would be completed in the very first moment, it would be impermanent by force, since in the second and subsequent moments it would not be acting — because acting and not-acting are contradictory in one and the same [entity].'

children.text: nitya-vādī punar evaṃ pramāṇayati: sarvaṃ nityaṃ sattvāt. kṣaṇike sad-asat-kālayor artha-kriyā-virodhāt, tal-lakṣaṇaṃ sattvaṃ nâvasthāṃ badhnātîti, tato nivartamānam ananya-śaraṇatayā nityatvaṃ sādhayati. tathā hi: kṣaṇiko 'rthaḥ sad vā kāryaṃ kuryāt, asad vā, gaty-antarâbhāvāt. na tāvad ādyaḥ pakṣaḥ, sama-samaya-vartini vyāpārâyogāt, sakala-bhāvānāṃ parasparaṃ kārya-kāraṇa-bhāva-prāptyâtiprasaṅgāc ca. nâpi dvitīyaḥ pakṣaḥ kṣodaṃ kṣamate, asataḥ kārya-karaṇa-śakti-vikalatvāt. anyathā śaśa-viṣāṇâdayo 'pi kārya-karaṇāyôtsaheran, viśeṣâbhāvād iti.
children.translated_text: The proponent of permanence, in turn, proves thus: 'Everything is permanent, because of existence. In the case of the momentary, causal efficacy would be contradicted in both the existent and non-existent phases; [therefore] existence (<s>sattva</s>), which has that [causal efficacy] as its defining characteristic, cannot maintain its position; and [existence], departing from there, having no other refuge, establishes permanence. For a momentary entity would either produce an effect while existent, or while non-existent, since there is no third alternative. The first position does not hold, because there can be no operation among things existing at the same moment, and because all entities would absurdly become mutually related as cause and effect. Nor does the second position withstand scrutiny, because a non-existent thing is devoid of the capacity to produce effects. Otherwise, even a hare's horns and the like would be capable of producing effects, since there would be no distinguishing ground.'

children.text: tad evam ekânta-dvaye 'pi ye ye hetavas te te yukteḥ samānatayā viruddhaṃ na vyabhicaranty; avicārita-ramaṇīyatayā mugdha-jana-dhy-āndhyaṃ côtpādayantîti virudhâvyabhicāriṇo 'naikāntikāḥ, sarva-vastu-dharmāṇāṃ vastuto 'nekânta-pratibaddhatvād iti. tasmād amī sarva eva hetavaḥ santo 'nekântam antareṇa nôpapadyanta iti tam eva pratipādayitum īśate; vimūḍha-buddhibhiḥ punaḥ vipakṣa-sādhanârtham upanyasyamānā vivakṣayâsiddha-viruddhânaikāntikatām ābibhratîti sthitam.
children.translated_text: Thus, in both one-sided positions, whatever reasons [are advanced], those very reasons, due to the equality of [the opposing] argument, do not deviate from the contradictory [conclusion]; and because of their charm when unexamined, they produce blindness in the meditation of the deluded — thus they are contradictory-unfailing and inconclusive, because all properties of all things are in reality bound to <s>anekānta</s> (non-one-sidedness). Therefore, all these reasons, being [real], cannot be sustained without <s>anekānta</s>, and hence they are capable of establishing only that [non-one-sidedness]; but when presented by those of confused intellect for the purpose of proving the counter-position, they assume — according to [each disputant's] intention — the character of being unestablished, contradictory, and inconclusive. This is established.

children.text: tad evaṃ hetv-ābhāsān pratipādya dṛṣtânta-lakṣaṇa-vyudastān dṛṣṭântâbhāsān āha:
children.translated_text: Having thus explained the fallacious reasons (<s>hetvābhāsa</s>), he now states the fallacious examples (<s>dṛṣṭāntābhāsa</s>), which are vitiated in their characteristics as examples:
The defects of examples based on positive concomitance (<s>sādharmya</s>) are stated here by the knowers of logic;
they arise from defective characteristics and include deficiency in the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum) and so forth. (NA_24)

those whose origination is from them are

children.text: ; idaṃ ca prāyikaṃ viśeṣaṇaṃ, samyag-ghetāv api vaktṛ-doṣa-vaśāt dṛṣṭântâbhāsatôpapatter, yathā: nityânityaḥ śabdaḥ, śrāvaṇatvād, ghaṭavad ity-ādi.
children.translated_text: and this is a general qualifier, since a fallacious example can arise even with a correct reason due to the fault of the speaker, as in: 'Sound is permanent/impermanent, because of being audible, like a pot' — and so forth.

children.text:
tatra sādhya-vikalo yathā: bhrāntam anumānaṃ, pramāṇatvāt, pratyakṣavat; pratyakṣasya bhrāntatā-vikalatvāt; tad-bhrāntatve sakala-vyavahārôccheda-prasaṅgāt, tad-ucchede ca pramāṇa-prameyâbhāvān na kiñcit kenacit sādhyata iti bhrānta-vādino mūkatâpanipadyeta. sādhana-vikalo yathā: jāgrat-saṃvedanaṃ bhrāntaṃ, pramāṇatvāt, svapna-saṃvedanavat; svapna-saṃvedanasya pramāṇatā-vaikalyāt tat-pratyanīka-jāgrat-pratyayôpanipāta-bādhitatvād iti. ubhaya-vikalo yathā: nâsti sarva-jñaḥ, pratyakṣâdy-anupalabdhatvāt, ghaṭavad; ghaṭasya sattvāt pratyakṣâdibhir upalabdhatvāc ca. sandigdha-sādhya-dharmo yathā: vīta-rāgo 'yaṃ, maraṇa-dharmatvād, rathyā-puruṣavad; rathyā-puruṣe vīta-rāgatvasya sandigdhatvād, viśiṣṭa-ceto-dharmāṇāṃ viśiṣṭa-vyāhārâdi-liṅga-gamyatvād rathyā-puruṣe tan-nirṇayasyâpy abhāvād iti. sandigdha-sādhana-dharmo yathā: maraṇa-dharmâyaṃ puruṣo, rāgâdimattvād, rathyā-puruṣavad; rathyā-puruṣe rāgâdimattvasya
 sandigdhatvād, vīta-rāgasyâpi tathā sambhavād iti. sandigdhôbhaya-dharmo yathâsarva-jño 'yaṃ, rāgâdimattvād, rathyā-puruṣavad; rathyā-puruṣe pradarśita-nyāyenôbhayasyâpi sandigdhatvād iti.
children.translated_text: Therein, deficient in <s>sādhya</s> is like: '<s>Anumāna</s> (inference) is erroneous, because it is a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge), like <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception)' — because <s>pratyakṣa</s> lacks the property of being erroneous; for if <s>pratyakṣa</s> were erroneous, the consequence would be the annulment of all practical activity; and upon such annulment, since there would be no <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge) and <s>prameya</s> (object of knowledge), nothing could be proved by anything, and the proponent of universal error would be reduced to silence. Deficient in <s>sādhana</s> is like: 'Waking cognition is erroneous, because it is a <s>pramāṇa</s>, like dream-cognition' — because dream-cognition lacks the property of being a <s>pramāṇa</s>, since it is contradicted by the waking cognition that arises as its opposite. Deficient in both is like: 'There is no omniscient being, because of non-apprehension by <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and other [<s>pramāṇas</s>], like a pot' — because the pot exists and is apprehended by <s>pratyakṣa</s> and other [<s>pramāṇas</s>]. Having a doubtful <s>sādhya</s>-property is like: 'This person is free from passion, because of being subject to death, like a person in the street' — because freedom from passion in a person in the street is doubtful, since the special qualities of mind are knowable through special indicators such as distinctive conduct, and there is no such determination regarding a person in the street. Having a doubtful <s>sādhana</s>-property is like: 'This person is subject to death, because of possessing passion (<s>rāga</s>) and the like, like a person in the street' — because the possession of passion and the like in a person in the street is doubtful, since even one free from passion could be [in the street] likewise. Having both properties doubtful is like: 'This person is not omniscient, because of possessing passion and the like, like a person in the street' — because both [properties] are doubtful in a person in the street, by the reasoning already shown.

children.text: nanu ca parair anyad api dṛṣṭântâbhāsa-trayam uktam, tad yathânanvayo 'pradarśitânvayo viparītânvayaś cêti. tatrânanvayo yathā: rāgâdimān vivakṣitaḥ puruṣo, vaktṛtvād, iṣṭa-puruṣavad iti. yady api kilêṣṭa-puruṣe rāgâdimattvaṃ vaktṛtvaṃ ca sādhya-sādhana-dharmau dṛṣṭau, tathâpi yo yo vaktā sa sa rāgâdimān iti vyāpty-asiddher ananvayo 'yaṃ dṛṣṭântaḥ. tathâpradarśitânvayo yathânityaḥ śabdaḥ, kṛtakatvād, ghaṭavad iti. atra yady api vāstavo 'nvayo 'sti, tathâpi vādinā vacanena na prakāśita ity apradarśitânvayo dṛṣṭântaḥ. viparitânvayo yathânityaḥ śabdaḥ, kṛtakatvād iti hetum abhidhāya yad anityaṃ tad kṛtakaṃ ghaṭavad iti, viparīta-vyāpti-darśanād viparītânvayaḥ, sādharmya-prayoge hi sādhanaṃ sādhyâkrāntam upadarśanīyam, iha tu viparyāsa-darśanād viparītatā. tad etad bhavadbhiḥ kasmān nôktam iti.
children.translated_text: Now, others have stated an additional triad of fallacious examples (<s>dṛṣṭāntābhāsa</s>), namely: the one lacking positive concomitance (<s>ananvaya</s>), the one with undemonstrated positive concomitance (<s>apradarśitānvaya</s>), and the one with reversed positive concomitance (<s>viparītānvaya</s>). Among these, the one lacking positive concomitance is illustrated as follows: 'The person under discussion possesses <s>rāga</s> (passion) and so forth, because of being a speaker, like a desired person.' Although in the desired person both the properties to be proved and the proving property — namely, possession of passion and being a speaker — are observed, nevertheless, since the pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>) 'whatever is a speaker possesses passion' is not established, this example lacks positive concomitance. The one with undemonstrated positive concomitance is as follows: 'Sound is non-eternal, because of being produced, like a pot.' Here, although the positive concomitance actually exists, it has not been made explicit by the proponent's statement, hence it is an example with undemonstrated positive concomitance. The one with reversed positive concomitance is as follows: after stating the reason 'Sound is non-eternal, because of being produced,' [one says] 'whatever is non-eternal is produced, like a pot.' Because the pervasion is shown in reverse, it has reversed positive concomitance. For in a positive agreement (<s>sādharmya</s>) formulation, the proving property should be shown as pervaded by the property to be proved; but here, because of a reversed presentation, there is reversal. 'Why has this not been stated by you?' — [the objector asks].

children.text: atrôcyate -- pareṣāṃ na suparyālocitam etad dṛṣṭântâbhāsa-trayâbhidhānam iti jñāpanârtham. tathā hi: na tāvad ananvayo dṛṣṭântâbhāso bhavitum arhati. yadi hi dṛṣṭânta-balena vyāptiḥ sādhya-sādhanayoḥ pratipādyeta, tataḥ syād anavayo dṛṣṭântâbhāsaḥ, sva-kāryâkaraṇād, yadā tu pūrva-pravṛtta-sambandha-grāhi-pramāṇa-gocara-smaraṇa-sampādanârthaṃ dṛṣṭântôdāhṛtir iti sthitaṃ, tadânanvayatva-lakṣaṇo na dṛṣṭântasya doṣaḥ, kiṃ tarhi hetor eva, pratibandhasyâdyâpi pramāṇenâpratiṣṭhitatvāt, pratibandhâbhāve cânvayâsiddheḥ. na ca hetu-doṣo 'pi dṛṣṭânte vācyo, 'tiprasaṅgād iti. tathâpradarśitânvaya-viparītânvayāv api na dṛṣṭântâbhāsatāṃ svī-kuruto, 'nvayâpradarśanasya viparyastânvaya-pradarśanasya ca vaktṛ-doṣatvāt, tad-doṣa-dvareṇâpi dṛṣṭântâbhāsa-pratipādane tad-iyattā viśīryeta, vaktṛ-doṣāṇāmānantyāt. vaktṛ-doṣatve 'pi parârthânumāne tat-kauśalam apekṣata iti. evaṃ côpanyāse na bubhutsitârtha-sādhakāv ato dṛṣṭântâbhāsāv etāv iti ced, evaṃ tarhi karaṇâpāṭavâdayo 'pi dṛṣṭântâbhāsā vācyāḥ. tathā hi: karaṇa-pāṭava-vyatirekeṇâpi na para-pratyāyanaṃ samasti, vispaṣṭa-varṇâgrahaṇe vyaktatayā tad-arthâvagamâbhāvād ity āstāṃ tāvat.
children.translated_text: To this we reply: [We have not stated it] in order to make known that this declaration of a triad of fallacious examples by the opponents has not been well considered. For: first, the one lacking positive concomitance (<s>ananvaya</s>) cannot properly be a fallacious example. If pervasion between the property to be proved and the proving property were established by the force of the example alone, then the one lacking positive concomitance would indeed be a fallacious example, due to its failure to accomplish its function. But when it is established that the citation of an example serves the purpose of occasioning the recollection of a cognition that has the scope of a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) grasping a previously existing connection, then the defect characterized as lacking positive concomitance is not a defect of the example, but rather of the reason (<s>hetu</s>) itself, because the invariable connection (<s>pratibandha</s>) has not yet been established by a <s>pramāṇa</s>; and in the absence of invariable connection, positive concomitance is not established. Nor should the defect of the reason be attributed to the example, due to over-extension. Similarly, the one with undemonstrated positive concomitance and the one with reversed positive concomitance are also not accepted as fallacious examples, because the failure to demonstrate positive concomitance and the demonstration of reversed positive concomitance are defects of the speaker. If fallacious-example-hood were established even through such [speaker's] defects, then the specification [of a definite number of fallacious examples] would collapse, since the speaker's defects are infinite. Even when it is a speaker's defect, in <s>parārthānumāna</s> (inference for the sake of others) skill in that [presentation] is required. If [it is objected that] 'in such a formulation, these two do not establish the intended meaning, and hence are fallacious examples,' then [we reply]: in that case, deficiency of articulative skill and so forth should also be called fallacious examples. For without articulative skill too, the persuasion of the other party does not take place, since without clear apprehension of the phonemes, there is no understanding of the meaning due to lack of distinctness. But let this be set aside for now.

children.text: tad evaṃ sādharmyeṇa dṛṣṭântâbhāsān pratipādya vaidharmyeṇâha:
children.translated_text: Thus, having set forth the fallacious examples by positive agreement (<s>sādharmya</s>), [the author] states [them] by negative agreement (<s>vaidharmya</s>):
The defects of the example by negative agreement (<s>vaidharmya</s>) have been declared by the knowers of logic:
from the non-exclusion of the pair of provable and prover, and from doubt. (NA_25)

children.text: sādhyâbhāvaḥ sādhanâbhāva-vyāptau darśayitum abhipreto yasmiṃs tad
children.translated_text: That in which the absence of the provable is intended to be shown as pervaded by the absence of the prover — that is
'the defects of the example have been declared by the knowers of logic' —
'Of the pair of provable and prover' —
[that is,] of both the indicated and the indicator;
the word 'and' (<s>ca</s>) is used in a non-adjacent connection;

children.text: ca nivṛtti-sandehāc cêty arthaḥ. tad anena ṣaḍ dṛṣṭântâbhāsāḥ sūcitās, tad yathā -- sādhyâvyatirekī, sādhanâvyatirekī, sādhya-sādhanâvyatirekī, tathā sandigdha-sādhya-vyatirekaḥ, sandigdha-sādhana-vyatirekaḥ, sandigdha-sādhya-sādhana-vyatirekaś cêti.
children.translated_text: and from doubt about exclusion — this is the meaning. By this, six fallacious examples are indicated, namely: one from which the provable is not excluded (<s>sādhyāvyatirekī</s>), one from which the prover is not excluded (<s>sādhanāvyatirekī</s>), one from which both the provable and prover are not excluded (<s>sādhya-sādhanāvyatirekī</s>), and likewise one of doubtful exclusion of the provable (<s>sandigdha-sādhya-vyatireka</s>), one of doubtful exclusion of the prover (<s>sandigdha-sādhana-vyatireka</s>), and one of doubtful exclusion of both provable and prover (<s>sandigdha-sādhya-sādhana-vyatireka</s>).

children.text: tatra sādhyâvyatirekī yathā: bhrāntam anumānam, pramāṇatvād iti. atra vaidharmya-dṛṣṭânto: yat punar bhrāntaṃ na bhavati na tat pramāṇaṃ, tad yathā svapna-jñānam iti; svapna-jñānād bhrāntatânivṛtteḥ sādhyâvyatirekitvam iti. sādhanâvyatirekī yathā: nirvikalpakaṃ pratyakṣaṃ, pramāṇatvād iti. atra vaidharmya-dṛṣṭânto: yat punaḥ savikalpakaṃ na tat pramāṇaṃ, tad yathânumānam; anumānāt pramāṇatânivṛtteḥ sādhanâvyatirekitvam iti. ubhayâvyatirekī yathā: nityânityaḥ śabdaḥ, sattvād iti. atra vaidharmya-dṛṣṭânto: yaḥ punar na nityânityaḥ sa na san, tad yathā -- ghaṭo; ghaṭād ubhayasyâpy avyāvṛtter ubhayâvyatirekitvam iti. tathā sandigdha-sādhya-vyatireko yathâsarva-jñā anāptā vā
children.translated_text: Among these, the one from which the provable is not excluded is illustrated as follows: 'Inference is errant, because of being a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge).' Here the negative-agreement example [is]: 'Whatever is not errant is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>, like dream-cognition.' Since errantness is not excluded from dream-cognition, it is one from which the provable is not excluded. The one from which the prover is not excluded is as follows: '<s>Nirvikalpaka</s> (non-conceptual cognition) is perception, because of being a <s>pramāṇa</s>.' Here the negative-agreement example [is]: 'Whatever is conceptual (<s>savikalpaka</s>) is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>, like inference.' Since <s>pramāṇa</s>-hood is not excluded from inference, it is one from which the prover is not excluded. The one from which both are not excluded is as follows: 'Sound is eternal and non-eternal, because of existence.' Here the negative-agreement example [is]: 'Whatever is not both eternal and non-eternal does not exist, like a pot.' Since both [properties] are not excluded from the pot, it is one from which both are not excluded. Similarly, the one of doubtful exclusion of the provable is as follows: '<s>Kapila</s> and others are not omniscient or not authoritative,

It is merely presented as one of doubtful exclusion of the provable because it appears so to those who are deficient in examining the capacity of the <s>pramāṇa</s> that refutes [the Four Noble Truths]. For although
