children.text: katham ete sarvâbhiprāya-saṅgrāhakā iti ced, ucyate: 'bhiprāyas tāvad artha-dvāreṇa śabda-dvāreṇa vā pravarteta, gaty-antarâbhāvād; arthaś ca sāmānya-rūpo viśeṣa-rūpo vā, śabdo 'pi rūḍhito vyutpattitaś ca, vyutpattir api sāmānya-nimitta-prayuktā tat-kāla-bhāvi-nimitta-prayuktā vā syāt. tatra ye kecanârtha-nirūpaṇa-pravaṇāḥ pramātr-abhiprāyās te sarve 'py ādye naya-catuṣṭaye 'ntar-bhavanti. tatrâpi ye paraspara-viśakalitau sāmānya-viśeṣāv icchanti tat-samudāya-rūpo naigamaḥ. ye punaḥ kevalaṃ sāmānyaṃ vāñchanti tat-samūha-sampādyaḥ saṅgrahaḥ. ye punar anapekṣita-śāstrīya-sāmānya-viśeṣaṃ loka-vyavahāram avatarantaṃ ghaṭâdikaṃ padârtham abhiprayanti tan-nicaya-janyo vyavahāraḥ. ye tu kṣaṇa-kṣayiṇaḥ paramâṇu-lakṣaṇā viśeṣāḥ satyā iti manyante tat-saṅghāta-ghaṭita ṛjusūtra iti. tathā ye rūḍhitaḥ śabdānāṃ pravṛttiṃ vāñchanti tan-nivaha-sādhyaḥ śabda iti. ye tu vyutpattito dhvanīnāṃ pravṛttiṃ vāñchanti nânyathā tad-vāra-janyaḥ samabhirūḍha iti. ye tu vartamāna-kāla-bhāvi-vyutpatti-nimittam adhikṛtya śabdāḥ pravartante nânyathêti manyante tat-saṅgha-ghaṭitaḥ khalv evambhūta iti. tad evaṃ na kaścid vikalpo 'sti vastu-gocaro yo 'tra naya-saptake nântar-yātîti sarvâbhiprāya-saṅgrāhakā ete iti sthitam.
children.translated_text: How are these all-encompassing of every viewpoint? It is said: A viewpoint would operate either through the medium of the object or through the medium of the word — there being no other possibility. And the object is either of the nature of a universal or of the nature of a particular; the word too [operates] either through conventional usage or through etymological derivation; and derivation too may be occasioned by a general ground or by a ground pertaining to the present time. Among these, all the viewpoints of knowers that are directed toward the determination of the object are included within the first four <s>nayas</s>. Among those, those who desire the universal and the particular as mutually undivided — the collection of those [viewpoints] constitutes the <s>Naigama</s> (figurative standpoint). Those who desire only the universal — the assemblage of those [viewpoints] constitutes the <s>Saṅgraha</s> (synthetic standpoint). Those who intend an object such as a pot, as it enters common usage without regard for the technical [categories of] universal and particular — the collection of those [viewpoints] produces the <s>Vyavahāra</s> (practical standpoint). Those who consider that the particulars characterized by atoms perishing in an instant are real — the aggregate constituted by those [viewpoints] is the <s>Ṛjusūtra</s> (straight-thread standpoint). Likewise, those who desire the operation of words through conventional usage — the assemblage accomplished by those [viewpoints] is the <s>Śabda</s> (verbal standpoint). Those who desire the operation of sounds through etymological derivation and not otherwise — that which is produced by those occasions is the <s>Samabhirūḍha</s> (etymological standpoint). Those who think that words operate on the basis of the etymological ground pertaining to the present time and not otherwise — that which is constituted by the assemblage of those [viewpoints] is indeed the <s>Evambhūta</s> (such-like standpoint). Thus, there is no conceptual alternative pertaining to a thing that does not fall within this sevenfold set of <s>nayas</s> — hence these are all-encompassing of every viewpoint; this is established.

children.text: sāmpratam eṣām eva pratyekaṃ matam upavarṇayāmaḥ. tatra gamanaṃ gamaḥ pariccheda ity arthaḥ. niścito gamo nigamo vivikta-vastu-grahaṇaṃ, sa eva, prajñâder ākṛti-gaṇatayā svârthikâṇ-pratyaya-vidhānān naigamaḥ. yadi vā nigamyante niyataṃ paricchidyanta iti nigamā arthās teṣu bhavo yo 'bhiprāyo niyata-pariccheda-rūpaḥ sa naigama iti. ayaṃ hi sattā-lakṣaṇaṃ mahā-sāmānyam avāntara-sāmānyāni ca dravyatva-guṇatva-karmatvâdīni tathântyān viśeṣān sakalâsādhāraṇa-rūpa-lakṣaṇān avāntara-viśeṣāṃś câpekṣayā para-rūpa-vyāvartana-kṣamān sāmānyād atyanta-vinirluṭhita-svarūpān abhipraiti. tathā hi: kila saṃvin-niṣṭhāḥ padârtha-vyavasthitayo, na ca sāmānya-grāhiṇi vijñāne viśeṣâvabhāso 'sty, 'nuvartamānâikâkāra-parāmarśena tad-grahaṇād, anyathā sāmānya-grāhakatvâyogāt. nâpi viśeṣa-grahaṇa-dakṣe saṃvedane sāmānyaṃ cakāsti, viśiṣṭa-deśa-daśâvacchinna-padârtha-grāhitayā tat-pravṛtter, anyathā viśeṣa-saṃvedanatvâyogāt. na câitau paraspara-vibhinnāv api pratibhāsamānau sāmānya-viśeṣau kathañcin miśrayitum yuktāv, atiprasaṅgād, vibhinna-pratibhāsinām api nikhilârthâtmanām aikya-prāpteḥ. evaṃ ca pramāṇayati: paraspara-viśliṣṭau sāmānya-viśeṣau, pārthakyenôpalabdher, iha yad yat pārthakyenôpalabhyate tat tat paraspara-viśliṣṭaṃ dravyaṃ, tad yathā -- devadatta-yajñadattāv iti, pārthakyena côpalabhyete sāmānya-viśeṣāv, ataḥ paraspara-vibhinnāv iti. na sāmānyāt pṛthag viśeṣôpalambha iti cet, kathaṃ tarhi tasyôpalambha iti vācyam. sāmānya-vyāptasyêti cen, na tarhi sa viśeṣôpalambhaḥ, sāmānyasyâpi tena grahaṇāt; tataś ca tena bodhena vivikta-viśeṣa-grahaṇâbhāvāt tad-vācakaṃ dhvaniṃ tat-sādhyaṃ ca vyavahāraṃ na pravartayet pramātā; na câitad asti, viśeṣâbhidhāna-vyavahārayoḥ pravṛtti-darśanāt. tasmād viśeṣam abhilaṣatā tatra ca vyavahāraṃ pravartayatā tad-grāhako bodho vivikto 'bhyupagantavyaḥ. tathā sāmānyam api viviktâkāratayā sva-grāhiṇi jñāne yadi na prakāśeta, tadā tad-gocarâbhimata-saṃvedanena viśeṣasyâpy ākalanāt sāmānyâbhidhāna-vyavahārayoḥ pravṛtter ucchedas tathâiva vaktavyo, vivikta-sāmānya-grāhi-bodha-mūlakatvāt tayos, tad-aniṣṭau tayor apy abhāvâpatteḥ. na ca sāmānyaṃ viśeṣaṃ vā tiras-kṛtya kevalasya viśeṣasya sāmānyasya vâbhyupagamaḥ kartuṃ yukto, dvayor api sva-grāhi-jñāne pratibhāsamānatayā viśeṣâbhāvāt. tasmād etau dvāv apîtarêtara-viśakalitāv aṅgī-karaṇârhāv iti naigamaḥ.
children.translated_text: Now we describe the view of each of these individually. Therein, 'going' (<s>gama</s>) means ascertainment, i.e., determination. A definite ascertainment (<s>nigama</s>) is the apprehension of a distinct object; and that itself, because <s>prajñā</s> (wisdom) and the like belong to the <s>ākṛti-gaṇa</s> (form-class), and thus by the rule prescribing the <s>svārthika aṇ-pratyaya</s> (affix denoting one's own meaning), is called <s>naigama</s> (figurative/teleological). Or alternatively, objects that are definitively ascertained — i.e., necessarily determined — are called <s>nigamas</s>; the view (<s>abhiprāya</s>) that has its being in those, having the form of definite determination, is the <s>naigama</s> [standpoint]. For this [standpoint] intends [to grasp] the great universal characterized by <s>sattā</s> (existence), and the subordinate universals such as <s>dravyatva</s> (substancehood), <s>guṇatva</s> (quality-hood), <s>karmatva</s> (action-hood), and so forth, as well as the ultimate particulars characterized by wholly unique forms, and the subordinate particulars that are capable of distinguishing from other forms by virtue of relative [consideration] — [these] universals being completely separated from particulars in their essential nature. For indeed: the determinations of the categories of objects are grounded in cognition, and in a cognition that grasps the universal there is no manifestation of the particular, because it is grasped through a cognition that comprehends a single recurring form; otherwise, its being a grasper of universals would be untenable. Nor does the universal shine forth in an awareness capable of grasping the particular, because its operation is directed toward grasping objects delimited by specific place and time; otherwise, its being an awareness of particulars would be untenable. And these two — universal and particular — though appearing as mutually distinct, cannot in any way be mixed, because of overextension: since even all objects, which appear as distinct, would then have to be unified. And he establishes this by argument: the universal and the particular are mutually separated, because they are apprehended as distinct. Here, whatever is apprehended as distinct is a mutually separated substance, just as <s>Devadatta</s> and <s>Yajñadatta</s>; and the universal and the particular are apprehended as distinct; therefore they are mutually different. If [you say] the particular is not apprehended separately from the universal — then it must be stated: how then is it apprehended at all? If [you say] as pervaded by the universal — then that is not an apprehension of the particular, since the universal too is grasped by that [same cognition]; and consequently, since there is no apprehension of a distinct particular by that cognition, the knower would not employ the word designating it nor the practical activity dependent on it; but this is not the case, since the employment of designation and practical activity pertaining to the particular is observed. Therefore, one who desires the particular and engages in practical activity regarding it must acknowledge a distinct cognition that grasps it. Similarly, if the universal too does not shine forth in the cognition that grasps it with a distinct form, then since even the particular would be apprehended by that awareness intended to have [the universal] as its object, the annulment of designation and practical activity pertaining to the universal should be stated in the same way, since these two are rooted in a cognition that grasps a distinct universal; and if that [cognition] is not accepted, the absence of both would follow. And it is not proper to accept only the particular alone or the universal alone while discarding the other, since there is no difference between the two, both appearing in cognitions that grasp their own [respective objects]. Therefore, both of these, though separated from each other, deserve to be acknowledged — such is the <s>naigama</s> [standpoint].

children.text: adhunā saṅgrahâbhiprāyo varṇyate. tatra saṅgṛhṇāty aśeṣa-viśeṣa-tiro-dhāna-dvāreṇa sāmānya-rūpatayā jagad ādatta iti saṅgrahaḥ. ayaṃ hi manyate: bhāva-lakṣaṇa-sāmānyād vyatiricyamāna-mūrtayo vā viśeṣāḥ parikalpyerann, avyatiricyamāna-mūrtayo vā, gaty-antarâbhāvāt. tatra yady ādyaḥ pakṣas, tadā niḥsvabhāvatāṃ te svī-kuryur, bhāva-vyatirekitvād, gagana-kusumâdivat. atha dvitīyaḥ kalpas, tarhi bhāva-mātram āpadyante. tathā hi: bhāva-mātraṃ viśeṣās, tad-avyatiriktatvād, iha yad yato 'vyatiriktaṃ tat tad eva bhavati, tad yathā -- bhāvasyâiva svarūpam, avyatirekiṇaś ca viśeṣā, atas tad-rūpā eva. nanu ca yadi bhāva-mātram eva tattvaṃ tadā tasya sarvatrâviśeṣād ya ete pratiprāṇi-prasiddhāḥ stambhêbha-kumbhâmbho-rūhâdi-viśiṣṭa-vastu-sādhyā vyavahārās te sarve 'pi pralayam āpadyerann, ato viśeṣā api vivikta-vyavahāra-hetavo 'bhyupagantavyāḥ. nâitad asti, vyavahārasyânādy-avidyā-bala-pravartitatvāt, tena pārāmarthika-pramāṇa-pratiṣṭhita-tattva-pratibandhâbhāvāt. kiṃ ca, viśeṣâgraho viśeṣeṇa tyājyo, viśeṣa-vyavasthāpaka-pramāṇâbhāvāt. tathā hi: bheda-rūpā viśeṣāḥ, na ca kiñcit pramāṇaṃ bhedam avagāhate, pratyakṣaṃ hi tāvad bhāva-sampādita-sattākaṃ tam eva sākṣat-kartuṃ yuktam, nâbhāvaṃ, tasya sakala-śakti-viraha-rūpatayā tad-utpādane vyāpārâbhāvād, anutpādakasya ca sākṣāt-karaṇe sarva-sākṣāt-karaṇa-prasaṅgāt, tathā ca viśeṣâbhāvāt sarvo draṣṭāsarva-darśīsyāt. aniṣṭam câitad bhavatāṃ, tasmād bhāva-grāhakam eva tad eṣṭavyam. sa ca bhāvaḥ sarvatrâviśiṣṭa iti tathâiva tena grāhyas, tad-uttara-kāla-bhāvī punar vikalpo ghaṭo 'yaṃ paṭâdir na bhavatîty evam-ākāro vyavahāraṃ racayann avidyā-mūlatvān na pramāṇaṃ, tan na pratyakṣād viśeṣâvagatiḥ. nâpy anumānâdeḥ, pratyakṣa-mūlakatvāc cheṣa-pramāṇa-vargasya, tasmāt sāmānyam eva paramârtho, na viśeṣā iti saṅgrahaḥ.
children.translated_text: Now the view of <s>saṅgraha</s> (collection/synthesis) is described. Therein, [it is so called because] it collects (<s>saṅgṛhṇāti</s>), i.e., it comprehends the world in the form of the universal through the concealment of all particulars — such is <s>saṅgraha</s>. For this [standpoint] holds: would the particulars, whose forms are distinguished from the universal characterized by existence (<s>bhāva</s>), be conceived as having forms that are different [from the universal], or as having forms that are not different? — there being no third alternative. Therein, if the first position, then they would assume the status of being without own-nature (<s>niḥsvabhāvatā</s>), because they are different from existence, like sky-flowers and the like. If the second alternative, then they amount to mere existence. For: the particulars are mere existence, because they are not different from it; here, whatever is not different from something is that very thing, just as the own-nature of existence itself; and since the particulars are non-different, they are of that very nature. Now, if mere existence is indeed the reality, then since there would be no distinction in it anywhere, all those practical activities well-known to every living being — those accomplished by specific objects such as posts, elephants, jars, trees, etc. — would all be annulled; therefore, the particulars too, as causes of distinct practical activities, must be acknowledged. This is not so, because practical activity is set in motion by the force of beginningless <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), and therefore there is no obstruction by a reality established by an ultimately valid <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge). Moreover, the non-apprehension of particulars should be abandoned specifically, because there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> that establishes the particulars. For: the particulars have the form of difference, and no <s>pramāṇa</s> grasps difference. For perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>), having its existence produced by what is existent, is suited only to directly apprehend that [existent], not absence — since [absence], being of the nature of the complete absence of all power, has no capacity to produce it; and if what is not a producer could be directly perceived, the absurd consequence would be the direct perception of everything; and thus, in the absence of the particular, every perceiver would perceive everything. And this is undesirable by you; therefore, that [perception] must be accepted as grasping only what is existent. And that existent is undifferentiated everywhere; therefore it must be grasped in just that way by it [i.e., perception]. The subsequent conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa</s>) — 'this is a pot, not a cloth, etc.' — having such a form, though it constructs practical activity, is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> because it is rooted in <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance); therefore there is no apprehension of the particular from perception. Nor from inference and the rest, because the remaining group of <s>pramāṇas</s> is rooted in perception. Therefore, the universal alone is the ultimate reality, not the particulars — such is the <s>saṅgraha</s> [standpoint].

children.text: sāmprataṃ vyavahāra-matam ucyate. tatra vyavaharaṇaṃ vyavahriyate vânena laukikair abhiprāyeṇêti vyavahāraḥ. ayaṃ tu manyate: yathā loka-grāham eva vastv astu, kim anayâdṛṣṭâvyavahriyamāna-vastu-parikalpana-kaṣṭa-piṣṭikayā? yad eva ca loka-vyavahāra-patham avatarati tasyânugrāhakaṃ pramāṇam upalabhyate, nêtarasya, na hi sāmānyam anādi-nidhanam ekaṃ saṅgrāhâbhimataṃ pramāṇa-bhūmis, tathânubhavâbhāvāt, sarvasya sarva-darśitva-prasaṅgāc ca. nâpi viśeṣāḥ paramâṇu-lakṣaṇāḥ kṣaṇa-kṣayiṇaḥ pramāṇa-gocaras, tathā pravṛtter abhāvāt. tasmād idam eva nikhila-lokâbādhitaṃ pramāṇa-prasiddhaṃ kiyat-kāla-bhāvi-sthūratām ābibhrāṇam udakâharaṇâdy-artha-kriyā-nirvartana-kṣamaṃ ghaṭâdikaṃ vastu-rūpaṃ pāramārthikam astu, pūrvôttara-kāla-bhāvi-tat-paryāya-paryālocanā punar ajyāyasī, tatra pramāṇa-prasarâbhāvāt, pramāṇam antareṇa ca vicārasya kartum aśakyatvāt. avastutvāc ca teṣāṃ, kiṃ tad-gocara-paryālocanena? tathā hi: pūrvôttara-kāla-bhāvino dravya-vivartāḥ kṣaṇa-kṣayi-paramâṇu-lakṣaṇā vā viśeṣā na kañcana loka-vyavahāram uparacayanti, tan na te vastu-rūpā, loka-vyavahārôpayogināṃ eva vastutvād iti vyavahāraḥ.
children.translated_text: Now the <s>vyavahāra</s> (practical/conventional) view is stated. Therein, 'convention' (<s>vyavahāra</s>) means that by which worldly people conduct their dealings, or that by which [things] are practically employed — such is <s>vyavahāra</s>. This [standpoint] holds: let the object be just as it is grasped by common people — what is the use of this laborious fabrication of inventing objects that are unseen and never employed in practice? And a <s>pramāṇa</s> that supports it is found only for that which enters the path of worldly convention, not for anything else. For the single beginningless and endless universal proposed by the <s>saṅgraha</s> [standpoint] is not the domain of any <s>pramāṇa</s>, because no such experience exists, and because of the absurd consequence that everyone would perceive everything. Nor are the particulars characterized as <s>paramāṇus</s> (atoms) that perish every moment the object of any <s>pramāṇa</s>, because no such cognitive operation occurs. Therefore, let this alone — the reality of objects such as pots and the like, which is uncontradicted by all people, established by <s>pramāṇa</s>, which endures for some time, possesses gross form, and is capable of accomplishing practical purposes such as fetching water — be the ultimate reality. The investigation of the transformations of that [object] occurring in prior and subsequent times, however, is not beneficial, because there is no operation of <s>pramāṇa</s> there, and because investigation cannot be carried out without <s>pramāṇa</s>. And since those [past and future states] are non-real, what is the point of investigating what pertains to them? For: the transformations of substance occurring in prior and subsequent times, or the particulars characterized as momentary atoms — they do not produce any worldly practical activity; therefore they are not real entities, since only what is useful for worldly practical activity has the status of reality — such is the <s>vyavahāra</s> [standpoint].

children.text: sāmprataṃ ṛjusūtrâbhiprāyaḥ kathyate. tatra rju praguṇam akuṭilam atītânagata-vakra-parityāgād vartamāna-kṣaṇa-vivarti-vastuno rūpaṃ sūtrayati niṣṭaṅkitaṃ darśayatîty ṛjusūtraḥ. tathā hy: asyâbhiprāyo -- 'tītasya vinaṣṭatvād anāgatasyâlabdhâtma-lābhatvāt khara-viṣāṇâdibhyo 'viśiṣyamāṇatayā sakala-śakti-viraha-rūpatvān nârtha-kriyā-nirvartana-kṣamatvam, artha-kriyā-kṣamaṃ ca vastu; tad-abhāvān na tayor vastutvam iti. vartamāna-kṣaṇâliṅgitaṃ ca punar vastu-rūpaṃ samastârtha-kriyāsu vyāpriyata iti tad eva pāramārthikam. tad api ca niraṃśam abhyupagantavyam, aṃśa-vyāpter yukti-riktatvād, ekasyâneka-svabhāvatām antareṇâneka-svâvayava-vyāpanâyogāt. aneka-svabhāvatâivâstv iti cen, na, virodha-vyāghrâghrātatvāt. tathā hi: yady ekaḥ svabhāvaḥ katham anekaḥ? anekaś cet katham ekaḥ? ekânekayoḥ paraspara-parihāreṇâvasthānāt; tasmāt svarūpa-nimagnāḥ paramâṇava eva parasparôpasarpaṇa-dvāreṇa kathañcin nicaya-rūpatām āpannā nikhila-kāryeṣu vyāpāra-bhāja iti ta eva svalakṣaṇaṃ, na sthūratāṃ dhārayat pāramārthikaṃ iti. kiṃ ca, pramāṇato 'rtha-vyavasthā, na ca pramāṇaṃ deśa-kāla-vyāpti-grahaṇe kiñcana pravartate, sarva-pramāṇānāṃ vartamāna-prakāśa-rūpatvāt. tathā hi: pratyakṣaṃ tāvad rūpâloka-manaskāra-cakṣur-lakṣaṇa-kāraṇa-catuṣṭayāl labdha-sattākaṃ vartamāna-kṣaṇa eva prakāśate, atīta-vartsyat-kṣaṇayor asannihitatvāt, tataś ca tat tat-kāla-sambaddham eva vastuno rūpaṃ sākṣāt-kartuṃ kṣamate na pūrvam aparaṃ vâsannidhānād eva. yadi punar vinaṣṭam api pūrva-kṣaṇa-varti-rūpamākalayet, tadā vinaṣṭatvâviśeṣān niravadhiḥ kṣaṇa-paramparā tatra pratīyeta, tathā ca sati saṅkalikayânādi-janma-paramparā-grāhi pratyakṣam anuṣajyeta. evam anāgata-kṣaṇa-grahaṇe 'pi yojyam; aniṣṭaṃ câitat, tasmāt tad vārtamānika-kṣaṇa-grahaṇa-dakṣam evêty abhyupagantavyam. nanu ca yadi kṣaṇa-bhaṅguratām arthâtmanām adhyakṣam avalokayati, tadā nīlatêva pratibhāsamānā sā vipratipatti-gocaraṃ na yāyād iti tad-viṣayo laukikānāṃ vyavahāraḥ pravarteta, na câitad asti, sthiratā-dvāreṇa vyavahāra-pravṛtter iti. atra pratividhīyate -- sākṣāt-kurvāṇā api kṣaṇa-vinaśvaratāṃ sadṛśâparâparôtpatti-vipralabdha-buddhayo mandā nâdhyavasyanty, anādi-kāla-prarūḍha-vāsanā-prabodha-samupajanita-mithyā-vikalpa-sāmarthyāc ca viparyasta-sthiratā-vyavahāraṃ pravartayanti, tan nâyam adhyakṣasyâparādho, 'pi tu pramātḥṇām eva. tathā ghanâkāro 'pi pratyakṣa-pṛṣṭha-bhāvi-mithyā-vikalpa-sandarśita eva, vivikta-darśane tat-pratibhāsâyogāt, kara-caraṇa-śiro-grīvâdayo hy avayavāḥ paraspara-vibhaktā eva tatra pratibhānti, na vyāpy-ākāro, na ca te 'pi svâṃśa-vyāpinaḥ pratibhānti, tad-avayavānām apîtarêtara-viśakalita-rūpāṇāṃ pratibhāsāt tāvad yāvat paramâṇava eva prathante, vyāpi-rūpasya vicārâkṣamatvād ity ukta-prāyam. nâpy anumānāt sthira-sthūra-vastu-siddhiḥ, pratyakṣa-parigṛhītaṃ hi sambandham āsādyânumānaṃ pravarteta, yadā ca tat kṣaṇa-bhaṅgura-viviktâṃśa-grahaṇa-cāturyam ābibhrad darśitaṃ tadânumānam api tat-pratibandha-mūlakaṃ tad-gocaram eva pāramparyeṇa pratiṣṭhāpayati, sva-pratibhāsino rūpasyâlīkatayā tat-pratiṣṭhāpana-dvāreṇâiva tasya prāmāṇyāt. nanu ca smaraṇa-pratyabhijñānâdīni sthira-sthūra-vastu-vyatirekeṇa nôpapadyante, pūrvam adṛṣṭe tad-abhāvāt, puruṣâdy-avayavināṃ smaraṇāt pratyabhijñānāc ca. nâitad asti, teṣām alīka-vāsanā-prabodhôtthāpitatvena prāmāṇyâyogāt. kiṃ ca, tāny api svayaṃ vartamāna-kṣaṇa eva prakāśante, viplava-vaśāt tu svarūpam eva vāsanā-sampāditâtītârtha-rūpatayā vyavasyanti, ghanâkāraṃ ca tasyâsantam adhyāropayanti; tan na tebhyo 'pi vyāpi-vastu-siddhiḥ. tasmād vyāpini rūpe pramāṇânavatārāt paraspara-viśliṣṭāḥ paramâṇava eva paramârthata iti rjusūtraḥ.
children.translated_text: Now the view of <s>ṛjusūtra</s> (the straight thread / direct standpoint) is stated. Therein, <s>ṛju</s> means straight, direct, not crooked — having abandoned the crookedness of past and future, the form of an object that exists in the present moment; one who threads (<s>sūtrayati</s>), i.e., clearly shows, that [form] is the <s>ṛjusūtra</s>. For the purport of this [standpoint] is: since the past has been destroyed and the future has not yet obtained its own existence, being no different from a donkey's horn and the like, and being of the nature of the complete absence of all power, they are not capable of accomplishing practical purposes (<s>artha-kriyā</s>); and a real entity is that which is capable of practical efficacy; therefore, in the absence of that, there is no reality in those two [past and future]. The real entity, however, embraced by the present moment, engages in all practical activities — therefore that alone is ultimately real. And that too must be acknowledged as partless, because the pervading of parts is devoid of reasoning: without having a manifold nature, a single [entity] cannot pervade its many constituents. If [you say] let it indeed have a manifold nature — no, because it would be bitten by the tiger of contradiction. For: if it is one nature, how is it many? And if many, how is it one? — since the one and the many exist by mutual exclusion. Therefore, atoms immersed in their own nature, having somehow attained the form of an aggregate through mutual approach, participate in all effects — they alone are the <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> (unique particular), and what bears gross form is not ultimately real. Moreover, the determination of objects is from <s>pramāṇa</s>, and no <s>pramāṇa</s> operates in grasping spatial and temporal extension, because all <s>pramāṇas</s> have the nature of illuminating the present. For: perception, having its existence produced from the fourfold cause of visible form, light, attention, and the eye, illuminates only in the present moment, because the past and future moments are not present; and therefore it is capable of directly apprehending only that form of the object connected with that time, not the earlier or later [form], due to their non-presence. If, however, it were to apprehend even the destroyed form existing in the prior moment, then, there being no difference in terms of being destroyed, an unlimited succession of moments would be cognized therein, and thus perception would absurdly follow the chain grasping the beginningless succession of births. The same should be applied to the apprehension of the future moment as well; and this is undesirable — therefore it must be acknowledged that [perception] is competent only to grasp the present moment. Now, if perception observes the momentariness of object-natures, then, just as blueness appears, that [momentariness] too would not enter the domain of disagreement, and thus the practical activity of common people regarding it would proceed; but this is not the case, since practical activity proceeds through [the appearance of] stability. To this the response is: even while directly perceiving momentary destruction, the dull-witted, deceived by the successive arising of similar [entities], do not ascertain [the momentariness]; and due to the power of false conceptual construction (<s>mithyā-vikalpa</s>) generated by the awakening of <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions) cultivated since beginningless time, they engage in the erroneously reversed practical activity of stability — therefore this is not a fault of perception, but rather of the perceivers themselves. Similarly, the form of solidity too is shown only by the false conceptual construction that follows in the wake of perception, because in distinct [i.e., analytical] seeing, that appearance would be impossible — for the parts such as hands, feet, head, neck, etc., appear in perception as mutually distinct, not in an all-pervading form; and they too do not appear as pervading their own parts, because even the parts of those parts appear as mutually separated — and this continues down to the atoms themselves being manifest, since the pervading form does not withstand scrutiny — this has been mostly stated already. Nor is the establishment of stable, gross objects from inference [possible], for inference would operate only upon attaining a relation grasped by perception; and when that [perception] has been shown to possess the skill of grasping momentary, distinct parts, then inference too, being rooted in that relation, establishes precisely that [momentary, distinct] domain mediately — because its validity consists precisely in establishing that, given that its own appearing form is false. Now, [if you say] memory, recognition, and the like are impossible without stable, gross objects — because in what has not been previously seen, those would be absent, and because there is memory and recognition of composite wholes such as persons — this is not so, because those [i.e., memory and recognition], being generated by the awakening of false <s>vāsanās</s>, cannot be valid means of knowledge. Moreover, they too themselves illuminate only in the present moment; but through error they ascertain their own nature as having the form of a past object produced by <s>vāsanā</s>, and they superimpose upon it the form of solidity, which is unreal; therefore, not even from these is the establishment of a pervading object possible. Therefore, since no <s>pramāṇa</s> descends upon a pervading form, the mutually separated atoms alone are ultimately real — such is the <s>ṛjusūtra</s> [standpoint].

children.text: tad idam artha-svarūpa-nirūpaṇa-nipuṇānāṃ nayānāṃ matam upavarṇitam; adhunā śabda-vicāra-caturāṇām upavarṇyate. tatra trayāṇām api śabdâdīnām idaṃ sādhāraṇamākūtaṃ, yad uta śabda eva paramārtho nârthas, tasya tad-avyatiriktatvāt. pārthakyena vastutva-siddheḥ katham avyatireka iti cet, pramāṇād iti brūmaḥ. tathā hi: na vyatirikto 'rthaḥ śabdāt, tat-pratītau tasya pratīyamānatvād, iha yat-pratītau yat pratīyate tat tato 'vyatiriktaṃ bhavati, tad yathā -- śabde pratīyamāne tasyâiva svarūpaṃ, pratīyate ca śabde pratīyamāne 'rtho, 'to 'sau tato 'vyatirikta iti. agṛhīta-saṅketasya ghaṭa-śabda-śravaṇe 'pi ghaṭa-pratīter abhāvād vyatirikta iti ced, evaṃ tarhi viṣasya māraṇâtmakatvaṃ tad-ajñasya na pratibhātîti tat tato vyatiriktam āpadyeta, na câitad asti, tad-vyatirekâviśeṣeṇa guḍa-khaṇḍavad viṣasyâpy amārakatvâpatteḥ, sambandhasya ca vyatiriktena saha prāg evâpāstatvāt; tan nâbuddha-pramātṛ-doṣeṇa vastuno 'nyathātvam, anyathândho rūpaṃ nêkṣata iti tad-abhāvo 'pi pratipattavya iti. ye nirabhidhānā vartante 'rthās teṣāṃ śabdāt pārthakyena vastutva-siddhir iti cen, na, nirabhidhānârthâbhāvāt, kevalaṃ kecid viśeṣa-śabdaiḥ saṅkīrtyante, kecit sāmānya-dhvanibhir ity etāvān viśeṣaḥ syāt. yadi vā sakalârtha-vācakā viśeṣa-dhavanayo na santîti nâsty atra pramāṇam. tataś ca sarve 'rthā vidyamāna-sva-vācakā, 'rthatvād, ghaṭârthavad iti pramāṇāt sarveṣāṃ sva-vācakatvena pūrvôkta-yukteḥ śabdād apārthakya-siddhiḥ. tasmān na paramârthato 'rthaḥ śabdâtirikto 'sty, upacārataḥ punar laukikair aparyālocita-paramârthair vyavahriyate. asāv apy aupacārikaḥ śabdâtmako vârthaḥ pratikṣaṇa-bhaṅguraḥ svī-kartavyo, varṇānāṃ kṣaṇa-dhvaṃsitā-pratīter, ṛjusūtra-pratipādita-yukti-kalāpāc ca.
children.translated_text: Thus the view of the <s>nayas</s> (standpoints) that are skilled in determining the nature of the object has been described; now [the view of] those skilled in the investigation of words is described. Therein, this is the common purport of all three — <s>śabda</s> (word) and the rest: the word alone is the ultimate reality, not the object, because the object is non-different from it. If [you ask] how can there be non-difference when objecthood is established through separateness — we say: from <s>pramāṇa</s>. For: the object is not different from the word, because when the word is cognized, the object too is cognized. Here, whatever is cognized when something [else] is cognized is non-different from that, just as when a word is being cognized, its own form [is cognized]; and the object is cognized when the word is being cognized; therefore it is non-different from it. If [you say] that even when one who has not grasped the convention hears the word 'pot,' there is no cognition of a pot — therefore [the object] is different — then in that case, since the killing nature of poison does not appear to one ignorant of it, that [nature] would be different from [the poison]; but this is not so, because without the difference of that [killing nature from the poison], the poison would absurdly become non-lethal like a lump of sugar; and because the relation [between them] has already been rejected as [holding] with something separate. Therefore, the nature of the object is not altered by the fault of the unknowing perceiver; otherwise, since a blind person does not see form, even its non-existence would have to be accepted. If [you say] those objects that exist without being designated — their reality is established through separateness from the word — no, because there are no undesignated objects; the only difference would be that some are named by specific words, and some by general sounds. Or, there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> for the claim that specific sounds designating all objects do not exist. And so, all objects have their own designators, because they are objects, like the object 'pot' — thus from this <s>pramāṇa</s>, since all [objects] have their own designators, by the previously stated reasoning, the non-difference of the object from the word is established. Therefore, there is no object ultimately other than the word; conventionally, however, common people who have not reflected on the ultimate reality do employ [the distinction]. That conventional object too, which has the nature of the word, should be accepted as momentarily perishing — because the momentary destruction of phonemes is cognized, and because of the collection of arguments demonstrated by the <s>ṛjusūtra</s> [standpoint].

children.text: sāmpratam eteṣām eva pratyekam abhiprāyaḥ kathyate. tatra śabdo: rūḍhito yāvanto dhvanayaḥ kasmiṃścid arthe pravartante; yathêndra-śakra-purandarâdayaḥ, teṣāṃ sarveṣām apy ekam artham abhipraiti kila pratīti-vaśād, yathā śabdâvyatireko 'rthasya pratipādyate tathâiva tasyâikatvaṃ vânekatvaṃ vā pratipādanīyaṃ; na cêndra-śakra-purandarâdayaḥ paryāya-śabdā vibhinnârtha-vācitayā kadācana pratīyante, tebhyaḥ sarvadâivâikâkāra-parāmarśôtpatter, askhalad-vṛttitayā tathâiva vyavahāra-darśanāt. tasmād eka eva paryāya-śabdānām artha iti śabdaḥ, śabdyata āhūyate 'nenâbhiprāyeṇârtha iti niruktād ekârtha-pratipādanâbhiprāyeṇâiva paryāya-dhvanīnāṃ prayogād iti.
children.translated_text: Now the individual view of each of these is stated. Therein, <s>śabda</s> (the word standpoint): however many sounds operate with respect to some object by convention — such as <s>Indra</s>, <s>Śakra</s>, <s>Purandara</s>, etc. — this [standpoint] intends that all of them indeed refer to a single object, on the strength of cognition. Just as the non-difference of the object from the word is demonstrated, so too its oneness or manyness should be demonstrated; and the synonymous words <s>Indra</s>, <s>Śakra</s>, <s>Purandara</s>, etc. are never cognized as denoting different objects, because from all of them there always arises a comprehension of one and the same form, and because practical activity is observed to proceed in just that way without stumbling. Therefore, the object of synonymous words is one alone — such is the <s>śabda</s> [standpoint]; because 'what is called (<s>śabdyate</s>), i.e., summoned, by this [word] is the object' — from this etymology, synonymous sounds are employed with the very purpose of conveying a single object.

children.text: sāmprataṃ samabhirūḍha-matam upavarṇyate. tatra sam ekī-bhāvenâbhirohati vyutpatti-nimittam āskandati śabda-pravṛttau yo 'bhiprāyaḥ sa samabhirūḍhaḥ. ayaṃ hi paryāya-śabdānāṃ prativibhaktam evârtham abhimanyate, tad yathêndanād indraḥ, paramâiśvaryam indra-śabda-vācyaṃ paramârthatas, tadvaty arthe punar upacārataḥ pravartate, na vā kaścit tadvān, sarva-śabdānāṃ paraspara-vibhaktârtha-pratipādakatayâśrayâśrayi-bhāvena pravṛtty-asiddheḥ. evaṃ śakanāc chakraḥ, pūr-dāraṇāt purandara ity-ādi bhinnârthatvaṃ sarva-śabdānāṃ darśayati; pramāṇayati ca: paryāya-śabdā vibhinnârthāḥ, prativibhakta-vyutpatti-nimittakatvād, iha ye ye prativibhakta-vyutpatti-nimittakās te te bhinnârthāḥ, yathêndra-ghaṭa-puruṣa-śabdā vibhinnârthā, vibhinna-vyutpatti-nimittakāś ca paryāya-śabdā apy, ato 'bhinnârthā iti. yat punar avicārita-pratīti-balād ekârthâbhidhāyakatvaṃ pratipādyate tad ayuktam, atiprasaṅgāt. tathā hi: yadi yukti-riktā pratītir eva śaraṇī-kriyate tadā manda-manda-prakāśe davīyasi deśe sanniviṣṭa-śarīrā vibhinnā api nimba-kadambâśvattha-kapitthâdaya eka-tarv-ākāratām ābibhrāṇāḥ pratīyanta ity ekatayâivâbhyupagantavyāḥ. na câitad asti, vivikta-tat-svarūpa-grāhi-pratyanīka-pratyayôpanipāta-bādhitatvena pūrva-pratīter viviktānām eva teṣām abhyupagamāt, tan nâikârtha-vācino dhvanayaḥ santi, rūḍhiḥ punar avicārita-tad-arthānām iti samabhirūḍhaḥ.
children.translated_text: Now the view of <s>samabhirūḍha</s> (the specifically conventional standpoint) is described. Therein, [it is so called because] the purport that ascends (<s>abhirohati</s>) to the etymological basis in a unified manner (<s>sam</s>, i.e., as one), that assails the occasion of the word's operation — that view is <s>samabhirūḍha</s>. For this [standpoint] holds that synonymous words have individually distinct meanings. For example: from 'delighting' (<s>indanāt</s>) [comes] <s>Indra</s>; supreme sovereignty is what is ultimately denoted by the word <s>Indra</s>; with respect to an object possessing that [quality], however, [the word] operates conventionally — or there may be no such possessor [at all], since, given that all words convey mutually distinct meanings, [their] operation through the relation of substratum and superstratum is not established. Similarly, from 'being able' (<s>śakanāt</s>) [comes] <s>Śakra</s>; from 'destroying cities' (<s>pūr-dāraṇāt</s>) [comes] <s>Purandara</s> — thus [this standpoint] shows the different meaning of all words. And it argues: synonymous words have different meanings, because they have individually distinct etymological bases. Here, whatever have individually distinct etymological bases have different meanings, just as the words <s>Indra</s>, 'pot,' and 'person' have different meanings; and synonymous words too have distinct etymological bases; therefore they have different meanings. Now, the claim that on the strength of unreflective cognition they denote a single object is untenable, because of overextension. For: if cognition devoid of reasoning is made the refuge, then neem, kadamba, fig, wood-apple, and other trees, though different, which appear in dim light at a distant place as bearing the form of a single tree, would have to be acknowledged as one; but this is not so, because the prior cognition is sublated by the onset of a contrary cognition that grasps their distinct natures, and therefore those [trees] are acknowledged as distinct. Therefore, no sounds denote a single object; convention (<s>rūḍhi</s>) is merely [the usage] of those who have not examined the [true] meaning — such is the <s>samabhirūḍha</s> [standpoint].

children.text: sāmpratam evambhūtâbhiprāyaḥ pratipādyate. tatrâivaṃ-śabdaḥ prakāra-vacanas, tataś câivaṃ yathā vyutpāditas taṃ prakāraṃ bhūtaḥ prāpto yaḥ śabdaḥ sa evambhūtaḥ; tat-samarthana-pradhāno 'bhiprāyo 'py evambhūtas, tad-viṣayatvāt, viṣaya-śabdena ca viṣayiṇo 'bhidhānāt. ayaṃ hi yasminn arthe śabdo vyutpādyate sa vyutpatti-nimittam artho yadâiva vivartate tadâiva taṃ śabdaṃ pravartamānam abhipraiti, na sāmānyena. yathôdakâdy-āharaṇa-velāyāṃ yoṣid-ādi-mastakârūḍho viśiṣṭa-ceṣṭāvān eva ghaṭo 'bhidhīyate, na śeṣo, ghaṭa-śabda-vyutpatti-nimitta-śūnyatvāt, paṭâdivad iti. atītāṃ bhāvinīṃ vā ceṣṭām adhikṛtya sāmānyenâivôcyata iti cen, na, tayor vinaṣṭânutpannatayā śaśa-viṣāṇa-kalpatvāt; tathâpi tad-dvāreṇa śabda-pravartane sarvatra pravartayitavyo, viśeṣâbhāvāt. kiṃ ca, yady atīta-vartsyac-ceṣṭâpekṣayā ghaṭa-śabdo 'ceṣṭāvaty api prayujyeta, kapāla-mṛt-piṇḍâdāv api tat-pravartanaṃ durnivāraṃ syāt, viśeṣâbhāvāt, tasmād yatra kṣaṇe vyutpatti-nimittam avikalam asti tasminn eva so 'rthas tac-chabdena vācya ity evambhūtaḥ.
children.translated_text: Now the view of <s>evambhūta</s> (the 'such-like' / actuality standpoint) is explained. Therein, the word '<s>evam</s>' denotes a manner; and thus, a word that has attained (<s>bhūta</s>, i.e., reached) the manner in which it was etymologically derived is <s>evambhūta</s>; the view that is predominantly concerned with establishing that is also [called] <s>evambhūta</s>, because it has that as its object, and because a subject is designated by the word for its object. For this [standpoint] holds that the meaning for which a word is etymologically derived — that etymological basis of meaning — only when it is actually present does it intend that word to be in operation, not in a general way. Just as at the time of fetching water and the like, only a pot that is mounted on a woman's head and engaged in a specific function is [properly] called [a pot], not the rest [of the time], because [those other states] are devoid of the etymological basis of the word 'pot,' just like cloth and the like. If [you say] that with reference to a past or future function, [the word] is used in a general way — no, because those [past and future functions], being destroyed and not-yet-arisen, are like a hare's horn. Even granting that, if the word were to operate through those [past/future states], it would have to operate everywhere, because there is no distinguishing feature. Moreover, if the word 'pot' were used even for something without [the relevant] function on the basis of past or future function, then its application even to potsherds, lumps of clay, etc. would be impossible to prevent, because there is no distinguishing feature. Therefore, only at that moment when the etymological basis is fully present is that object to be denoted by that word — such is the <s>evambhūta</s> [standpoint].

children.text: tad evam aneka-dharma-parītârtha-grāhikā buddhiḥ pramāṇaṃ, tad-dvārâyātaḥ punar eka-dharma-niṣṭhârtha-samarthana-pravaṇaḥ parāmarśaḥ śeṣa-dharma-svī-kāra-tiras-kāra-parihāra-dvāreṇa vartamāno nayaḥ, sa ca dharmāṇām ānantyād ananta-bhedas, tathâpi sarva-saṅgrāhakâbhiprāya-parikalpana-mukhenâivaṃ sapta-bhedo darśitaḥ. ayam eva ca svâbhipreta-dharmâvadhāraṇâtmakatayāśeṣa-dharma-tiras-kāra-dvāreṇa pravartamāṇaḥ parāmarśo durnaya-saṃjñām aśnute; tad-bala-prabhāvita-sattākā hi khalv ete para-pravādāḥ. tathā hi: naigama-naya-darśanânusāriṇau
children.translated_text: Thus, cognition (<s>buddhi</s>) that grasps an object invested with multiple properties is <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid knowledge); the conceptual determination (<s>parāmarśa</s>) that comes through that [cognition], however — which is inclined toward establishing the object as possessing a single property, operating by way of setting aside, concealing, or excluding the remaining properties — is <s>naya</s> (standpoint). And since the properties are infinite, the <s>naya</s> has infinite divisions; yet, by way of devising a comprehensive classification, it has been shown as sevenfold in this manner. And this very conceptual determination, when it operates by way of concealing all remaining properties through the exclusive assertion of its preferred property, acquires the designation <s>durnaya</s> (false standpoint); for indeed these rival doctrines (<s>para-pravāda</s>) have their existence empowered by the force of that [exclusivist tendency]. children.text: . śabdâdi-naya-matâvalambino vaiyākaraṇâdaya iti. athêttham abhidadhīthā, yathā: katham ete 'vadhāraṇa-dvāreṇa svakam arthaṃ samarthayantas tad-viparītaṃ nirākurvāṇā durnayatāṃ pratipadyanta ity, atrôcyate -- evaṃ pravṛttau nirgocaratvān, nirgocarasya nayatvâyogāt. tathā hi: nayati kenacid aṃśena viśiṣṭam arthaṃ prāpayati yo 'bhiprāyaḥ sa nayaḥ, svâbhipreta-dharmāc cheṣa-dharma-pratikṣepa-dvāreṇa tu pravṛtto na kiñcin nayaty, eka-dharmâliṅgitasya vastuno 'sambhavād, bahir antaś câneka-dharma-parikarita-svabhāvasya tasya pratibhāsāt, tad-apahnava-kāriṇāṃ kadabhiprāyāṇāṃ pratibhāsa-bādhitatvenâlīkatvāt.
children.translated_text: Those who follow the views of the <s>śabda</s> (word) and other standpoints are the grammarians (<s>vaiyākaraṇas</s>) and others. Now if you were to say thus: how do these [standpoints], when establishing their own object through exclusive assertion while refuting the opposite, come to be <s>durnayas</s> (false standpoints)? — to that it is said: because when operating in that manner, they become objectless (<s>nirgocara</s>), and what is objectless cannot be a <s>naya</s>. For: a <s>naya</s> is a view that 'leads' (<s>nayati</s>), i.e., makes one reach a distinguished object through some particular aspect; but when operating through the rejection of the remaining properties from its preferred property, it does not lead to anything, because an object characterized by a single property is impossible — since that [object] appears both externally and internally as having a nature invested with multiple properties; and because those perverse views that deny that [multiplicity] are false, being contradicted by [the object's] appearance.
