tathā hi: yaḥ tāvan naigama-nayaḥ paraspara-viśliṣṭau sāmānya-viśeṣau pratyapīpadat, tad ayuktam. tayos tathā kadācana pratibhāsâbhāvāt. yac côktam: anuvartamānâikâkāra-parāmarśa-grāhyaṃ sāmānyaṃ yatra na tatra viśeṣa-pratibhāso, yatra ca viśiṣṭa-deśa-daśâvacchinna-bodha-nirgrāhyo viśeṣo na tatra sāmānyâvagatis, tad-vacana-mātram eva, dhava-khadira-palāśâdi-samasta-viśeṣâpasāraṇe vṛkṣatvâdi-sāmānya-pratibhāsâbhāvāt. dūrād viśeṣâgrahaṇe 'pi kevalaṃ tac cakāstîti cen, na, tatrâpy abhyantarī-bhūta-viśeṣa-pratibhāsāt, tad-virahe śaśa-viṣāṇa-rūpatvāt. evaṃ viśeṣā api na sāmānyād atyanta-vyatirekiṇaḥ pratibhānti, tan-nimagnānām eva teṣāṃ grahaṇād, itarathā sattāto 'tiricyamānā bhāvā niḥsvabhāvatām ātmasāt-kurvanti. tathā vṛkṣatvâdi-sāmānyebhyo 'pi bhedino vṛkṣâdayo na syus, tad-abheda-nibandhanatvāt tat-svarūpa-sthiteḥ. tasmāt tad eva saṃvedanam upasarjanī-kṛta-vaiṣamyaṃ pradhānī-kṛtâikâkāraṃ sāmānyaṃ gṛhṇātîty ucyate, nyak-kṛta-samatvam utkalita-nānātvaṃ punar viśeṣa-grahîti, samatva-nānātvayoḥ kathañcid bhedâbhedinoḥ parasparaṃ sarvârtheṣu bhāvāt, tad-abhāve tathā-vidha-pratibhāsânupapatteḥ. etena yad avādi "na câitau vibhinnāv api pratibhāsamānau sāmānya-viśeṣau kathañcin miśrayituṃ yuktāv" ity-ādi, tad apāstam avagantavyaṃ, vibhinnayoḥ pratibhāsâbhāvāt. vyavahāro 'pi sarvaḥ pradhānôpasarjana-dvāreṇa kathañcid itarêtarâvinirluṭhita-sāmānya-viśeṣa-sādhya eva; na hi sāmānyaṃ doha-vāhâdi-kriyāyām upayujyate, viśeṣāṇām eva tatrôpayogān, nâpi viśeṣā eva tat-kāriṇaḥ, gotva-śūnyānāṃ teṣāṃ vṛkṣâdy-aviśiṣṭatayā tat-karaṇa-sāmarthyâbhāvāt. kiṃ câtyanta-vyatireke sāmānya-viśeṣayor vṛkṣaṃ chindhîti coditaḥ kim iti tad-viśeṣe palāśâdauchedaṃ vidhatte? tatra tasya samavāyād iti cen, na, samavāya-grāhaka-pramāṇâbhāvād, bhāve 'pi viśliṣṭayor abheda-buddhy-utpādanâkṣamatvāt, tasyâpi vyatiriktatayā padârthântarâviśeṣān nityatvâikatva-sarva-gatatvâdibhiś ca sarvatra tat-karaṇa-prasaṅgāc ca. yat punar avādīr, yad uta: yadi sāmānyaṃ viśeṣa-niṣṭhaṃ, viśeṣo vā sāmānya-vyāptaḥ samupalabhyeta, tato viviktayos tayoḥ kvacid anupalambhād yo 'yaṃ vivikteṣu sāmānyeṣu viśeṣeṣu câbhidhānârtha-kriyā-lakṣaṇo vyavahāraḥ sa samastaḥ pralayaṃ yāyāl, lolī-bhāvena tad-vivekasya kartum aśakyatvāt, tad apy asamīcīnaṃ, yato yady api parasparâviviktayoḥ sāmānya-viśeṣayoḥ sarvatrôpalambhas, tathâpi yatrâiva pramātur arthitvaṃ tad eva sāmānyaṃ, viśeṣān vā pradhānī-kṛtya tad-gocaraṃ dhvanim artha-kriyāṃ vā pravartayatîtarasyâpy upasarjana-bhāvena tatra vyāpārāt, tad-vikalasyêtarasyâpi śaśa-viśāṇāyamānatayā kvacid anupayogāt. kiṃ câtyanta-vyatirekiṇi viśeṣebhyaḥ sāmānye vṛtti-vikalpôpalambha-nūtana-viśeṣa-sambandhâdi-dvāreṇa dūṣaṇa-mudgara-kadambakaṃ mūrdhani patad durviṣahaṃ syāt. tathā hi: tat teṣu kathaṃ varteta -- sāmastyenâikadeśena vā? sāmastya-pakṣe prativiśeṣaṃ parisamāptatayā sāmānya-bahutva-prasaṅgo, 'niṣṭaṃ câitad, ekatvâbhupagama-kṣateḥ. ekadeśena vartane punar yāvanto viśeṣās tāvantas tad-aṃśāḥ prasajanti, na câitad asti, sāmānyasya niravayavatvāt; sâvayavatve 'pi punas te 'bhinnā bhinnā vā. yady abhinnā viśeṣās, tarhy abhedinaḥ kiṃ nêṣyante, viśeṣâbhāvāt. bheda-pakṣe punas teṣv api tat kathaṃ varteta -- sāmastyenâikadeśena vêti? tad eva codyam alabdha-pariniṣṭham avatarati, tan nâtyanta-bhedino vṛttiḥ sambhavati. kiṃ ca, yady ekaṃ sāmānyaṃ bhedavat samasta-viśeṣeṣu varteta, tadâika-viśeṣôpalambha-kāle tad upalambhyate na vā? yady ādyaḥ pakṣas, tasyâikatayā sarvatrôpalambhāt, vyāpya-grahaṇâbhāve vyāpaka-grahaṇâsiddher, nikhila-tad-vyāpya-viśeṣa-grahaṇam āsajyeta, na câitad asti, puro-varti-viśeṣasyâiva sākṣāt-karaṇāc, cheṣa-viśeṣāṇām asannidhānāt; sannihita-viśeṣa-niṣṭham eva tad upalabhyate. tasyâiva tad-vyañjakatvād, itareṣāṃ tad-abhāvād iti cen nâika-svabhāvasya khaṇḍaśo vyañjanâyogāt sannihita-viśeṣa-vyañjitam eva tat sarvatra svabhāvântarâbhāvāt sarva-viśeṣa-gataṃ ca tad-rūpam, atas tad-darśanaṃ kena vāryeta. atha dvitīyaḥ kalpas, tathā sati yathâika-viśeṣôpalambha-samaye nôpalabhyate, tathā śeṣa-viśeṣôpalambha-kāle 'pi nôpalabhyeta, viśeṣâbhāvāt. atas tad-abhāva evôktaḥ syāt, kevalasyôpalambhâbhāvāt. upalambhe 'pi sva-svabhāva-sthiter viśeṣa-rūpatâpattiḥ. tathā cirantana-viśeṣa-vyavasthita-sattākaṃ tan nūtana-viśeṣôtpāde sati kathaṃ tena saha sambandham anubhavet? na tāvad viśeṣântarebhyas tad utpitsu-viśeṣa-deśaṃ gantum arhati,
niṣkriyatvāt. nâpi tatrâivâbhavad, viśeṣôtpādāt prāk tad-deśe tad-upalambhâbhāvāt. nâpi viśeṣeṇâiva sahôtpadyate, nityatvān, nityasya côtpatti-virodhāt. athâitad-doṣa-parijihīrṣayā tat sakriyākam abhidhīyeta, tathâpi pūrva-vyakti-tyāgena vā nūtana-viśeṣa-deśam ākrāmet, tad-abhāvena vā? na tāvad adyaḥ pakṣaś, cirantana-vyaktīnāṃ sāmānya-vikalatayā tat-sambandha-sādhya-buddhi-dhvani-viraha-prasaṅgāt. na câitad asty, aparâpara-viśeṣôtpāde 'pi prācīna-vyaktiṣu tad-darśanāt. atha dvitīyaḥ kalpas, tad apy asambaddhaṃ, niravayavasya pūrva-vyakti-tyāga-vaikalye saty utpitsu-vyaktiṃ pratigamanâbhāvāt. sâvayava-pakṣasya punaḥ prāg evâpāstatvān, nâitad-abhyupagama-dvāreṇa parihāraḥ śreyān. anyac ca: vyatirikta-sāmānya-sambandhād yadi bhāvāḥ samānā, na svarūpeṇa, tadā sattva-sambandhāt prāg bhāvāḥ santo 'santo vā. santaś ced apārthakaḥ sattā-sambandho, 'nyathânavasthā prasajyeta, punaḥ-sattântara-sambandhânivāraṇāt. asantaś ced atyantâsatām api gaganâravindâdīnāṃ sattā-sambandhād bhāva-rūpatâpadyeta. evaṃ dravyatva-guṇatva-karmatva-gotvâdi-sāmānyeṣv api samastam etad vācyam, eka-yoga-kṣematvāt, tan na parasparam atyanta-vyatirekiṇau sāmānya-viśeṣau kathañcana ghaṭām āṭīkete. ata eva tat-samarthana-pravaṇas tat-tādātmya-pratikṣepako 'bhiprāyo nirālambanatvān naigama-durnaya-vyapadeśam āskandati, tādātmyôpekṣayâiva sāmānya-viśeṣa-vyatireka-samarthakasya naigama-nayatvād, vyatirekiṇor api tayor vastuni kathañcid bhāvād, itarathā vivakṣayâpi tathā darśayitum aśakyatvāt, pradhānôpasarjana-bhāvasya dvaya-niṣṭhatvāt, atyanta-tādātmye tat-kāriṇyā vivakṣāyā api nirgocaratā-prasaṅgāt. tasmāt kathañcid bhedâbhedināv evâitau, tad-anyatara-samarthakaḥ punar nirālambanatvād durnayatāṃ svī-karotîti sthitam.
children.translated_text: For: as regards the <s>naigama-naya</s> (figurative standpoint) that maintained that the universal and the particular are mutually separated — that is untenable, because there is never an appearance of them as such [i.e., completely separated]. And what was stated — namely that 'the universal, graspable through a cognition comprehending a single recurring form, is such that where it is, there is no manifestation of the particular; and where the particular, graspable by a cognition directed toward objects delimited by specific place and time, is present, there is no apprehension of the universal' — that is mere verbiage, because in the absence of all the particulars such as <s>dhava</s>, <s>khadira</s>, <s>palāśa</s>, etc., there is no appearance of the universal such as 'tree-ness.' If [you say] that even when the particular is not grasped from a distance, that [universal] alone shines forth — no, because even there the particular is internally present in the appearance; in its absence, [the universal] would be like a hare's horn. Similarly, the particulars too do not appear as completely different from the universal, since they are grasped only as immersed in it; otherwise, entities separated from <s>sattā</s> (existence) would assume the condition of being without own-nature. Likewise, trees and the like, being different from the universals such as 'tree-ness,' would not exist, because the persistence of their nature depends on non-difference from that [universal]. Therefore, it is that very cognition which, having subordinated the dissimilarity and made dominant the one recurring form, is said to grasp the universal; while that which, having suppressed the sameness and brought forth the diversity, [grasps] the particular — since sameness and diversity, being somehow both different and non-different, exist in all objects mutually; in their absence, such an appearance would be impossible. By this, what was said — namely 'these two, universal and particular, though appearing as distinct, cannot in any way be mixed,' etc. — should be understood as refuted, because there is no appearance of [them as completely] distinct. All practical activity too is accomplished only through universal and particular that are somehow not completely separated from each other, by way of the principal and the subordinate. For the universal is not employed in activities such as milking, carrying, etc., since only the particulars are useful there; nor are the particulars alone the agents of that, because without 'cow-ness,' they, being no different from trees and the like, would lack the capacity to do that. Moreover, if the universal and particular were completely different, why does one who is told 'cut the tree' perform the cutting on a particular [tree] such as <s>palāśa</s>? If [you say] because of <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) of that [universal] in that [particular] — no, because there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> that grasps <s>samavāya</s>; and even if it existed, it would be incapable of producing a cognition of identity between two separated things; and since that [<s>samavāya</s>] too is separate, being no different from another category, and because of its permanence, unity, and omnipresence, there would be the absurd consequence of it producing that [identity-cognition] everywhere. And what you further stated — namely: if the universal were apprehended as residing in the particular, or the particular as pervaded by the universal, then, given that in some cases neither is apprehended in its distinct form, the entire practical activity of designation and efficacy pertaining to distinct universals and particulars would be annulled, since their distinction cannot be made through wavering — that too is improper. For although the universal and the particular, being mutually inseparable, are apprehended everywhere, nevertheless, whichever — whether the universal or the particulars — the knower is interested in, it is precisely that which, by making it principal, generates the sound or practical activity pertaining to it, while the other too operates there in a subordinate capacity; and the other, being deprived of that [role], since it amounts to a hare's horn, is of no use somewhere. Moreover, if the universal were completely different from the particulars, a cluster of refutation-hammers would fall unbearably upon its head through [problems of] inherence, conceptual alternative, apprehension, connection with novel particulars, and so forth. For: how would it inhere in them — in its entirety or in part? In the position of entirety, since it would be completely present in each particular, there would be the absurd consequence of the universal being many, and this is undesirable, since it would violate the acceptance of its unity. In the position of partial inherence, however, as many particulars as there are, so many parts of it would absurdly follow; but this is not so, because the universal is partless. Even if it had parts, are they non-different or different [from each other]? If the particulars are non-different, then why are they not accepted as non-different [from the universal], since there is no [ground for] particular difference? In the position of difference, how would it [the universal] inhere in those [different parts] too — in its entirety or in part? The very same objection descends without resolution — therefore inherence in completely different [things] is not possible. Moreover, if the one universal, being multi-located, were to inhere in all the particulars, then at the time of apprehending one particular, would it be apprehended or not? If the first position — then since it is one, being apprehended everywhere, and since in the absence of grasping the pervaded the grasping of the pervader is not established, the grasping of all the particulars pervaded by it would absurdly follow; but this is not so, since only the particular in front is directly perceived, the remaining particulars being absent. [If you say] that it [the universal] is apprehended only as residing in the present particular because only that [particular] manifests it, while the others lack that [manifesting capacity] — no, because what has a single nature cannot be manifested piecemeal; being manifested by the present particular alone, since there is no other nature elsewhere, and since that form is present in all particulars, by what would its perception be prevented? If the second alternative — then in that case, just as it is not apprehended at the time of apprehending one particular, so too it would not be apprehended at the time of apprehending the remaining particulars, since there is no distinguishing feature. Hence, the absence of that [universal] alone would be stated, since it is never apprehended by itself. Even if apprehended, since it persists in its own nature, it would turn out to have the nature of a particular. Similarly, since that [universal] has its existence established in long-standing particulars, how would it experience a relation with a newly arising particular? It cannot go from other particulars to the place of the about-to-arise particular, because it is actionless. Nor did it already exist there, because prior to the arising of the particular, it is not apprehended in that place. Nor is it produced together with the particular, because it is eternal, and production is contradictory with eternality. If, wishing to avoid this defect, one declares it to be capable of action — even then, would it move to the place of the new particular by abandoning the prior instances, or without abandoning them? Not the first alternative, because the long-standing instances, being deprived of the universal, would absurdly lack the cognition, speech, etc. that are accomplished through relation with it; but this is not so, because even when subsequent particulars arise, that [universal] is observed in the prior instances. If the second alternative, that too is incoherent — because for a partless [entity], when there is no deficiency in [being present in] the prior instances, there would be no going toward the about-to-arise instance. Since the position of having parts has already been refuted, a resolution through that acceptance would not be preferable. Furthermore: if entities are similar due to relation with a separate universal, and not by their own nature, then prior to the relation with <s>sattā</s> (existence), are the entities existent or non-existent? If existent, then the relation with <s>sattā</s> is pointless; otherwise an infinite regress would follow, since a further relation with another <s>sattā</s> cannot be prevented. If non-existent, then even completely non-existent things such as sky-lotuses would become real entities through relation with <s>sattā</s>. The same entire [set of objections] should be stated for the universals such as <s>dravyatva</s> (substancehood), <s>guṇatva</s> (quality-hood), <s>karmatva</s> (action-hood), <s>gotva</s> (cow-ness), etc., since they share the same logical fate. Therefore, the universal and the particular, being completely different from each other, cannot in any way be made to fit together. Precisely for this reason, the view that is inclined toward establishing that [complete difference] and that rejects their identity — being without foundation, it incurs the designation of <s>naigama-durnaya</s> (false figurative standpoint), because the <s>naigama-naya</s> consists precisely in establishing the difference of the universal and particular with due regard to their identity; and because even those two, though different, somehow exist in the object; otherwise, it would be impossible to show them as such even through a statement of intent; because the relation of principal and subordinate depends on both; and because in absolute identity, even the statement of intent that produces that [distinction] would absurdly become objectless. Therefore, these two are indeed somehow both different and non-different; the view that establishes only one of the two, however, being without foundation, assumes the status of a <s>durnaya</s> (false standpoint) — this is established.

children.text: tathā saṅgraho 'py aśeṣa-viśeṣa-pratikṣepa-mukhena sāmānyam ekaṃ samarthayamāno durnayaḥ, tad-upekṣā-dvāreṇâiva tasya nayatvāt, viśeṣa-vikalasya sāmānyasyâsambhavāt. tathā hi: yat tāvad uktaṃ -- yad uta "viśeṣāḥ sāmānyād vyatirekiṇo 'vyatirekiṇo vā. vyatireka-pakṣe niḥsvabhāvatvaṃ, niḥsattākatvāt. avyatireka-pakṣe bhāva-mātraṃ, tad-avyatiriktatvāt, tat-svarūpavad" iti -- tad ayuktaṃ, viśeṣa-vādino 'py evaṃ-vidha-vikalpa-sambhavāt. tathā hi: viśeṣebhyaḥ sāmānyaṃ vyatiriktam avyatiriktaṃ vā. vyatiriktaṃ cen, na tarhi sāmānyaṃ, sva-svarūpa-vyavasthitatayā viśeṣa-rūpatvāt. avyatiriktaṃ cet, tathâpi na sāmānyaṃ, viśeṣâvyatiriktatvād eva tat-svarūpavat. yad apy avādy -- "anādy-avidyā-bala-pravṛtto viśeṣa-vyavahāras, tāttvikaṃ sāmānyaṃ" -- tad api vacana-mātram eva, yukti-riktatvāt, sāmānyam evânādy-avidyā-darśitaṃ, viśeṣāḥ punaḥ pāramārthikā iti viśeṣa-vādino 'pi vadato vaktra-bhaṅgâbhāvāt. yat punar viśeṣa-grāhaka-pramāṇâbhāvaṃ pratipādayatâbhyadhāyi, yad uta "pratyakṣaṃ bhāva-sampādita-sattākaṃ tam eva sākṣāt-karoti nâbhāvaṃ, tasyânutpādakatvād" ity-ādi, tad ayuktataraṃ, yataḥ kenêdaṃ bhavato 'tyanta-suhṛdā niveditaṃ: "bhāva eva kevalaḥ pratyakṣam utthāpayati, na punar abhāvo 'pi" [iti]? abhāva-vyāpārâbhāva-pratipādaka-yukti-kalāpenêti ced mugdha-vipratārito 'si, tad-vyāpārâbhāvâsiddheḥ, sad-asad-rūpa-vastunaḥ samasta-kriyāsu vyāpārād, bhāva-tādātmyena vyavasthitasyâbhāvasya vyāpāre virodhâbhāvāt. kathaṃ bhāvâbhāvayos tādātmyaṃ, virodhād? iti cen, na, pramāṇa-prasiddhe virodhâbhāvāt. tathā hi: ghaṭâdikaḥ padârthâtmā svarūpeṇa san, na paṭâdi-rūpeṇâpîti bhāvâbhāvâtmakaḥ. yadi punaḥ kathañcin nâbhāvâtmakaḥ syāt, tadā paṭâdi-rūpeṇâpi bhāvāt sarvâtmakaḥ prāpnoti. yuktam etad, ata eva bheda-prapañca-vilaya-siddhir iti cet, syād evâitad, yadi paṭâdy-abhāvâikântāc
children.translated_text: Likewise, the <s>saṅgraha</s> (synthesis standpoint) too, when establishing the universal as one through the rejection of all particulars, is a <s>durnaya</s> (false standpoint), because its status as a <s>naya</s> consists only in the disregard [rather than rejection] of [the particulars], and because a universal deprived of particulars is impossible. For: as regards what was stated — namely 'the particulars are either different from the universal or not different. In the position of difference, they would be without own-nature, because they lack existence. In the position of non-difference, they amount to mere existence, because they are non-different from it, like its own nature' — that is untenable, because the same kind of dilemma is possible for the proponent of particulars too. For: is the universal different from the particulars or non-different? If different, then it is not a universal, because it has the nature of a particular by being established in its own separate form. If non-different, then too it is not a universal, because being non-different from the particular, it is of the latter's nature. And what was said — 'practical activity pertaining to particulars is set in motion by the force of beginningless <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance); the universal is the reality' — that too is mere verbiage, being devoid of reasoning; since the proponent of particulars too can say without any awkwardness that the universal alone is shown by beginningless <s>avidyā</s>, while the particulars are ultimately real. And what was asserted while demonstrating the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s> that grasps the particular — namely 'perception, having its existence produced by the existent, directly apprehends only that [existent], not absence, since [absence] is not its producer,' etc. — that is even more untenable. For who, being your dear friend, informed you that 'only the existent alone generates perception, but absence does not'? If [you say] by the collection of arguments demonstrating the absence of the operation of absence — you have been deceived like a fool, because the absence of that operation is not established, since the object, having the nature of both being and non-being, operates in all activities; and because there is no contradiction in the operation of absence that is established as identical with being. How can there be identity of being and non-being, given that they are contradictory? — no, because in what is established by <s>pramāṇa</s>, there is no contradiction. For: an object-nature such as a pot, being existent in its own form, is not [existent] in the form of cloth, etc. — thus it is of the nature of both being and non-being. If, however, it were in no way of the nature of non-being, then since it would exist even in the form of cloth, etc., it would become the nature of everything. [If you say] this is correct — precisely this establishes the dissolution of the manifold of difference — [we reply]: this would be so if from the absolute absence of cloth, etc.

children.text: 'pi mano-ratha-pūraṇaṃ na syāt; tathā hi: paṭâdi-vivikto ghaṭo 'nubhūyate, na ca paṭâdy-abhāvo bhāvena saha tādātmyam anubhavati, tasmād abhāvâtmaka evâyam, evaṃ paṭâdayo 'pîtarêtarâpekṣayêti śūnyatvâpattiḥ. tasmāt svarūpam ābibhrāṇaṃ para-rūpebhyo vyāvṛttam eva vastu sarva-kriyāsu vyāpriyata iti bhāvâbhāvâtmakasyâiva vyāpāraḥ, svarūpa-dhāraṇasya bhāvatvāt, para-rūpa-vyāvartanasyâbhāvatvād iti. evaṃ sva-gocara-pratyakṣôtpādane 'pi vyāpriyate, tataś ca tad-rūpam eva tat sākṣāt-kuryād iti svarūpa-niyate para-rūpebhyo vyāvṛtta eva vastuni pratyakṣaṃ pravartate, taj-janyatvān, na bhāva-mātre, tasya kevalasya svarūpâvyavasthiter utpādakatvâyogāt. na ca janakatvād artho grāhyo janyatvād vā jñānaṃ grāhakam, atiprasaṅgād ity uktaṃ, kiṃ tarhy āvaraṇa-vicchedâder labdha-sattākaṃ grahaṇa-pariṇāmāj jñānaṃ gṛhṇāty, arthas tu sannidhānâder gṛhyate, sa cânuvartamāna-vyāvartamāna-rūpa eva pratīyata iti tathā-bhūto 'bhyupagantavyo, na kevala-sāmānya-rūpa iti. sad-asad-aṃśayoḥ katham ekatrâvasthānam iti cet, tādātmyenêti brūmaḥ. nanu tādātmye bhāva-mātram abhāva-mātraṃ vâpadyetêtarêtarâvyavatiriktatvād, itarêtara-svarūpavat, tan nôbhaya-rūpa-vastu-siddhiḥ. nâitad asti, tādātmyasya sambandhatvāt, sambandhasya ca dvaya-niṣṭhatvāt, tad-abhāve kasya kena sambandho, nirgocaratvāt? tasmād etau sad-asad-aṃśau dharmi-rūpatayâbhedinau, vastunaḥ sad-asad-rūpasyâikatvād, dharma-rūpatayā punar vivakṣitau bhedam anubhavataḥ, svarūpeṇa bhāvāt, para-rūpeṇa tv abhāvād iti. tad evaṃ pratyakṣe vivikta-vastu-grāhiṇi sakala-pramāṇa-praṣṭhe prasādhite śeṣa-pramāṇāny api tad-anusāritayā viviktam eva sva-gocaraṃ sthāpayantîti. tad-apalāpī kevala-sāmānya-pratiṣṭhāpakaḥ kad-abhiprāyaḥ saṅgraha-durnaya-vyapadeśaṃ svī-kurute, viśeṣâpekṣayâiva sāmānya-sthāpakasya saṅgraha-nayatvād iti.
children.translated_text: too would have their wish fulfilled; but [they would not]: for a pot is experienced as distinct from cloth, etc., and the absence of cloth, etc. does not experience identity with the existent [pot] — therefore this [pot] is of the nature of absence precisely [insofar as it is not cloth, etc.], and similarly cloth and the like too, in relation to each other — hence the absurd consequence of voidness (<s>śūnyatva</s>) [would follow]. Therefore, it is the object, bearing its own form, distinguished from other forms, that engages in all activities — thus it is the operation of what is of the nature of both being and non-being: the bearing of its own form being its existence (<s>bhāvatva</s>), and the exclusion from other forms being its non-existence (<s>abhāvatva</s>). Thus, even in producing the perception that is its own object, it operates; and therefore that [perception] would directly apprehend precisely that form — thus perception operates with respect to an object that is determined by its own form and excluded from other forms, being produced by that [determinate object], not with respect to mere being, since that alone, lacking determination of its own form, would be incapable of being a producer. And it has been said that the object should not be considered the grasped merely because it is a cause, nor knowledge the grasper merely because it is an effect, due to overextension; rather, knowledge grasps through the transformation of grasping, having obtained its existence from the removal of obscuration and the like; and the object is grasped due to its presence and the like. And that [object] is cognized as having both persisting and changing forms — therefore it should be acknowledged as being of such a nature, not as having merely the form of a universal. If [you ask] how can the aspects of being and non-being coexist in one [thing] — we say: through identity (<s>tādātmya</s>). But in identity, [would it] not turn out to be mere being or mere non-being, since each is non-different from the other, and would be of the other's nature — and so the reality having both natures would not be established? This is not so, because identity is a relation, and a relation depends on two [terms]; in its absence, what would be related to what, since there would be no object [for the relation]? Therefore, these two aspects of being and non-being, as the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>), are non-different — because the object, having the nature of both being and non-being, is one; but when intended as properties (<s>dharma</s>), they admit of difference — existing in their own form, but not existing in other forms. Thus, once perception, the chief of all <s>pramāṇas</s>, has been established as grasping the distinct object, the remaining <s>pramāṇas</s> too, following it, establish their own object as distinct. The perverse view that denies that and establishes mere universals alone assumes the designation of <s>saṅgraha-durnaya</s> (false synthesis standpoint), because the <s>saṅgraha-naya</s> consists in establishing the universal only with due regard to the particular.

children.text: tathā vyavahāro 'pi pramāṇa-prasiddhaṃ vastu-svarūpaṃ nihnuvāno yukti-riktam avicārita-ramaṇīyaṃ loka-vyavahāra-mārgânusāri samarthayamāno durnayatām ātmani nidhatte, loka-vyavahāra-prasādhakasyâpîtarâniṣṭau vyavasthānâbhāvāt. tathā hi: yad idaṃ kiyat-kāla-bhāvi sthūratām ābibhrāṇaṃ loka-vyavahāra-kāri ghaṭâdikaṃ bhavatas tāttvikam abhipretaṃ tan nâkasmikaṃ, kiṃ tarhi nitya-paramâṇu-ghaṭitam, itarathā niṣkāraṇatvena sarvadā bhāvâbhāva-prasaṅgāt. na te paramâṇavas tathā pratibhāntîti cen, nâta eva teṣām anumānataḥ siddhiḥ. yadi punar yad eva sākṣān na viśada-darśane cakāsti tat sakalam apalapyeta, hanta bahv idānīm apalapanīyaṃ, ghaṭâdi-vastuno 'py arvāg-bhāga-varti-tvaṅ-mātra-pratibhāsān madhya-para-bhāgâdīnām apalāpa-prasaṅgāt, tathā ca loka-vyavahāra-kāritâpi viśīryeta, tāvatā tad-asiddheḥ. athâtrânumāna-balena vyavahāra-kṣama-sampūrṇa-vastunaḥ sādhanam, evaṃ tarhi bhūta-bhāvi-paryāya-paramâṇu-sādhanam api kriyatāṃ, viśeṣâbhāvāt. tathā hi: yathā bāhya-tvaṅ-mātra-pratibhāse 'pi sarva-vastūnāṃ tāvatā vyavahārâbhāvān madhya-bhāgâdi-sādhanena sampūrṇāni tat-samarthāni tāni sādhyante, tathâiva kiyat-kāla-bhāvi-ghanâkāra-darśane 'py anādy-ananta-paramâṇu-tādādmya-vyavasthita-śarīrāṇi tāni sādhyantāṃ, tad-abhāve 'pi teṣām anupapatteḥ. tathā hi: vyavahārâvatāriṇo darśana-yogyasyâdya-paryāyasya tāvad atīta-paryāyânabhyupagame nirhetukatvaṃ, tatra côkto doṣaḥ. tad-utpādakânantara-paryāyêṣṭau punas taj-janaka-paryāyo 'py abhyupagantavya ity anādi-paryāya-paramparā siddhim adhyāsīta. tathā vyavahārâvatāri-vastu-paryanta-paryāyasya paryāyântarânutpādakatve balād avastutvam āḍhaukate, bhavan-nīter evârtha-kriyā-karaṇa-vaikalyāt. tad-utpādakatve punar asāv apy apara-paryāyôtpādaka ity ananta-paryāya-mālôpapadyate. tathā ghanâkāro 'pi viśada-darśanena sākṣāt-kriyamāṇo niṣpradeśa-paryantâvayava-vyatirekeṇa nôpapadyate, kara-caraṇâdy-avayavānāṃ khaṇḍaśo bhidyamānatayâvayavi-rūpatvāt, tad-avayavānām apy avayavântara-ghaṭitatvāt. paramâṇava eva paryantâvayavāḥ paramârthato ghanâkāra-hetavas; tad-abhāve punar ākasmiko 'sau sarvatrôpalabhyeta, na vā kvacid, viśeṣâbhāvāt. etena yad avādi: loka-vyavahārâvatāriṇaḥ pramāṇam anugrāhakam asti vastuno nêtarasyêty-ādi, tad api pratikṣiptam avagantavyaṃ, dṛśyamānârthânyathânupapattyâiva tat-sādhanāt. yat punar uktaṃ: "kiṃ teṣām atītânāgata-paryāya-paramâṇv-ādīnāṃ paryālocanena loka-vyavahārânupayogitayâvastutvād" ity-ādi, tad ayuktam, upekṣayā vārtamānika-vastuno 'nupayogitvenâvastutva-prāpteḥ, sarvasya sarva-lokânupayogitvāt. kasyacid upayogitayā vastutve teṣām api sā samasty eva, sarva-jña-jñānâdi-gocaratvād ity āstāṃ tāvat. tad evaṃ pramāṇa-prasiddhârthâpalāpitvād vyavahāro durnayaḥ, tad-upekṣayā vyavahārânupāti-vastu-samarthakasya vyavahāra-nayatvād iti.
children.translated_text: Likewise, the <s>vyavahāra</s> (conventional standpoint) too, denying the real nature of things established by <s>pramāṇa</s> and establishing [instead] what is devoid of reasoning and charming only when unexamined, following the path of worldly convention — assumes the status of a <s>durnaya</s> (false standpoint) upon itself, because even [the standpoint] that establishes worldly convention cannot maintain its position when the other [i.e., the pramāṇa-established reality] is not accepted. For: this [object] of yours — a pot, etc. — that endures for some time, possesses gross form, and produces worldly practical activity, which you consider to be the ultimate reality — it is not without a cause; rather, it is constituted by eternal atoms, since otherwise, being without a cause, there would be the absurd consequence of its existing or not existing at all times. If [you say] those atoms do not appear as such — precisely for that reason they are established through inference. If, however, everything that does not clearly shine forth in direct perception is to be denied — well then, much is now to be denied, since even for the object such as a pot, because only the outermost skin-surface appears, there would be the absurd consequence of denying the middle and far portions, etc.; and thus even its capacity for worldly practical activity would be shattered, since it would not be established by that much [alone]. If here the establishment of a complete object capable of practical activity is through the force of inference — then let the establishment of past and future modes, atoms, etc. also be carried out, since there is no distinguishing feature. For: just as, even when only the outermost skin-surface appears, since practical activity would not be possible for all objects on that basis alone, the objects are established as complete and capable of that [practical activity] through the establishment of the middle portion, etc. — in exactly the same way, even when only a gross form enduring for some time is perceived, let those objects be established as having bodies constituted by the identity of beginningless and endless atoms, since even those [objects] would be impossible without them. For: if the prior mode of the first mode that enters into practical activity and is fit for perception is not accepted, it would be causeless — and that defect has been stated. If, however, a mode immediately preceding that, which produces it, is accepted, then the mode that generates that mode too must be acknowledged — thus a beginningless succession of modes would be established. Similarly, if the final mode of the object that enters into practical activity does not produce another mode, it would by force assume the status of non-reality, because by your own principle, it would lack the capacity to perform practical efficacy. If it does produce [another mode], then that [subsequent mode] too would produce yet another — thus an endless chain of modes is established. Similarly, the gross form too, when directly apprehended through clear perception, is impossible without parts down to the partless ultimate constituents — because parts such as hands, feet, etc. have the nature of composite wholes as they can be progressively divided, and because the parts of those parts too are constituted by further parts. The atoms alone are the ultimate parts and the real causes of the gross form; in their absence, that [gross form] would either appear everywhere spontaneously, or nowhere at all, since there would be no distinguishing feature. By this, what was said — 'there is a <s>pramāṇa</s> that supports only the object that enters worldly practical activity, not the other,' etc. — should also be understood as refuted, because that [worldly object] itself is established only through the otherwise-impossible-to-explain nature of what is observed. And what was further stated — 'what is the point of investigating those [past and future modes, atoms, etc.], since they are non-real because useless for worldly practical activity,' etc. — that is untenable, because through neglect, even the present object would turn out to be non-real as useless, since everything is useless for all [possible] people [in the world]. If reality consists in being useful to someone, then that same [usefulness] fully applies to those [past/future modes, atoms] as well, since they are the objects of the omniscient one's knowledge and the like — but let that suffice for now. Thus, because it denies the object established by <s>pramāṇa</s>, the <s>vyavahāra</s> is a <s>durnaya</s> (false standpoint), since its status as a <s>naya</s> consists in establishing reality that accords with convention only by disregarding [rather than denying the pramāṇa-established reality].

children.text:
atha ṛjusūtro 'pi dṛṣṭâpalāpenâdṛṣṭam eva kṣaṇa-kṣayi-paramâṇu-lakṣaṇaṃ vastu-svarūpaṃ paramârthatayā manyamāno durnayatām āskandati, dṛśyamāna-sthira-sthūrârthâpahnave nirmūlatayā svâbhipreta-vastu-samarthaka-parāmarśasyôtthānâbhāvāt. tathā hi: svâvayava-vyāpinaṃ kālântara-saṃcariṣṇum ākāraṃ sākṣāl lakṣayan paścāt kuyukti-vikalpena vivecayed, yad utâiṣa sthira-sthūro dṛśyamānaḥ khalv ākāro na ghaṭām iyarti. vicārâkṣamatvād ity-ādinā na ca dṛṣṭam adṛṣṭa-sandarśakaiḥ kuyukti-vikalpair bādhituṃ śakyaṃ, sarvatrânāśvāsa-prasaṅgāt. athâbhidadhīthā: "manda-manda-prakāśe pradeśe rajjau viṣa-dhara-bhrāntiḥ prāktanī yathôdīcīnena tan-nirṇaya-kāriṇā vikalpena bādhyate, tathêdam api sthira-sthūra-darśanaṃ kṣaṇa-kṣayi-paramâṇu-prasādhaka-parāmarśena, kim atrâyuktam?" nâitad asti, rajju-pratibhāsasyâiva prāk-pravṛtta-viṣa-dhara-bhrānty-apanoda-dakṣatvāt, tad-abhāve ca vikalpa-śatair api nivartayitum aśakyatvāt. atrâpy atīta-vartsyator vinaṣṭânutpannatayâsannihitatvāt, sthūrâvayavānāṃ ca svâvayaveṣu bhedâbheda-dvāreṇa paryālocyamānānām avasthānâbhāvāt kṣaṇa-kṣayi-paramâṇava eva pratibhānti, tataś ca pratibhāsa eva sthira-sthūra-darśanasya bādhaka iti ced, evaṃ tarhi pratibhāsasyôpadeśa-gamyatânupapattes, tathâiva vyavahāraḥ pravarteta. pāścātya-mithyā-vikalpa-viplavān na pravartata iti cen, nânyatrâpy asyôttarasya viplava-hetutvāt. tathā hi: dhavale jalajâdau pratibhāte 'pi nīlo 'yam adhyakṣeṇâvalokitaḥ; pāścātya-mithyā-vikalpa-viplavāt tu dhavalaḥ pratibhātîti bhavan-nyāyena śaṭhaḥ pratijānānaḥ kena vāryeta. tan na dṛṣṭâpalāpaḥ kartuṃ śakya iti sthira-sthūra-vastu-siddhis, tasyâiva darśanād, itarasya tad-darśana-dvāreṇa sādhyamānasyânumeyatvāt, tad-aniṣṭau tasyâpy asiddheḥ. etena sthira-sthūra-vastuno 'rtha-kriyā-viraha-pratipādanam api prativyūḍhaṃ, tathā-vidhasyâiva sarva-kriyāsu vyāpāra-darśanāt kṣaṇa-kṣayiṇo 'rtha-kriyā-niṣedhāc ca, yathôktaṃ prāk: "kṣaṇa-bhaṅguro hy arthâtmā svakṣane pūrvaṃ paścād vā kāryaṃ kuryād ity-ādi. kiṃ ca, sattva-puruṣatva-caitanyâdibhir bāla-kumāra-yuva-sthaviratva-harṣa-viṣādâdibhiś cânuvartamāna-vyāvartamāna-rūpasya sarvasya vastunaḥ pratīter dravya-paryāyâtmakatvam, abhedasya dravyatvād, bhedasya paryāya-rūpatvād iti. tataś ca bhūta-bhāvi-kṣaṇayor asannidhāna-dvāreṇa vārtamānika-kṣaṇasyâivârtha-kriyā-kāritva-pratipādanaṃ nâsmād-bādhā-karaṃ, paryāyāṇāṃ krama-bhāvitayā vartamāna-paryāyâliṅgitasyâiva dravyasyârtha-kriyā-karaṇa-caturatvāt. [na] kevalaṃ tat tri-kāla-vyāpi, draṣṭâpi dravya-rūpatayā tathā-bhūta eva. tataś ca kṣaṇika-paryāya-tiro-dhāna-dvāreṇa tad-rūpa-saṅkalanāt sthiram evêdaṃ samasta-kriyāsu vyāpriyata iti pratīti-vīthim avatarati, sthairyasyâpi tāttvikatvāt, kṣaṇika-paryāyāṇāṃ vidyamānānām apy agrahaṇāt, prākṛta-loka-jñānasyâvaraṇa-kṣayôpaśamâpekṣitayā katicid-aṃśa-viṣayatvāt. yadi punar dravya-buddhiḥ paryāya-paramparā-darśana-balâyātatvād atāttvikī kalpyeta, tadā pūrva-paryāyasyôttara-paryāyôtpādane sânvayatvaṃ niranvayatvaṃ vā vaktavyaṃ, gaty-antarâbhāvāt. sânvayatve dravyaṃ paryāyântareṇâbhihitaṃ syān; niranvayatve punar nirhetutayôttara-paryāyânutpāda-prasaṅgaḥ. tan nôbhaya-rūpa-vastu-vyatirekeṇârtha-kriyā-siddhiḥ. na cârtha-kriyā vastu-lakṣaṇaṃ, śabda-vidyut-pradīpâdi-carama-kṣaṇānāṃ kṣanântarânārambhakatvenâvastutva-prāptes, tad-avastutve punar upāntya-kṣaṇasyâpi vastuni vyāpārâbhāvād; evaṃ yāvat sarva-kṣaṇānāṃ saṅkalikayā vastutvam. atha kṣaṇântarânārambhe 'pi sva-gocara-jñāna-janakatvam artha-kriyā parikalpyeta, tathā saty atīta-bhāvi-paryāya-paramparâpi yogi-jñāna-gocaratāṃ yātîti vastutvaṃ svī-kuryāt. tan nârtha-kriyā vastu-lakṣaṇam, api tûtpāda-vyaya-dhrauvya-yuktatā, pramāṇa-pratiṣṭhitatvāt. utpāda-vyayau dhrauvyena saha viruddhāv iti cet, kuto 'yaṃ virodhaḥ: pramāṇād apramāṇād vā? na tāvad ādyaḥ pakṣaḥ, sarva-pramāṇānāṃ bahir antaś ca tathā-vidhā-vastu-dyotana-paṭiṣṭhatayā prasādhitatvāt. nâpi dvitīyo, 'pramāṇasyâkiñcit-karatvāt. etena sthūratā-dūṣaṇam api pratikṣiptaṃ, pratibhāsa-hatatvāt, tad-apahnavena virodhôdbhāvanasya nirmūlatayā pralāpa-mātratvāt. yat punar vartamāna-prakāśa-rūpatayā tat-sambaddha-vastu-grāhitvaṃ sarva-pramāṇānām udagrāhi, tad ayuktaṃ, teṣām ekântena vārtamānikatvâsiddheḥ, kathañcid ātmā-vyatirekitvāt, tasya ca kāla-traya-vyāpakatvāt, tad-rūpatayā teṣām apy avasthānāt. tataś câtmano 'rtha-grahaṇa-pariṇāma-rūpatvāt, sarva-pramāṇānāṃ pariṇāminy eva vastuni vyāpāro, na kṣaṇike. na câtītânāgata-kṣaṇa-varti-vastu-grahaṇe 'py anādy-ananta-janma-paramparā-grahaṇa-prasaṅga, āvaraṇa-viccheda-sāpekṣatvāt, tasyâiva paramârthataḥ saṃvedanâvir-bhāvântara-kāraṇatvād, grāhyâder bahir-aṅgatvāt. sāmastyena punar āvaraṇa-vilaye sati samasta-vastu-vistārânādy-ananta-kṣaṇa-paramparā-grahaṇa-prasaṅgo na no bādhā-kārîṣṭatvāt. tad eka-deśa-kṣayôpaśame punas tad-anusāriṇī bodha-pravṛttir iti kiyat-kāla-bhāvini sthūre vastuni
prākṛta-loka-jñānāni pravartante, na sampūrṇe. na ca tāny alīkāni, tad-grāhyâṃśasyâpi vastuni bhāvāt, tāvatâiva vyavahāra-siddher iti. yac côktaṃ: kṣaṇikatāṃ gṛhṇanto 'pi sadṛśâparâparôtpatti-vipralabdhatvān mandā nâdhyavasyanti, mithyā-vikalpa-vaśāt sthiratā-vyavahāraṃ ca pravartayanti, tad ayuktaṃ, bhavad-ākūṭena sādṛśyâbhāvāt, tad-abhāve tad-utpādyâbhimata-bhrānter nirbījatayôtpatter asambhavāt. tathā sthiratâropo 'pi kvacid gṛhīta-sthiratvasyâiva yukto nânyathā, yathā dṛṣṭa-viṣa-dharasya manda-prakāśe rajju-darśane viṣa-dharâropaḥ. na ca bhavatāṃ kadācana sthiratā pratīti-gocara-cāritām anubhavati, tat kathaṃ pratikṣaṇam udayâpavarga-saṃsargiṇi sakale vastuni pratyakṣeṇâvalokite 'pi tad-āropa iti. tasmāt tiro-hita-kṣaṇa-vivartam alakṣita-paramâṇu-vaiviktyaṃ vastu sarva-sāṃvyavahārika-pramāṇair gocarī-kriyata iti tat-tiras-kāra-dvāreṇâdṛṣṭa-kṣaṇa-kṣayi-paramâṇu-pratiṣṭhāpako 'bhiprāya ṛjusūtra-durnaya-saṃjñām aśnute, tad-upekṣayâiva tad-darśakasya nayatvād iti.
children.translated_text: Now, the <s>ṛjusūtra</s> (direct standpoint) too, denying what is observed and considering the real nature of objects to be ultimately characterized as momentary and atomic, assumes the status of a <s>durnaya</s> (false standpoint), because in the denial of observed stable and gross objects, the conceptual determination that would establish the object it intends is rootless and cannot arise. For: one should first directly perceive a form that pervades its own parts and persists across time, and only afterwards analyze it through erroneous conceptual reasoning — [thinking] 'this observed stable and gross form cannot indeed withstand [scrutiny], being incapable of bearing examination,' etc. But what is observed cannot be sublated by erroneous conceptual reasoning that demonstrates the unobserved, because of the absurd consequence of a complete loss of confidence everywhere. If you were to say: 'Just as in a dimly lit place, the prior delusion of [seeing] a snake in a rope is sublated by the subsequent conceptual determination that ascertains [the true nature of] the rope, so too is this perception of stable and gross [objects sublated] by the conceptual determination that establishes momentary atoms — what is untenable in this?' — this is not so, because it is the very appearance of the rope that is capable of dispelling the prior delusion of a snake; and in its absence, even a hundred conceptual constructions could not dispel [the delusion]. Here too [you might say]: since the past and future, being destroyed and not-yet-arisen, are not present, and since the gross parts, when examined through the pair of [alternatives of] difference and non-difference from their own parts, cannot maintain their status — atoms that perish every moment alone appear; and therefore appearance itself is the sublator of the perception of the stable and gross — if so, then since the appearance is not something that can be communicated through instruction, practical activity would proceed in precisely that way [i.e., following the stable, gross appearance]. [If you say] it does not proceed [that way] because of the error of the subsequent false conceptual construction — [we reply] not so, because this response too is a cause of error elsewhere. For: even when a white lotus appears, a rogue arguing according to your logic — 'this blue [thing] was perceived by direct perception; but it appears white due to the error of a subsequent false conceptual construction' — by whom could he be stopped? Therefore, the denial of what is observed cannot be carried out — hence the establishment of stable and gross reality, because that alone is observed; while the other [i.e., momentary atoms], being established through the medium of observing that [stable, gross reality], is [merely] something to be inferred; and if that [observed reality] is not accepted, the latter too would not be established. By this, the demonstration that stable and gross objects lack practical efficacy is also countered, because that very type [of stable, gross object] is observed to operate in all activities, and because practical efficacy must be denied to what is momentary, as was stated before: 'For an object-nature that is momentary — would it produce its effect in its own moment, before, or after?' etc. Moreover, since all objects are cognized as having both persisting and changing forms — through [persisting properties like] existence, personhood, consciousness, etc., and through [changing properties like] childhood, youth, maturity, old age, joy, sorrow, etc. — they have the nature of both <s>dravya</s> (substance) and <s>paryāya</s> (mode): because non-difference constitutes substancehood, and difference constitutes modal nature. And therefore, the demonstration that only the present moment is the agent of practical efficacy — through the non-presence of past and future moments — does not sublate our [position], because the modes, being sequential, it is precisely the substance embraced by the present mode that is skilled in performing practical activity. [The substance is] not merely that [present moment]; it extends across three times; the perceiver too, as having the nature of substance, is of such a nature. And therefore, through the concealment of momentary modes, by aggregating those forms [into a whole], this very [substance] — 'it is stable and engages in all activities' — enters the pathway of cognition, because stability too is real; because the momentary modes, though existing, are not grasped [separately]; and because the ordinary knowledge of common people, being dependent on the diminution and subsidence of <s>āvaraṇa</s> (obscuration), has only a limited number of aspects as its object. If, however, the cognition of substance is supposed to be non-real because it arises from the force of seeing a succession of modes — then it must be stated whether the prior mode's [role in] producing the subsequent mode involves continuity or no continuity, since there is no third alternative. If there is continuity, then substance would be designated by another term for mode. If there is no continuity, then because of being causeless, there would be the absurd consequence that the subsequent mode does not arise. Therefore, practical efficacy is not established apart from an object having both natures [substance and mode]. Nor is practical efficacy the defining characteristic of reality, because the final moments of sounds, lightning, lamps, etc., since they do not produce a subsequent moment, would turn out to be non-real; and if those were non-real, then even the penultimate moment would lack operation with respect to the real — and so on, until by a chain [of reasoning], the reality of all moments [would be lost]. If, however, even without producing a subsequent moment, being the generator of cognition pertaining to its own object is conceived as practical efficacy — then in that case, even the succession of past and future modes, having become the object of yogic knowledge, would acquire the status of reality. Therefore, practical efficacy is not the defining characteristic of reality; rather, it is the conjunction of origination, decay, and permanence (<s>utpāda-vyaya-dhrauvya</s>), because it is established by <s>pramāṇa</s>. If [you say] origination and decay are contradictory with permanence — whence comes this contradiction: from <s>pramāṇa</s> or from non-<s>pramāṇa</s>? Not the first, because all <s>pramāṇas</s> have been established as revealing reality that is of precisely such a nature, both externally and internally. Nor the second, because what is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> has no efficacy. By this, the objection against grossness is also countered — because it is contradicted by appearance; and because demonstrating a contradiction through denying that [appearance] is rootless and amounts to mere prattle. And what was boldly declared — namely that all <s>pramāṇas</s>, being of the nature of illuminating the present, grasp only the object connected with it — that is untenable, because their being exclusively of the present is not established, since the self (<s>ātman</s>) is somehow different from [any single moment of] them, and since it extends across the three times, and they [the <s>pramāṇas</s>] too persist in the form of that [self]. And since the self has the nature of transformation that constitutes the grasping of objects, all <s>pramāṇas</s> operate with respect to an object that undergoes transformation, not one that is merely momentary. Nor does the apprehension of objects existing in past and future moments entail the absurd consequence of grasping a beginningless and endless succession of births, because it depends on the removal of obscuration; because that [removal of obscuration] alone is ultimately the cause of the manifestation of additional awareness; and because the graspable object and the like are external [conditions]. In general, however, when obscuration is completely removed, the absurd consequence of grasping the entire extent of all objects and the beginningless, endless succession of moments does not harm us, because that is accepted [by us, as omniscience]. But in the case of partial diminution and subsidence [of obscuration], the cognitive activity follows accordingly — thus the ordinary knowledge of common people operates with respect to a gross object enduring for some time, not with respect to the complete [reality]. Nor are these [cognitions] false, because even the aspect grasped by them exists in the object, and practical activity is accomplished by just that much. And what was said — 'even while grasping momentariness, the dull-witted, being deceived by the successive arising of similar [entities], do not ascertain [it], and due to the power of false conceptual construction, engage in the practical activity of stability' — that is untenable, because according to your purport, there is no similarity [between successive moments]; and in its absence, the delusion intended to be produced by it, being seedless, could not arise. Similarly, the superimposition of stability is proper only for one who has [at some point] grasped stability, not otherwise — just as the superimposition of a snake on a rope in dim light [is possible] for one who has [previously] seen a snake. But in your [system], stability never enters the domain of cognition — so how can there be superimposition of it upon all objects, even when they are perceived by direct perception as being associated with arising and perishing at every moment? Therefore, reality — whose momentary transformations are concealed and whose atomic distinctness is unnoticed — is made the object by all conventional <s>pramāṇas</s>; and the view that, through concealing that [observed reality], establishes unobserved momentary atoms, assumes the designation of <s>ṛjusūtra-durnaya</s> (false direct standpoint), because its status as a <s>naya</s> consists only in showing that [momentary reality] through disregard [of the stable, gross reality, rather than its denial].

children.text: tathā śabdâdayo 'pi sarvathā śabdâvyatirekam arthasya samarthayanto durnayās, tat-samarthanârtham upanyastasya tat-pratītau pratīyamānatva-lakṣaṇasya hetor anaikāntikatvāt. tathā hi: nâyam ekânto yat-pratītau yat pratīyate tat tato 'vyatiriktam eva, vyatiriktasyâpi pāvakâder anyathânupapannatva-lakṣaṇa-sambandha-balād dhūmâdi-pratītau pratīyamānatvāt. evaṃ śabdo 'pi vyatiriktam apy arthaṃ vācakatvāt pratyāyayiṣyaty, avyatirekasya pratyakṣâdi-bādhitatvāc, chabdād vivekenâivânubhūyamānatvāt. asmiṃś ca hetāv anaikāntike sthite sarvârthānāṃ sasva-vācakatva-sādhana-dvāreṇa śabdâvyatireka-sādhanam api dūrâpāstam eva. na câtrâpi pratibandha-grāhi pramāṇaṃ -- yo yo 'rthas tena tena sasva-vācakena bhavitavyaṃ -- ghaṭâdi-dṛṣṭânta-mātrāt tad-asiddheḥ, kṣaṇikâlakṣya-dravya-vivartānāṃ saṅketa-grahaṇôpāyâbhāvenâbhilapitum aśakyatayânabhilāpyatva-siddheś ca. kṣaṇa-bhaṅguratā-pratijñānaṃ punar amīṣāṃ apy ṛjusūtravan nirasitavyam. tathā pratyeka-matâpekṣayâpi svâbhipretaṃ pratiṣṭhāpayantas tad-viparītaṃ śabdârthaṃ tiras-kurvāṇā durnayatām ātmasāt-kurvanti. etāvad dhi pramāṇa-pratiṣṭhitaṃ, yad uta vidhi-mukhena śabdo 'rthasya vācaka iti; na punar ayaṃ niyamo yathâyam asyâiva vācako nânyasya, deśa-kāla-puruṣa-saṅketâdi-vicitratayā sarva-śabdānām aparâparârtha-pratipādakatvenôpalabdher ananta-dharmatayâparâpara-yogyatā-dvareṇâparâparârthâbhidhāyakatvôpapatter, arthānām apy ananta-dharmatvād evâparâpara-śabda-vācyatvâvirodhāt, tathâivâvigānena vyavahāra-darśanāt, tad-aniṣṭau tal-lopa-prasaṅgāt. tasmāt sarva-dhvanayo yogyatayā sarvârtha-vācakā, deśa-kṣayôpaśamâdy-apekṣayā tu kvacit kathañcit pratītiṃ janayanti. tataś ca kvacid anapekṣita-vyutpatti-nimittā rūḍhitaḥ pravartante, kvacit sāmānya-vyutpatti-sāpekṣāḥ, kvacit tat-kāla-varti-vyutpatti-nimittâpekṣayêti na tatra prāmāṇikena niyatârthâgraho vidheyaḥ. ato 'mī śabdâdayo yadêtarêtarâbhimata-śabdârthôpekṣayā svâbhimataṃ śabdârthaṃ darśayanti, tadā nayās, tasyâpi tatra bhāvāt. paraspara-bādhayā pravartamānāḥ punar durnaya-rūpatāṃ bhajanti, nirālambanatvād iti.
children.translated_text: Likewise, the <s>śabda</s> (word) and other [standpoints] too, when establishing the non-difference of the object from the word in every respect, are <s>durnayas</s> (false standpoints), because the reason adduced for that purpose — namely 'being cognized when [the word] is cognized' — is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>). For: this is not an invariable rule — that whatever is cognized when something [else] is cognized is non-different from it — because even what is different, such as fire and the like, is cognized when smoke and the like are cognized, through the force of a relation characterized by otherwise-impossibility (<s>anyathānupapannatva</s>). Similarly, the word too, being a designator, will make known even a different object; and the non-difference [of object from word] is sublated by perception and the like, since the object is experienced as distinct from the word. And when this reason is established as inconclusive, the establishment of non-difference from the word — through the means of proving that all objects have their own designators — is also far removed. Nor is there a <s>pramāṇa</s> that grasps the invariable connection here — [namely] that every object must have its own designator — because that is not established merely from the example of 'pot' and the like, and because the momentary, imperceptible transformations of substance, lacking any means of grasping a convention [for them], cannot be expressed and are thus established as inexpressible. The assertion of momentariness by these [word-standpoints] too should be refuted just as in the case of the <s>ṛjusūtra</s>. Similarly, even with respect to their individual views, when establishing their own preferred [position] and concealing the opposing word-meaning, they assume the status of <s>durnayas</s>. For this much is established by <s>pramāṇa</s>: that in a positive sense, a word is a designator of an object; but this rule does not hold — that this [word] is the designator of this [object] alone and not of another — because, due to the variety of place, time, person, convention, etc., all words are observed to convey one meaning after another; and because through the infinite properties [of objects], by way of one capacity after another, the capacity of [words] to designate one object after another is tenable; and because objects too, being of infinite properties, are not contradicted in being denotable by one word after another; and because practical activity is observed [to proceed] in just that way without disagreement; and if that [variety] is not accepted, there would be the absurd consequence of the annulment of that [practical activity]. Therefore, all sounds are, by capacity, designators of all objects, but due to the diminution and subsidence of [karmic] obscuration pertaining to place, etc., they generate cognition of some particular [meaning] in some particular way. And thus, in some cases [words] operate by convention without regard to etymological basis, in some cases depending on a general etymological derivation, and in some cases depending on the etymological basis present at that time — therefore, the one who follows <s>pramāṇa</s> should not insist on a fixed meaning-apprehension there. Hence, when these <s>śabda</s> (word) and other [standpoints], by disregarding the word-meaning accepted by each other, show their own preferred word-meaning, they are <s>nayas</s>, because that [meaning] too exists there. But when they operate through mutual sublation, they assume the nature of <s>durnayas</s> (false standpoints), because they are without foundation.

children.text: nanu ca yady ekâika-dharma-samarthana-parāyaṇāḥśeṣa-dharma-tiras-kāra-kāriṇo 'bhiprāyā durnayatāṃ pratipadyante, tadā vacanam apy eka-dharma-kathana-dvāreṇa pravartamānaṃ sâvadhāraṇatvāc ca śeṣa-dharma-pratikṣepa-kāry alīkamāpadyate. tataś cânanta-dharmâdhyāsita-vastu-sandarśakam eva vacanaṃ yathâvasthitârtha-pratipādakatvāt satyaṃ; na câivaṃ vacana-pravṛttir, ghaṭo 'yaṃ śuklo mūrta ity-ādy ekâika-dharma-pratipādana-niṣṭhatayā vyavahāre śabda-prayoga-darśanāt, sarva-dharmāṇāṃ yaugapadyena vaktum aśakyatvāt, tad-abhidhāyakānām apyānantyāt. na câikâika-dharma-sandarśakatve 'py amūni vacanāny alīkāni vaktuṃ pāryante, samasta-śābda-vyavahārôccheda-prasaṅgāt, tad-alīkatve tataḥ pravṛtty-asiddher iti. atrôcyata -- iha tāvad dvaye vastu-pratipādakā, laukikās tattva-cintakāś ca. tatra pratyakṣâdi-prasiddham artham arthitva-vaśāl laukikās tāvan madhyastha-bhāvena vyavahāra-kāle vyapadiśyanti, yad uta nīlam utpalaṃ sugandhi komalam iti, na tu tad-dharmi-gata-dharmântara-grahaṇa-nirākaraṇayorādriyante, 'narthitvāt, tāvatâiva vivakṣita-vyavahāra-parisamāpteḥ. na ca tad-vacanānām alīkatā, śeṣa-dharmântara-pratikṣepâbhāvāt, tat-pratikṣepa-kāriṇām evâlīkatvāt. "sarvaṃ vacanaṃ sâvadhāraṇam" iti-nyāyāt teṣām api śeṣa-dharma-tiras-kāra-kāritva-siddher bhavan-nītyâlīkatâpadyata iti cen, na, avadhāraṇasya tad-asambhava-mātra-vyavacchede vyāpārād; yathâneka-puruṣa-sampūrṇe sadasi dvārâdau sthitasya kim atra devadattaḥ samasti nâstîti vā dolāyamāna-buddheḥ kenacid abhidhīyate -- yathā devadatto 'stîti. atra yady apy upanyasta-pada-dvayasya sâvadhāraṇatā gamyate, 'nyathā tad-uccāraṇa-vaiyarthya-prasaṅgāt, tathâpy avadhāraṇaṃ tad-asambhava-mātraṃ vyavacchinatti, na śeṣa-puruṣântarāṇi; nâpi para-rūpeṇa nāstitvaṃ, tad-vyavacchedâbhiprāyeṇa prastuta-vākya-prayogāt, prayoktr-abhiprāyâdi-sāpekṣatayâiva dhvaneḥ svârtha-pratipādana-sāmarthyāt. na ca vācya-vācaka-bhāva-lakṣaṇa-sambandhânarthakyaṃ, tad-abhāve prayoktr-abhiprāya-mātreṇa rūpasyâiva niyoktum aśakyatvāt. na ca samasta-dharma-yuktam eva vastu pratipādayad vacanaṃ satyam ity abhidadhmahe, yenâikâika-dharmâliṅgita-vastu-sandarśakānām alīkatā syāt, kiṃ tarhi sambhavad-artha-pratipādakaṃ satyam iti, sambhavanti ca śeṣa-dharmâpratikṣepe vacana-gocarâpannā dharmās; tasmāt tat-pratipādakaṃ satyam eva. yadā tu durnaya-matâbhiniviṣṭa-buddhibhis tīrthântarīyais tad-dharmi-gata-dharmântara-nirākaraṇâbhiprāyeṇâiva sâvadhāraṇaṃ tat prayujyate, yathânityam eva vastu nityam eva vêty-ādi, tadā nirālambanatvād alīkatāṃ prāpnuvat kena vāryeta? tattva-cintakāḥ punaḥ pratyakṣâdi-pramāṇa-siddham anekântâtmakaṃ vastu darśayanto dvedhā darśayeyus, tad yathā -- vikalâdeśena sakalâdeśena vā. tatra vikālâdeśo nayâdhīnaḥ, sakalâdeśaḥ pramāṇâyattaḥ. tathā hi: yadā madhyastha-bhāvenârthitva-vaśāt kiñcid dharmaṃ pratipipādayiṣavaḥ śeṣa-dharma-svī-karaṇa-nirākaraṇa-vimukhayā dhiyā vācaṃ prayuñjate, tadā tattva-cintakā api laukikavat sammugdhâkāratayâcakṣate, yad uta "jīvo 'sti kartā pramātā bhoktêty-ādi". ataḥ sampūrṇa-vastu-pratipādanâbhāvād vikalâdeśo 'bhidhīyate, naya-matena sambhavad-dharmāṇāṃ darśana-mātram ity arthaḥ. yadā tu pramāṇa-vyāpāram avikalaṃ parāmṛśya pratipādayitum abhiprayanti, tadâṅgī-kṛta-guṇa-pradhāna-bhāvâśeṣa-dharma-sūcaka-kathañcit-paryāya-syāc-chabda-bhūṣitayā sâvadhāraṇayā ca vācā darśayanti ‘syād asty eva jīva'; ity-ādikayā. ato 'yaṃ syāc-chabda-saṃsūcitâbhyantarī-bhūtânanta-dharmakasya sākṣād-upanyasta-jīva-śabda-kriyābhyāṃ pradhanī-kṛtâtma-bhāvasyâvadhāraṇa-vyavacchinna-tad-asambhavasya vastunaḥ sandarśakatvāt sakalâdeśa ity ucyate, pramāṇa-pratipanna-sampūrṇârtha-kathanam iti yāvat. tad uktaṃ:
children.translated_text: Now, if intentions that are devoted to establishing each single property and that cause the concealment of the remaining properties fall into the status of false reasoning, then speech too, which proceeds by way of stating a single property and which, being determinative, causes the rejection of the remaining properties, becomes false. In that case, only speech that reveals the object as endowed with infinite properties would be true, since it would convey the object as it really is. But verbal usage does not operate in that way, since in ordinary practice we observe the use of words in a manner terminating in the expression of each single property, such as 'this is a pot,' 'it is white,' 'it is corporeal,' and so forth, because it is impossible to state all properties simultaneously, and because the terms that would express them are also infinite. Nor can these statements, even though they reveal the object through a single property, be called false, because there would follow the annulment of all verbal transactions — for if they were false, engagement based on them would be impossible. To this we reply: In this world, there are two [kinds of] agents who convey the nature of objects — ordinary people and investigators of reality. Among these, ordinary people, impelled by their practical needs, with an impartial disposition, designate at the time of transaction an object that is well-known through perception and other means — such as 'a blue, fragrant, soft lotus' — but they do not concern themselves with either the apprehension or the rejection of other properties belonging to that property-bearer, because they have no interest [in doing so], since the intended transaction is completed by just that much. Nor is there falsity in those statements, because there is no rejection of the remaining other properties — for falsity belongs only to those [statements] that cause the rejection of [other properties]. If it is objected that, by the principle 'every statement is determinative,' even those [ordinary statements] are established as causing the concealment of the remaining properties and therefore, by your own reasoning, fall into falsity — no, because the function of determination extends only to the exclusion of the mere impossibility of that [property]; just as when, in an assembly full of many persons, someone standing at the door, whose mind is wavering as to whether <s>Devadatta</s> is present there or not, is told by someone: '<s>Devadatta</s> is [indeed] here.' Here, although the determinative force of the two words presented is understood — otherwise there would be the absurd consequence of the utterance being pointless — nevertheless, the determination excludes only the mere impossibility of that [presence], not the remaining other persons; nor [does it exclude] the non-existence [of <s>Devadatta</s>] in the form of another, because the statement in question is employed with the intention of excluding that [impossibility alone], since language has the capacity to convey its own meaning only in dependence upon the speaker's intention and so forth. Nor is the relation characterized by the signifier-signified relationship rendered purposeless, because in the absence of that [relation], the [particular] form cannot be assigned by the speaker's intention alone. Nor do we assert that only a statement that conveys the object as endowed with all properties is true — for in that case there would be the falsity of [statements] that reveal the object as embraced by each single property — rather, [we say that] what conveys a possible object is true, and properties that have come within the range of speech are possible when there is no rejection of the remaining properties; therefore, a statement that conveys them is indeed true. When, however, adherents of other schools (<s>tīrthāntarīyas</s>), whose intellects are attached to wrong doctrines, employ that [statement] determinatively with the very intention of rejecting other properties belonging to that property-bearer — such as 'the object is impermanent only' or 'permanent only' and the like — then, since it has no basis [in reality], what would prevent it from becoming false? The investigators of reality, however, who reveal the object as possessing a manifold nature established by <s>pramāṇas</s> such as perception, may reveal it in two ways: through a partial viewpoint (<s>vikalādeśa</s>) or through a complete viewpoint (<s>sakalādeśa</s>). Of these, the partial viewpoint depends on <s>naya</s> (standpoint), and the complete viewpoint depends on <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge). For when, with an impartial disposition and impelled by practical need, wishing to convey some particular property, they employ speech with an intellect that is averse to either accepting or rejecting the remaining properties, then even the investigators of reality speak in the manner of ordinary people, with an appearance of bewilderment, such as 'the <s>jīva</s> (soul) exists, is an agent, a knower, an experiencer,' and so forth. Therefore, since there is no conveyance of the complete object, it is called a partial viewpoint — meaning that it is merely the showing of possible properties according to the <s>naya</s> doctrine. But when they intend to convey by fully grasping the unimpaired operation of <s>pramāṇa</s>, then they show it by means of determinative speech adorned with the <s>syāt</s>-word (the conditional 'perhaps') — a word that, having adopted a hierarchy of principal and subordinate, indicates all properties without remainder, expressed in the mode of 'in a certain sense' — such as '<s>syād asty eva jīvaḥ</s>' ('In a certain sense, the <s>jīva</s> certainly exists'), and so forth. Therefore, because this [statement], through the <s>syāt</s>-word that indicates the infinite properties internalized within, and through the directly presented word '<s>jīva</s>' and the verbal action [denoting existence] that make the essential nature primary, reveals the object whose impossibility [of being otherwise] is excluded by the determination — it is called the complete viewpoint, meaning the statement of the complete object as apprehended by <s>pramāṇa</s>. Thus it has been said:
That cognition of the knowable particular is of the nature of <s>naya</s> (standpoint) and <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge); therein,

children.text: sakala-grāhi tu mānaṃ vikala-grāhī nayo jñeyaḥ //
children.translated_text: <s>pramāṇa</s> is that which grasps the whole, while <s>naya</s> is to be understood as that which grasps partially.

children.text: tad idam uktaṃ bhavati: naya-pramāṇâbhijñaḥ syād-vādī sakala-vikalâdeśāv adhikṛtya vastu-svarūpa-pratipipādayiṣayā yad yad brūte tat tat satyaṃ, sambhavad-artha-gocaratvāt. durnaya-matâvalambinaḥ punar ekânta-vādino yad yad ācakṣate tat tad alīkam, asambhavad-artha-viṣayatvād iti.
children.translated_text: Thus the meaning stated is: The <s>syādvādin</s> (proponent of conditional predication), who is conversant with <s>naya</s> and <s>pramāṇa</s>, whatever he states with the intention of conveying the true nature of the object through the complete and partial viewpoints — all that is true, because it has as its range a possible object. But the <s>ekāntavādins</s> (absolutists), who rely on wrong doctrines, whatever they declare — all that is false, because it has as its range an impossible object.

children.text: sāmpratam amum evârthaṃ draḍhayan siddhânte 'py ekâika-naya-mata-pravṛttāni sūtrāṇi na sampūrṇârthâbhidhāyakānîty, api tu tat-samudāyâbhiprāya-pravṛttam avikala-vastu-nivedakam iti darśayann āha:
children.translated_text: Now, strengthening this very point, showing that even in [Jain] scripture the <s>sūtras</s> that proceed according to each individual <s>naya</s> doctrine are not conveyors of the complete meaning, but rather it is their aggregate that, proceeding with the intention of [all nayas combined], communicates the unimpaired object — [the author] says:
Because the <s>nayas</s> (standpoints), each devoted to a single [aspect], operate within the path of scripture,
the <s>syādvāda-śruta</s> (scripture of conditional predication) is said to be that which ascertains the complete meaning. (NA_30)

children.text: iha trividhaṃ śrutaṃ, tad yathā -- mithyā-śrutaṃ naya-śrutaṃ syād-vāda-śrutaṃ ca. tatra śrūyata iti śrutam āgamaḥ. mithyâlīkaṃ śrutaṃ mithyā-śrutaṃ, tac ca durnayâbhiprāya-pravṛttaṃ tīrthika-sambandhi, nirgocaratvāt. tathā nayair hetu-bhūtaiḥ śrutaṃ naya-śrutam, etac cârhad-āgamântar-gatam evâika-nayâbhiprāya-pratibaddhaṃ, yathā "paḍuppaṇṇe neraïë viṇassaï" ity-ādy, ṛjusūtra-nayâbhiprāyeṇa kṣaṇikatvasyâpi tatra sambhavāt. tathā nirdiśyamāna-dharma-vyatiriktâśeṣa-dharmântara-saṃsūcakena syātā yukto vādo 'bhipreta-dharma-vacanaṃ syād-vādaḥ, tad-ātmakaṃ śrutaṃ syād-vāda-śrutam. tat kiṃ-bhūtam ucyata ity āha:
children.translated_text: Here, scripture (<s>śruta</s>) is threefold: <s>mithyā-śruta</s> (false scripture), <s>naya-śruta</s> (standpoint-scripture), and <s>syādvāda-śruta</s> (scripture of conditional predication). Therein, that which is heard (<s>śrūyate</s>) is <s>śruta</s>, i.e., <s>āgama</s> (authoritative tradition). False (<s>mithyā</s>) scripture is <s>mithyā-śruta</s>, and that proceeds according to wrong doctrines and belongs to the heterodox (<s>tīrthika</s>), because it has no [real] domain. Likewise, scripture [understood] through <s>nayas</s> that serve as causal factors is <s>naya-śruta</s>; and this too is contained within the <s>Arhat</s>'s scripture itself, bound to the intention of a single <s>naya</s> — as for example '<s>paḍuppaṇṇe neraïe viṇassaï</s>' ('a being born in hell perishes'), and so forth, because even momentariness is possible there according to the <s>ṛjusūtra-naya</s> (straight-thread standpoint). Likewise, <s>syādvāda</s> is a discourse (<s>vāda</s>) on the intended property accompanied by <s>syāt</s> — [a word] that indicates all remaining properties other than the one being stated — and scripture of that nature is <s>syādvāda-śruta</s>. What kind [of scripture] is it said to be? He says:
that is, unimpaired; and that is the

children.text: tan-nirṇaya-hetutvād evam abhidhīyate; paramârthataḥ punaḥ samasta-vastu-svarūpa-pratipādîty arthaḥ, śabdâtmakatvān, niścayasya bodha-rūpatvād iti. naya-śrutaṃ tarhi sampūrṇârtha-viniścāyi kasmān na bhavatîty āha:
children.translated_text: it is so called because it is the cause of the determination of that [complete meaning]; but in the ultimate sense, it means that which conveys the true nature of the entire object — because it is of the nature of words, and because ascertainment has the form of understanding. Why then does <s>naya-śruta</s> not ascertain the complete meaning? He says:
those whose scope terminates in the apprehension of a single property,

children.text: pravartanān na tad ekâikâbhiprāya-pratibaddhaṃ sampūrṇârtha-viniścāyi, tat-samudāyasyâiva sampūrṇârtha-viniścāyakatvād ity-ākūṭam.
children.translated_text: because they operate [thus], that [<s>naya-śruta</s>], being bound to each individual standpoint's intention, does not ascertain the complete meaning — the implication being that only their aggregate ascertains the complete meaning.

children.text: tad evaṃ naya-pramāṇa-svarūpaṃ pratipādyâdhunâśeṣa-naya-pramāṇa-vyāpakaṃ teṣāṃ tatra tādātmyenâvasthānāt pramātāram abhidhātukāma āha:
children.translated_text: Having thus elucidated the nature of <s>naya</s> and <s>pramāṇa</s>, now wishing to describe the knower (<s>pramātā</s>) who pervades all <s>nayas</s> and <s>pramāṇas</s> — since they subsist in him through identity — [the author] says:
The knower (<s>pramātā</s>) is the <s>jīva</s> (soul), which illuminates both itself and others, is an agent and an experiencer, possesses transformation,
is established through self-awareness (<s>sva-saṃvedana</s>), and is not of the nature of earth and the like. (NA_31)
Therein, because it lives through the three times,
meaning the <s>ātman</s> (self) that sustains life (<s>prāṇa</s>); that [<s>jīva</s>] measures (<s>pramiṇoti</s>), hence it is the

children.text: prameya-paricchedakaḥ. kiṃ-bhūtaḥ sann ity āha: svânyāv ātma-parau nirbhāsitum uddyotayituṃ śīlam asyêti
children.translated_text: one who delimits the <s>prameya</s> (knowable object). What kind [of knower] is it? He says: 'self' and 'other' — meaning the self and what is external — [that which has as] its nature the illumination, i.e., the manifesting [of these], thus it is

children.text: , sva-svarūpârthayoḥ prakāśaka iti yāvat. tathā karotîti
children.translated_text: meaning one that makes manifest both its own nature and objects. Likewise, [that which] acts is the

children.translated_text: 'Self' (<s>sva</s>) is the <s>ātman</s>; that by which it is experienced is <s>sva-saṃvedana</s> (self-awareness); by that, well-established, i.e., grounded, i.e., cognized, is

children.text: . kṣitiḥ pṛthivy ādir yeṣāṃ tāni kṣity-ādīny, ādi-śabdād ambu-tejo-vāyv-ākāśāni gṛhyante; na vidyata
children.translated_text: <s>Kṣiti</s> (earth) is the element earth; those having that as their initial [member] are <s>kṣity-ādi</s> (earth and the like); by the word '<s>ādi</s>' (and so forth), water, fire, air, and space are included. There does not exist
