'<s>kṣity-ādy-anātmaka</s>' (not of the nature of earth and the like) —
meaning it does not have the essential nature of earth and so forth.

children.text: ty-anena ye pāramārthikaṃ pramātāraṃ nâbhyupagacchanty, api tu vijñāna-kṣaṇa-paramparânubhava-bala-prabodhitânādi-prarūḍha-vāsanā-sampādita-sattākaṃ mithyā-vikalpa-parikalpitam apāramārthikaṃ taṃ manyante pratikṣaṇa-vilaya-vādinaḥ tān nirācaṣṭe, kṣaṇa-vilayasya prāg eva pratiṣiddhatvād, bahir antaś ca pariṇāmi-vastunaḥ prasādhanāt.
children.translated_text: by this [statement], those who do not accept an ultimately real knower, but rather consider him to be a falsely constructed product of <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction) — whose existence is brought about by <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions) that have grown since beginningless time and are awakened by the force of the experience of the successive series of consciousness-moments — [consider him to be] non-ultimate, [namely] the proponents of momentary destruction — [the author] refutes them, since momentary destruction has been previously refuted, and since a transforming entity, both external and internal, has been established.

children.text: nanu ca ghaṭâdayas tāvad vināśam āviśanto dṛśyante, teṣāṃ ca vināśo lakuṭâdi-kāraṇa-kalāpenâvinaśvara-svabhāvānāṃ vā kriyeta, vinaśvara-svabhāvānāṃ vā. yady ādyaḥ kalpas tad ayuktaṃ, svabhāvasya pracyāvayitum aśakyatvāt, tasya niyata-rūpatvād, anyathā svabhāvatvâyogāt. athâivaṃ-bhūta eva tasya svabhāvaḥ sva-kāraṇa-balâyāto yad uta vināśa-kāraṇam āsādya vinaṅkṣyatîti brūṣe, tathâpi tad-vināśa-kāraṇa-sannidhānaṃ kiṃ yādṛcchikam uta tat-svabhāva-sampādyam eva. yadâdyaḥ kalpas, tadā sannihitasyâpi tat-pratyanīka-pratyayôpanipātena nivartanāt, tat-sannidhāpaka-hetūnāṃ api sva-sannidhāpaka-kāraṇa-kalāpa-sāpekṣatvāt, sannihitānām api pratidvandvinā nivartanād, yādṛcchikatvāc ca nâvaśyaṃ-bhāvi tat-sannidhānaṃ; tataś câsannihita-sva-vināśa-kāraṇa-kadambakaḥ kaścid ghaṭâdir na vinaśyed apy, aniṣṭaṃ câitat, sarva-kṛtakānāṃ vināśâvigānāt. atha dvitīyaḥ pakṣas, tathā sati paścād api tad-balād vināśa-hetavaḥ sannidhāsyantîti prathama-kṣaṇa eva sannidadhatu, tathâpi kṣaṇikatâivârthasya. sva-hetor eva niyata-kālāt parato 'yaṃ sva-vināśa-hetuṃ sannidhāpayiṣyatîty evaṃ-rūpo jāta iti cen, nâivam api kṣaṇa-bhaṅguratâyātā. tathā hi: sva-hetunā kilâsau varṣāt parataḥ sva-vināśa-hetu-sannidhāpana-kṣama-svabhāvo vyadhāyi; sa ca tasyôtpāda-kṣaṇād dvitīya-kṣaṇe svabhāvo 'sti vā na vā? asti cet, tathā sati punar varṣaṃ tena sthātavyam, evaṃ yāvad varṣôpāntya-kṣaṇe 'pi yadi tat-svabhāva evâsau tadâparam api varṣântaraṃ sthitir āpadyeta, tadā cânanta-kalpa-sthāyī-bhāvaḥ syād, apracyuta-varṣa-sthāyi-svabhāvatvād iti. atha dvitīya-kṣaṇe nâsti sa svabhāva iti brūṣe, hanta kṣaṇikatvam evâḍhaukate, 'tādavasthyasya tal-lakṣaṇatvāt. kiṃ ca, vināśa-hetur bhāvasya vināśaṃ vyatiriktam avyatiriktaṃ vā kuryāt? vyatirikta-karaṇe na kiñcit kṛtaṃ syāt, tataś ca bhāvas tādavasthyam anubhavet. tat-sambandhaḥ kriyata iti cen, na sambandhasya tādātmya-tad-utpatti-vyatiriktasya pratiṣedhāt. na cânayor anyataraḥ sambandho 'tra samasti, vyatirekiṇā sârddhaṃ tādātmyâyogād, anya-hetukasya paścād utpannasya tad-utpatti-vaikalyāt. tan na vyatirikto vināśaḥ kartuṃ yuktaḥ. avyatirikta-karaṇe punas tam eva bhāvaṃ vināśa-hetuḥ karotîti prāptam, avyatirekasya tad-rūpatā-lakṣaṇatvāt. na câsau kartavyaḥ, sva-hetor eva niṣpannatvāt, tat-karaṇe ca tasyâvasthānam eva syān, na pralayaḥ. tan nâvinaśvara-svabhāvānāṃ paścāt kathañcid api vināśaḥ kartuṃ śakyo, vinaśvara-svabhāvānāṃ punaḥ sva-hetu-balâyātatvāt prāg api pratikṣaṇa-bhāvī, na kāraṇântarâpekṣaḥ, svabhāvasya niyata-rūpatvāt; tasmāt prāṇity adyâpi pratikṣaṇa-vilaya iti.
children.translated_text: But [the Buddhist objects:] pots and such are indeed seen undergoing destruction, and their destruction would be brought about by an assemblage of causes such as a club either upon things whose nature is non-perishable or upon things whose nature is perishable. If the first option — that is untenable, because one's intrinsic nature cannot be dislodged, since it has a fixed form; otherwise it would not qualify as an intrinsic nature. If [you say] its intrinsic nature is precisely of such a kind — derived from the force of its own cause — that it will perish upon encountering a cause of destruction, even so: is the proximity of that cause of destruction accidental, or necessarily produced by its own nature? If the first option, then since even when proximate, [the cause of destruction] may be averted by the occurrence of a counteracting condition, and since the agents that bring it into proximity are themselves dependent on their own assemblage of proximity-producing causes, and since even when proximate, [the cause] may be averted by a countervailing [force], and since being accidental, that proximity is not necessarily forthcoming — consequently, some pot or such, whose assemblage of causes of its own destruction is not proximate, might never perish, and this is undesirable, since the destruction of all produced things is undeniable. If the second position — in that case, since by the force of that [nature], the causes of destruction will be proximate even afterward, let them be proximate from the very first moment; even so, the object would be momentary. [If you say] it was produced with a nature such that it will bring about the proximity of its own cause of destruction only after a fixed time from its own cause — even this does not escape momentariness. For: that [object] was supposedly endowed by its own cause with a nature capable of bringing about the proximity of the cause of its own destruction after a year; but does that nature exist in the second moment after the moment of its production, or not? If it does, then it must persist for another year, and likewise even at the penultimate moment of the year — if its nature is still the same, then it would persist for yet another year, and thus there would be permanence for infinite <s>kalpas</s> (aeons), since the nature of year-long persistence has not been relinquished. If [you say] that nature does not exist in the second moment — well then, momentariness is exactly what is established, since that is its defining characteristic of non-abidingness. Moreover, does the cause of destruction produce a destruction that is distinct from the entity, or non-distinct? If it produces a distinct [destruction], then nothing would have been accomplished, and consequently the entity would persist unchanged. If [you say] a connection [between entity and destruction] is produced — no, because any connection other than identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) or causal origination (<s>tadutpatti</s>) has been denied. And neither of these two connections obtains here: identity is impossible with something that is distinct, and causal origination fails because [the destruction], arising subsequently from another cause, lacks origin from [the entity itself]. Therefore, it is not proper to hold that a distinct destruction is produced. If a non-distinct [destruction] is produced, then it follows that the cause of destruction produces that very entity, since non-distinction is characterized by being of that same nature. And it [the entity] need not be produced [again], since it has already been accomplished by its own cause; and in its production [by the destruction-cause], the entity would simply persist, not perish. Therefore, destruction cannot in any way be subsequently produced in things whose nature is non-perishable; and for things whose nature is perishable, since [that nature] is derived from the force of their own cause, [destruction] occurs at every moment even beforehand, not dependent on another cause, since intrinsic nature has a fixed form. Therefore, [the entity] lives today too, [yet] dissolution at every moment [also obtains].

children.text: atrôcyate -- satyam etat, kiṃ tu yathā vināśa-kāraṇâyogāt pratikṣaṇa-bhāvī vināśo bhavadbhiḥ pratipadyate, tathâiva sthity-utpattī pratikṣaṇa-bhāvinyau kiṃ na pratipadyete, tad-dhetūnām api vicāryamāṇānām ayogāt. tathā hi: sthiti-hetunā tāvat svayam asthira-svabhāvā bhāvāḥ sthāpyeran sthira-svabhāvā vā? na tāvat prathamaḥ pakṣaḥ kṣodaṃ kṣamate, svabhāvasyânyathā kartum aśakyatvāt, tasya pratiniyata-rūpatvāc, cetanâcetana-svabhāvavad, anyathā svabhāvatā-hāneḥ. dvitīya-pakṣe punaḥ svayaṃ sthira-svabhāvānāṃ kiṃ sthiti-hetunā? sthitir nêṣyata eva, tenânabhyupagatôpālambha evâyam iti ced, hanta hato 'sy, evaṃ hi bhāvāḥ kṣaṇa-mātram api na tiṣṭheyuḥ. kṣaṇa-bhāvinîṣyata evêti cet, sā tarhy asthiti-svabhāvānāṃ hetu-śatair api kartuṃ na pāryata iti brūmaḥ, tat-svabhāvatve punar hetu-vyāpāra-nairarthakyāt. ahetukā satī sakala-kālaṃ bhavatîti datto jalâñjaliḥ pratikṣaṇa-vilayasya. tathôtpāda-hetur api tat-svabhāvasyôtpattiṃ vidadhyād atat-svabhāvasya vā? na tāvad ādyaḥ pakṣaḥ kakṣī-kartuṃ yuktaḥ, svayam utpādakasyôtpādane vyāpriyamāṇo hi hetuḥ piṣṭaṃ pinaṣṭi, śaṅkhaṃ dhavalayati, tad-abhāve 'pi sva-yogyatayôtpatteḥ. nâpi dvitīyaḥ kalpo 'ṅgī-karaṇârhaḥ, svayam anutpatti-dharmakasyôtpādayitum aśakyatvād, anyathā śaśa-viṣāṇâdayo 'py utpādya-koṭim adhyāsīran, viśeṣâbhāvāt; tataś ca na kaścid atyantâbhāvaḥ syāt. tad yathā nirhetukatvān nāśaḥ pratikṣaṇa-bhāvī, tathâiva darśita-yukteḥ sthity-utpattī apîti trayâkrāntaṃ sakalaṃ vastu jātam abhyupagantavyaṃ; tathā sati jīvo 'pi jīvatva-caitanya-dravyatvâdibhiḥ sthemānaṃ ābibhrāṇa eva harṣa-viṣādâdibhir aparâparârtha-grahaṇa-pariṇāmaiś côtpāda-vyaya-dharmakaḥ pāramārthikaḥ pramātêti balāt siddhim adhyāste.
children.translated_text: Here it is said: This is true. However, just as you accept that destruction occurs at every moment because of the impossibility of a cause of destruction, why do you not likewise accept that persistence and origination too occur at every moment, since their causes too, when examined, are [equally] impossible? For: would things that are by nature unstable be made to persist by a cause of persistence, or things that are by nature stable? The first position does not withstand scrutiny, because intrinsic nature cannot be made otherwise, since it has a determinate form — like the nature of sentient and insentient [things] — and otherwise the status of being an intrinsic nature would be lost. In the second position, what need is there of a cause of persistence for things whose nature is itself stable? If [you say] persistence is not accepted at all, and thus this is [merely] an objection against what is not admitted — well then, you are undone! For on that [view], entities would not persist even for a single moment. If [you say] persistence for one moment is accepted — we say that even so, persistence cannot be produced in things whose nature is non-persistent even by a hundred causes, and if it were their nature, the operation of a cause would be pointless. [If you say it is] causeless and exists for all time — then farewell to momentary dissolution! Likewise, does the cause of origination produce the origination of something whose nature is to originate, or of something whose nature is not to originate? The first position is not fit to be accepted, because a cause that busies itself producing something that produces itself is grinding what is already ground, whitening what is already white — since even in its absence, [the thing] would originate by its own fitness. Nor is the second option worthy of acceptance, because it is impossible to cause the origination of something whose nature is not to originate — otherwise even hare's horns and the like would enter the category of producible things, since there is no distinguishing feature; and consequently there would be no absolute non-existence at all. Therefore, just as destruction, being causeless, occurs at every moment, so too persistence and origination, by the reasoning demonstrated — and thus all reality is to be accepted as pervaded by the triad [of origination, persistence, and destruction]. That being so, the <s>jīva</s> (soul) too, while maintaining stability through [its attributes of] soul-hood, consciousness, substantiality, and the like, and [simultaneously] being subject to origination and destruction through transformations consisting of the apprehension of different objects [accompanied by] joy, sorrow, etc. — [the <s>jīva</s>] forcefully establishes itself as the ultimate knower (<s>pramātṛ</s>).

children.text: nanu ca yady utpāda-vyaya-sthitīnāṃ nirhetukatvāt sakala-kāla-bhāvitā bhavadbhiḥ sādhyate, tadânvaya-vyatirekābhyāṃ pratyakṣâdi-pramāṇa-prasiddhaḥ khalv ayaṃ tat-kāraṇa-kalāpa-vyāpāraḥ kathaṃ neyaḥ? na câyam apahnotuṃ śakyaḥ! tathā hi: kulālâdi-kāraṇa-vrāta-vyāpāre ghaṭâdayaḥ samupalabhyante, tad-abhāve ca nôpalambhyanta iti taj-janyā ity ucyante. sthitir api vināśa-kāraṇa-sannidhānāt prāk tad-balād eva, tathā nāśo 'pi mudgarâdi-sannidhānâsannidhānābhyāṃ sad-asattām anubhavaṃs tat-kṛtaḥ pratīyate, nâhetukaḥ. tat katham etad iti?
children.translated_text: But [the opponent objects:] if you establish the presence at all times of origination, destruction, and persistence due to their causelessness, then how is the operation of their causal assemblage, which is well-established through positive and negative concomitance by <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and other <s>pramāṇas</s>, to be explained? And this cannot be denied! For: pots and such are apprehended when the causal assemblage of the potter, etc. operates, and are not apprehended in its absence — hence they are said to be produced by it. Persistence too, prior to the proximity of the cause of destruction, exists by the force of that [cause's absence]; and likewise destruction too, experiencing existence and non-existence through the proximity and non-proximity of a hammer, etc., is understood to be produced by that, not causeless. How then is this [to be explained]?

children.text: atrôcyate -- na vayaṃ sarvathā hetūnāṃ vyāpāraṃ vārayāmaḥ, kiṃ tarhi svayam utpāda-vyaya-sthity-ātmanā vivartamānasya dravyasya hetavas tad-viśeṣa-karaṇe vyāpāram anubhavanti, tenâiva sârddhaṃ teṣām anvaya-vyatirekânukaraṇa-darśanād, dṛṣṭasya câpahnave 'smākam apravṛttatvāt, pratīti-yukti-lakṣaṇa-dvaya-pakṣa-pātitvāt; kevalaṃ pratīti-vikalāṃ yuktiṃ yukti-vinākṛtāṃ vā pratītiṃ nâṅgī-kurmahe, 'sambhavad-artha-gocaratayā nirālambanatvāt tasyā ity āstāṃ tāvat.
children.translated_text: Here it is said: We do not deny the operation of causes in every respect. Rather, for a substance that is itself undergoing transformation in the form of origination, destruction, and persistence, causes play a role in the particularization of those [transformations] — because the observation of their positive and negative concomitance is with that [particularization] alone, and because we do not engage in denying what is observed, and because [our position] falls within both criteria of cognition and reasoning. We merely do not accept reasoning devoid of cognition, or cognition devoid of reasoning, since [such would be] without foundation, having as its object something that is not possible — but let that be for now.

children.text: -mataṃ vikuṭṭayati, kartā san bhoktâpîti kākvôpanyāsād, akartur bhogânupapatter, bhuji-kriyā-nirvartana-samarthasyâiva bhoktṛtvāt. japā-kusumâdi-sannidhāna-vaśāt sphaṭike raktatâdi-vyapadeśavad akartur api prakṛty-upadhāna-vaśāt sukha-duḥkhâdi-bhoga-vyapadeśo yuktas; tathā hi: prakṛti-vikāra-darpaṇâkāra-buddhi-saṅkrāntānāṃ sukha-duḥkhâdy-ātmakānām arthānāṃ puruṣaḥ sannidhāna-mātreṇa bhojako vyapadiśyate, "buddhy-adhyavasitam arthaṃ puruṣaś cetayata" iti-vacanād iti cen, na, kathañcit sakriyākatā-vyatirekeṇa prakṛty-upadhāne 'py anyathātvânupapatter, apracyuta-prācīna-rūpasya vyapadeśânarhatvāt, tat-pracyave ca prāktana-rūpa-tyāgenôttara-rūpâdhyāsitayā sakriyatvam āpatatîti-nyāyāt; sphaṭika-dṛṣṭânte 'pi japā-kusumâdi-sannidhānād andhôpalâdau raktatânāvir-bhavantī tatra punar āvir-bhavantī tasya tathā-vidhaṃ pariṇāmaṃ lakṣayaty, anyathândhôpalavat tatrâpi na prāduḥṣyāt. tan nâkriyasya bhoktṛtôpapadyata iti.
children.translated_text: doctrine, since by the implied rhetorical sense of 'being an agent, [it] is also an experiencer,' enjoyment is impossible for a non-agent, because only one capable of performing the action of enjoying can be an experiencer. [The Sāṃkhya objects:] Just as redness and such are predicated of a crystal due to the proximity of a <s>japā</s>-flower (<s>hibiscus</s>) and such, so too the predication of the enjoyment of pleasure, pain, etc. is fitting even for a non-agent [<s>puruṣa</s>] due to the superimposition of <s>prakṛti</s> (primordial nature). For <s>puruṣa</s> is designated as the enjoyer merely through proximity of objects consisting of pleasure, pain, etc. that have been transmitted to the mirror-like intellect (<s>buddhi</s>), which is a transformation of <s>prakṛti</s>, as stated [in the <s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s>]: '<s>Puruṣa</s> perceives the object determined by the intellect.' [Response:] No, because without some [form of] being active as distinguished from [complete] inactivity, the superimposition of <s>prakṛti</s> too cannot produce an alteration [in <s>puruṣa</s>], since one whose prior form has not been relinquished is not worthy of [new] predication, and if that [form] is relinquished, then by the principle that activity is entailed by the abandonment of the former form and the assumption of a subsequent form, [<s>puruṣa</s> becomes active]. Even in the crystal analogy, since redness does not appear in a dark stone, etc. from the proximity of a <s>japā</s>-flower, but does appear in the crystal, [this] indicates a transformation of that particular kind in [the crystal]; otherwise, it would not manifest there either, just as in a dark stone. Therefore, enjoyership is not possible for a non-active [entity].

children.text: di-prakalpitaṃ pramātāraṃ nirasyati, sarvathâvicalita-rūpasyârtha-grahaṇa-pariṇāmânupapatteḥ. vyatirikta-jñāna-samavāyād ekânta-nityo 'pi pramiṇotîti cen, na, samavāyasya prāg eva pratikṣiptatvāt, sambandhântarasya ca vyatirekiṇā sākam anupapatter, anyatrânyathânupapannatvāt. na ca vyatirekiṇi jñāne tat samasti, tad-grāhaka-pramāṇâbhāvād, avyatirekânubhavasya ca tad-bādhakatvāt. kiṃ ca, yadi samavāya-balād ātmani jñānaṃ samavaiti, tadâtmanāṃ samavāyasya ca vibhutvād eka-rūpatvāc ca sarvâtmasu kiṃ na samavaiti, viśeṣâbhāvāt? tathā ca devadatta-jṭānena yajṭadattâdayo 'py artha-tattvaṃ buddhyeran. anyac ca vijṭānôdaya-samaye 'pi yādṛśaḥ prāg-avasthāyāṃ tādṛśa eva santiṣṭhamānaḥ prāg apramātā paścāt pramātêti bruvāṇaḥ khalûnmattatām ātmany āvir-bhāvayati, nâparam ity āstāṃ tāvat.
children.translated_text: and others as absolutely permanent and without transformation, because the apprehension-transformation of an object is impossible for one whose form is entirely unshaken. If [you say] even an absolutely permanent [self] knows through the inherence (<s>samavāya</s>) of a distinct knowledge — no, because <s>samavāya</s> has already been previously rejected, and because another type of relation is impossible with something distinct, since it cannot be established otherwise. And that [<s>samavāya</s>] does not obtain in distinct knowledge, because there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> to apprehend it, and because the experience of non-distinction contradicts it. Moreover, if knowledge inheres in the self by the force of <s>samavāya</s>, then since both the selves and <s>samavāya</s> are all-pervading and uniform, why does it not inhere in all selves, since there is no distinguishing feature? And thus <s>Yajñadatta</s> and others would also cognize the truth of objects through <s>Devadatta</s>'s knowledge. Furthermore, one who, even at the time of the arising of cognition, remains exactly as he was in the prior state, and yet declares 'I was previously a non-knower and am now a knower' — he is surely manifesting madness in himself, and nothing more — but let that be for now.

children.text: paścârddhena punar bhūta-vyatirekiṇaṃ sva-saṃvedana-pratyakṣa-nirgrāhyaṃ jīvaṃ darśayaṃś
children.translated_text: By the latter half [of the verse], showing that the <s>jīva</s> (soul) is distinct from the material elements and is directly apprehended by self-awareness (<s>sva-saṃvedana-pratyakṣa</s>), [the author refutes]

children.text:
-darśanaṃ tiras-kurute, jaḍâtmaka-bhūtâvyatireke hi tad-vilakṣaṇa-bodha-rūpa-harṣa-viṣādâdi-vivartânubhavâbhāva-prasaṅgāt. nanu ca kāyâkāra-pariṇatāni bhūtāny evâtma-vyatirekiṇīṃ cetanām utkālayanti; sā ca tathā-vidha-pariṇāma-pariṇateṣu teṣu santiṣṭhate, tad-abhāve punas teṣv eva nilīyata iti; tad-vyatirekânubhave 'pi na para-loka-yāyi-jīva-siddhir, iyatâiva dṛṣṭa-vyavahārôpapatteḥ. nâitad asti, dvayaṃ hi tāvad etat saṃyogam anubhavad upalababhyate -- paṭca-bhūtâtmakaṃ śarīraṃ cetanā ca. tatrâpi śarīraṃ bahir-mukhâkāreṇa bodhenârtha-rūpatayā jaḍam anubhūyate, cetanā punar antar-mukhâkāreṇa sva-saṃvedana-pratyakṣeṇa sākṣāt-kriyate; 'ta evâvyatireka-pakṣaḥ pratibhāsa-nirākṛtatvān nâśaṅkitaḥ. vyatirekiṇoḥ punaḥ prakāśamānayor yadi bhūtāny eva cetanām utkālayantîti bhavadbhiḥ parikalpyate, tadā cetanâiva bhavântarād utpatti-sthānamāyātā paṭca-bhūta-bhrānti-janakaṃ śarīraṃ nirvartayet, punar bhavântaraṃ yātukāmā muṭcet, tat tayâdhiṣṭhitaṃ gamanâdi-ceṣṭāṃ kuryāt, tad-viyuktaṃ punaḥ kāṣṭhavat tiṣṭhed iti jīva-sampādyam eva śarīraṃ, na punar asau tat-sampādya ity, etat parikalpanaṃ yuktataraṃ paśyāmaḥ, jīvasya cetanāvataḥ sakarmakatayâparâpara-bhava-bhramaṇâparâpara-śarīra-nirvartanayor upapadyamānatvāt. bhavântarād āgacchan utpatti-sthānaṃ jīvo 'dhyakṣeṇa nôpalabhyata iti ced, bhūtāny api tarhi kāyâkāra-dhāraṇa-dvāreṇa cetanām utkālayantîti pratyakṣeṇa nôpalakṣyanta iti samāno nyāhaḥ. atha kāyâkāra-pariṇateṣv eva bhūteṣu cetanôpalabhyate, nânyadêty-anyathânupapatti-vaśāt taj-janyêti parikalpyata, evaṃ tarhi mṛtâvasthāyāṃ kāyâkāram ābibhrāṇeṣv api nôpalabdhā, kāyâkāra-pariṇāmo vā kādācitkatayā hetv-antarâpekṣîty-anyathânupapatti-vaśād eva tan-nirvartana-kṣamā cetanā bhavântarâgata-jīva-sambandhinîti pratipadyāmahe. kiṃ ca, jīvas tāvat karma-caitanya-sambandhāc charīra-nirvartanârthaṃ pravarata iti yuktam evâitad, bhūtāni punaḥ kiṃ-bhūtāni cetanā-karaṇe pravarteran: sacetanāni niścetanāni vā? yady ādyaḥ kalpas, tato vikalpa-yugalam avatarati: tac caitanyaṃ tebhyo bhinnam abhinnam vā? yadi bhinnaṃ, tadā puruṣa-śarīravat tatrâpi bhūtaiḥ saha vartamānam api bhūta-vilakṣaṇam ātma-kāraṇam anumāpayatîti tad-avasthâiva jīva-siddhiḥ. athâbhinnaṃ, tathā sati samasta-bhūtānām aikyaṃ prasajaty, eka-caitanyâvyatiriktatvāt, tat-svarūpavat. nija-nija-caitanyâvyatirekīṇi bhūtāni tenâyam adoṣa iti cen, na, tat-sampādya-puruṣa-śarīre 'pi taj-janya-pañca-caitanya-prasaṅgāt. pañcâpi sambhūya bṛhat-puruṣa-caitanyaṃ bahavas tilā iva taila-ghaṭaṃ janayantîti cet, tat tarhi puruṣa-caitanyaṃ kiṃ teṣām eva saṃyogo yad vā tad-utpādyam, anyad eva? yady ādhyaḥ kalpas, tad ayuktaṃ, caitanyānāṃ parasparaṃ miśraṇâbhāvena saṃyoga-virodhād, itarathā bahu-puruṣa-caitanyāni sambhūya bṛhattama-caitanyântaram ārabheran. atha dvitīyaḥ pakṣas, tatrâpi teṣāṃ kim anvayo 'sti nâsti vā? yady asti, tad ayuktaṃ, prāgvat taj-janya-caitanya-pañca-rūpatâpatteḥ. atha nâsti, tad apy acāru, niranvayôtpādasya pramāṇa-bādhitatvāt. tan na sacetanāni bhūtāni cetanā-karaṇe vyāpāra-bhāñji bhavitum arhanti. nâpi niścetanāni, teṣām atyanta-vilakṣaṇatayā caitanyôtpāda-virodhād, itarathā sikatâdayas tailâdi-karaṇe vyāpriyeran. kiṃ ca, tat-samudāya-mātra-sādhyaṃ vā caitanyaṃ syād viśiṣṭa-tat-pariṇāma-sādhyaṃ vā. na tāvad ādyā kḷptir, ilā-jalânalânila-nabhas-tala-mīlane 'pi cetanânupalabdheḥ. dvitīya-vikḷptau punaḥ kiṃ tad vaiśiṣṭyam iti vācyam. kāyâkāra-pariṇāma iti cet, sa tarhi sarvadā kasmān na bhavati? kutaścid dhetv-antarâpekṣaṇād iti cet, tat tarhi hetv-antaraṃ bhavântarâyāta-jīva-caitanyam ity anumimīmahe, tasyâiva kāyâkāra-pariṇāma-sādhya-caitanyânurūpôpādāna-kāraṇatvāt, tad-virahe kāyâkāra-pariṇāma-sadbhāve 'pi mṛtâvasthāyāṃ tad-abhāvād gamanâdi-ceṣṭânupalabdheḥ; tan na kāyākāra-pariṇāma-janyaṃ caitanyam, api tu sa eva taj-janya iti yuktaṃ paśyāmaḥ. na pratyakṣād anyat pramāṇam asti, na ca tena para-loka-gamanâgamanâdikaṃ caitanyasyôpalakṣyate, tena dṛṣṭāny eva bhūtāni tat-kāraṇatayā kalpanīyānîti cen, na, kevala-pratyakṣa-pratikṣepeṇa pramāṇântarāṇāṃ prāg eva prasādhitatvāt, tathā ca bhūyāṃsy anumānāni para-lokânuyāyi-jīva-sādhakāni pravarteran. tad yathā -- tad-ahar-jāta-bālakasyâdya-stanâbhilāṣaḥ pūrvâbhilāṣa-pūrvako, 'bhilāṣatvād, dvitīya-divasâdi-stanâbhilāṣavat.
tad idam anumānam ādya-stanâbhilāṣasyâbhilāṣântara-pūrvakatvam anumāpayad arthâpattyā para-loka-yāyi-jīvamākṣipati, taj-janmany abhilāṣântarâbhāvāt. evam anyad apy udāhāryam ity āstāṃ tāvat.
children.translated_text: [the author] refutes the view [of the <s>Cārvākas</s>]. For if [the <s>jīva</s>] were non-different from the material elements (<s>bhūtas</s>), which are insentient in nature, the absurd consequence would follow that there is no experience of transformations such as joy, sorrow, etc., which are of the nature of consciousness and dissimilar [to matter]. [The opponent objects:] But the elements, having assumed the configuration of a body, simply produce consciousness, which is distinct from themselves; and that [consciousness] abides in them when they are transformed in such a configuration, and in its absence it dissolves back into those very [elements]. Therefore, even granting the experience of [something] distinct from them, the establishment of a <s>jīva</s> (soul) that transmigrates to another world does not follow, since practical activity as observed can be explained by just this much. [Response:] This is not so. For two things are observed experiencing conjunction: the body, which consists of the five elements, and consciousness. Of these, the body is experienced as inert (<s>jaḍa</s>), as having the nature of an object, through an externally-directed cognition; consciousness, however, is directly apprehended through the internally-directed <s>sva-saṃvedana-pratyakṣa</s> (self-awareness perception). Therefore, the non-difference thesis, being refuted by [direct] appearance, is not to be entertained. But of the two that are manifest as distinct — if you postulate that the elements alone produce consciousness, then [we say:] consciousness itself, having arrived from another existence as its place of origination, might construct the body that generates the illusion of the five elements, and then, wishing to depart for another existence, might release it; [the body] when inhabited by it would perform activities such as movement, etc., and when separated from it would remain like a log. Thus the body is produced by the <s>jīva</s>, not the reverse — we see this postulation as more reasonable, since for the <s>jīva</s>, being possessed of consciousness and having <s>karma</s> (action), both transmigration through successive existences and the construction of successive bodies are explicable. If [you object:] the <s>jīva</s> arriving from another existence at its place of birth is not apprehended by <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) — well then, the elements too, producing consciousness through the means of assuming a bodily configuration, are likewise not perceived by <s>pratyakṣa</s>; so the reasoning is equal. If [you argue:] since consciousness is apprehended only in elements that have assumed bodily configuration and not elsewhere, by the force of the impossibility-of-otherwise (<s>anyathānupapatti</s>) it is postulated to be produced by them — well then, equally: since [consciousness] is not apprehended in the state of death even when [elements] maintain bodily configuration, and since the transformation into bodily configuration, being occasional, requires another cause — by the force of that very impossibility-of-otherwise, we understand that the consciousness capable of effecting that [bodily configuration] belongs to a <s>jīva</s> that has come from another existence. Moreover, the <s>jīva</s>, through its connection with <s>karma</s> (action) and <s>caitanya</s> (consciousness), proceeds to construct a body — this is entirely fitting. But what kind of entities would the elements be to proceed to produce consciousness? Are they conscious or unconscious? If the first alternative, then a twofold alternative descends: is that consciousness of theirs different from them or non-different? If different, then just as in the human body, even while existing together with the elements, being dissimilar to the elements, it causes the inference of its own [distinct] cause — and thus the establishment of the <s>jīva</s> stands as before. If non-different, then it would follow that all elements are identical, since they would be non-different from one single consciousness, just like its own nature. [If you say:] since the elements are non-different from their own respective consciousnesses, this is no fault — no, because even in the human body produced by them, the absurd consequence of five [separate] consciousnesses produced by them [would follow]. If [you say:] all five, combining together, produce the great consciousness of the person, just as many sesame seeds produce a jar of oil — well then, is that consciousness of the person merely the conjunction of those [five], or rather something distinct produced by them? If the first alternative, that is untenable, because of the contradiction of conjunction due to the impossibility of consciousnesses mutually blending; otherwise, the consciousnesses of many persons, combining, would produce yet another greater consciousness. If the second alternative — even there, is there continuity (<s>anvaya</s>) of them [in the product] or not? If there is, that is untenable, as before, because of the absurd consequence of the product-consciousness having a fivefold nature. If there is not, that too is unacceptable, because production without continuity is contradicted by <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition). Therefore, conscious elements cannot be capable of operating to produce consciousness. Nor [can] unconscious [elements], because due to their being utterly dissimilar [to consciousness], the production of consciousness is contradicted; otherwise, sand and the like would be operative in producing oil and such. Furthermore, would consciousness be producible by a mere assemblage of those [elements], or by a specific transformation of them? The first supposition does not [hold], because consciousness is not apprehended even when earth, water, fire, air, and space are mixed together. As for the second supposition: what is that specific characteristic? [you must state]. If [you say] it is the transformation into bodily configuration — then why does it not [produce consciousness] at all times? If [you say] because it requires some other cause — then we infer that that other cause is the consciousness of a <s>jīva</s> that has come from another existence, since precisely that is the material cause (<s>upādāna-kāraṇa</s>) appropriate to the consciousness producible by bodily configuration, and since in its absence, even when bodily configuration exists, [consciousness] is absent in the state of death and activities such as movement are not apprehended. Therefore, consciousness is not produced from bodily configuration; rather, that [bodily configuration] is produced by it — this we see as correct. [If you say:] there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> other than <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), and the coming and going of consciousness to another world is not perceived by it, therefore the elements that are seen should be postulated as its cause — no, because <s>pramāṇas</s> other than mere <s>pratyakṣa</s> have already been established earlier. And thus many <s>anumānas</s> (inferences) can be adduced that establish a <s>jīva</s> that transmigrates to another world. For example: the desire of a newborn infant for the breast on the very day of birth is preceded by a prior desire, because it is a desire, like the desire for the breast on the second day and so forth. This inference, inferring that the first desire for the breast is preceded by another desire, draws in by <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) a <s>jīva</s> that transmigrates to another world, since there is no other desire in that [current] birth. Likewise, other [examples] could be cited — but let that be for now.

children.text: tad ayaṃ sva-para-prakāśakaḥ kartā bhoktā nityânityâtmako bhūta-vilakṣaṇaḥ sākṣāt-kṛta-katicin-nija-paryāyânumitânādy-ananta-kāla-bhāvi-nijânanta-paryāya-vivartaḥ pramāṇa-pratiṣṭhitaḥ pāramārthiko jīvaḥ sakala-naya-pramāṇa-vyāpakaḥ pramātêti sthitam.
children.translated_text: Thus, this <s>jīva</s> (soul) — illuminating both self and other, an agent, an experiencer, of both permanent and impermanent nature, distinct from the material elements, having some of its own modes directly apprehended and its beginninglessly infinite future modes inferred as transforming — is established by <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition), is ultimately real, pervades all <s>nayas</s> (standpoints) and <s>pramāṇas</s>, and is the knower (<s>pramātṛ</s>). This is established.
Now, concluding the subject matter of the treatise with a final verse, [the author] says:
This arrangement of <s>pramāṇas</s> (valid cognition) and the rest, whose nature is without beginning or end,
though well-established for all who engage in practical activity, has [nevertheless] been proclaimed. || 32 ||
by the word '<s>ādi</s>,' the <s>nayas</s> (standpoints) are included. Of those,
meaning the orderly determination (<s>maryādā</s>) in the form of their respective definitions, etc. — that
is the syntactic connection. Of what nature? He says:

children.text: paryanto, na vidyete ādi-nidhane yasyâsau tathā-vidha
children.translated_text: meaning 'terminus.' That of which beginning and end do not exist — [that is] of such a nature;
meaning 'essential nature' — that of which [this is the nature], that
'of all who engage in practical activity' (<s>sarva-saṃvyavahartṛṇām</s>) —
meaning of all those who possess practical activity, differentiated by the distinctions of worldly persons, <s>tīrthikas</s> (heterodox teachers), and so on;

children.text: rūḍhâpi, tad-aprasiddhau nikhila-vyavahārôccheda-prasaṅgāt, tad-ucchede ca vicārânutthāne na kasyacit tattvasya pratiṣṭhitiḥ.
children.translated_text: though firmly rooted — since if it were not well-established, the absurd consequence of the cessation of all practical activity would follow, and upon that cessation, since inquiry would not arise, no truth whatsoever would be established.

children.text: saṃśabditâvyutpanna-vipratipanna-vyāmohâpohāyêti gamyate; pramāṇa-prasiddhe 'py arthe prabalâvaraṇa-kudarśana-vāsanâditaḥ keṣāñcid anadhyavasāya-viparyāsa-rūpa-vyāmoha-sadbhāvāt, tad-apanodârthaṃ ca sati sāmarthye karuṇāvatāṃ pravṛtter iti.
children.translated_text: meaning 'has been declared' — it is understood: for the removal of the confusion of the unlearned and the wrongly-learned. Because even regarding objects well-established by <s>pramāṇa</s>, for some, due to powerful obscuration, false seeing, <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions), and the like, confusion in the form of non-determination and wrong apprehension exists; and for the purpose of dispelling that, those possessed of compassion, when they have the capacity, proceed [to teach].

The heterodox deer (<s>kutīrthi-mṛga</s>) who have taken refuge in [mere partial] standpoints (<s>naya</s>), frightened by the terrifying roar of the lion of <s>syādvāda</s> (the doctrine of conditional predication), fleeing with trembling rolling eyes,

children.translated_text: having no other refuge — [this] reason, abandoning them, goes to the <s>Jina</s>; take refuge in Him! // NAV_32.1:1 //
